stories.Headline: Meta faces massive AI bills and legal troubles. Mark Zuckerberg keeps finding ways to come out on top.
stories.Summary:
Meta's AI bet has turned from a source of doubt into a source of optimism for Mark Zuckerberg, according to Business Insider's October 23, 2026 report. The company spent hundreds of billions of dollars on AI with largely unproven results, and Zuckerberg himself questioned the wager at the end of last year. Those bets, along with major layoffs and a reorganization, now appear to be paying off after Meta released its AI assistant, Muse, and a frontier AI model. Muse has reached more than 10 million downloads in North America and shot to the top of the app store a week after launch.

Meta also faces heavy costs and legal pressure that the article describes in some detail. The company remains deep in spending on AI without a clear financial return, and Muse is losing money because of high compute costs. In the second quarter of this year, 98% of revenue still came from traditional advertising. Meta trimmed staff beginning in March, then laid off about 10% of its workforce in May, and it reshuffled another 7,000 workers into an AI-focused reorganization. Meta was found negligent in a landmark youth mental health trial and is appealing, and a New Mexico jury ordered it to pay $25 billion over the Cambridge Analytica scandal, a verdict the company plans to appeal.

Zuckerberg's position has strengthened in the boardroom and with shareholders. After he told key board members in September that he would sell his Palo Alto estate in response to California's proposed billionaire tax, a special committee offered him $20 billion in immediate liquidity to cover the tax, if it passes, without reducing his controlling stake. Meta also planned new AI fundraising so that it would not dilute his control. The company said in a press release that its track record of value creation for shareholders is largely due to his strong leadership, unique vision, and management abilities. Meanwhile, Meta settled a multistate attorneys general lawsuit by agreeing to app changes such as daily time limits and overnight notification pauses.

The article makes clear the outcome is still uncertain. Investors sent Meta's stock down 7% the day after strong earnings as they weighed hundreds of billions of dollars in future spending commitments. Business Insider quoted portfolio manager David Wagner, who said Zuckerberg has won the narrative but has not yet proven the return. An analyst at Investing.com, Jesse Cohen, said Meta is cool again, crediting the Muse effect. Whether the strategy holds up over time remains open, and the article notes the next period of chaos may arrive before that question is settled.

Articles.Title: Meta faces massive AI bills and legal troubles. Mark Zuckerberg keeps finding ways to come out on top.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA vs. AMD vs. Apple — Here's What the Numbers Actually Say About Which AI Machine Is Right For You
stories.Summary:
The Entrepreneur article compares three local AI hardware options, NVIDIA, AMD and Apple, to help readers decide which machine fits their work. Its central argument is that the right choice depends on the ecosystem a team already uses rather than on a benchmark or a budget alone. The piece explains that a local AI machine is meant for keeping sensitive data off outside servers, avoiding metered API costs during frequent iteration, and owning a fixed, predictable system, while cloud GPUs remain better for large training runs and burst capacity. NVIDIA's DGX Spark, with 128GB of unified memory and a Grace Blackwell GB10 chip, is presented as the lowest-friction option for teams already built on CUDA, since existing PyTorch, TensorRT and cuDNN code runs without modification. Its drawback is memory bandwidth of 273 GB/s, which the article says is the slowest of the three for moving large amounts of model data.

AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395 chip appears in two very different products, and the article points out that third-party mini PCs such as the GMKtec EVO-X2 and the Framework Desktop sell for far less than AMD's own Ryzen AI Halo Developer Platform despite sharing the same processor and 128GB of memory. The article cites LTT Labs as saying that the premium on AMD's official kit pays for curated software configurations, which it calls AI Playbooks, along with first-party support rather than extra hardware. It also notes that AMD's ROCm software is more mature on Linux than on Windows, and that the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 was the first consumer processor to run OpenAI's gpt-oss 120B at up to 30 tokens per second on the 128GB configuration. LTT Labs reportedly found that Apple Silicon Mac Studios generated tokens two to three times faster than the AMD machines in its tests.

Apple's Mac Studio, offered with the M5 Max chip and up to 128GB of unified memory or the M5 Ultra with up to 512GB, is described as the leader on memory bandwidth, reaching up to 614 GB/s on the M5 Max and 1.2 TB/s on the M5 Ultra. The article says its 512GB ceiling can load models that the other two machines cannot hold without heavy quantization, though it remains too small for the largest open models. Its main cost is that code must run through Apple's stack, though the article notes that tools such as llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio let users load GGUF files without writing MLX code. The article concludes that no option is universally best and advises readers to choose the ecosystem their workflow already depends on before comparing hardware. More to follow.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA vs. AMD vs. Apple — Here's What the Numbers Actually Say About Which AI Machine Is Right For You

stories.Headline: Meta puts Muse agent at heart of AI strategy, plans new stock to power investments
stories.Summary:
Meta has put its new personal AI agent, Muse, at the center of its strategy, with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg calling it "the centerpiece" of the company's vision on Wednesday's earnings call. Sensor Tower data shows Muse reached 9 million U.S. downloads in 36 days, while it took Anthropic's Claude 670 days to hit the same mark. Zuckerberg said adoption was so fast that Meta had to work with payment processor Stripe to raise credit limits. Meta's stock has gained 5.7% since the launch, though it fell 6% on Wednesday even after a solid earnings report, as markets worried about rising AI spending, debt and equity issuance.

On the numbers, Citi analysts estimate Muse could bring Meta $27 billion in subscription and transaction revenue over the next several years. Consensus forecasts expect Meta's revenue to grow from $255 billion this year to $430 billion in 2029, with Muse and related revenue helping to drive it. Ahead of the report, analysts tracked by Visible Alpha expected third-quarter revenue of $63.42 billion, up 23.8% from a year earlier, and capital spending of $41.68 billion. Meta's capital spending for the full year could reach $145 billion, according to company guidance reported by CNBC, and analysts estimated the company would use $8.52 billion in free cash flow in the quarter. Deutsche Bank's Benjamin Black said Muse has put Meta back in the discussion of frontier AI, and the bank kept a buy rating with an $820 price target.

Not everyone is welcoming the agents. Amazon blocked Meta's Muse in September, and a spokesperson said third-party apps that buy on customers' behalf should operate openly and respect the decisions of service providers. Craig Moffett of MoffettNathanson warned that AI apps might route purchases outside Apple's in-app payment system to avoid its fees, and said text-based agents such as Instinct leave Apple with no way to profit. Privacy is a further worry, with Calli Schroeder of the Electronic Privacy Information Center cautioning that an agent could combine what it learns with data bought from brokers to build extremely specific profiles. Security firm Claroc found that shared Muse pages could be discovered with a single query, exposing personal files and internal company documents, and Meta said it has paused that feature while it reviews the report.

Meta says it built a dedicated cloud-based virtual machine to run Muse, with strong privacy and security protections. The company is also facing a wider legal burden, as a New Mexico judge ordered it on Wednesday to pay $25 billion in penalties over some of its data practices, a ruling Meta said it would appeal. Rivals are moving into the same space, including OpenAI's Dots and SpaceXAI's Grok Bot. Analysts say personal agents could add a new source of demand for AI computing, but they have yet to show they will produce material revenue growth, which is what would ease worries about the industry's spending and debt.

stories.Headline: Fix Your Downsampling ASAP! Aliasing and Sinc Artifact Free Pooling in the Fourier Domain
stories.Summary:
Researchers have published a paper in the International Journal of Computer Vision, dated October 5, 2026, proposing a new way to downsample the images and feature maps used by convolutional neural networks. The paper introduces Frequency Low Cut Pooling, called FLC Pooling, and a refined version called Aliasing and Sinc Artifact-free Pooling, or ASAP. The work is a substantial extension of an earlier conference paper presented at ECCV 2022 that first described FLC Pooling. The authors say standard downsampling methods such as MaxPooling, average pooling and strided convolution are prone to aliasing, which earlier research has linked to a network's vulnerability to distribution shifts and adversarial attacks.

The new methods perform downsampling in the frequency domain. According to the article, FLC Pooling avoids aliasing without requiring additional hyperparameters, while ASAP goes further by using a Hamming window in the frequency domain and by considering appropriate padding to reduce sinc interpolation artifacts, which appear as ringing in the spatial domain. The authors tested the methods on the ImageNet-1k, ImageNet-C and CIFAR datasets across several CNN architectures. They report that networks using FLC Pooling and ASAP learn more stable features, as measured by robustness to common corruptions and adversarial attacks, while keeping clean accuracy similar to the baseline models. They also say that combining these methods with FGSM and PGD adversarial training helps models avoid catastrophic overfitting.

The article credits its authors, whose names are not included in the excerpt provided, with the research and the design of the two pooling methods. The authors state that even aliasing-free pooling, such as FLC Pooling, can still produce spectral corruption, which motivated the development of ASAP. The article frames its contribution against prior work that reduced aliasing with blur filters, learned filters, wavelet-based pooling and related techniques, noting that those approaches did not fully remove aliasing or address other spectral leakage artifacts. The excerpt does not say whether the methods have been adopted in any commercial system or what follow-up work is planned.

Articles.Title: Fix Your Downsampling ASAP! Aliasing and Sinc Artifact Free Pooling in the Fourier Domain

stories.Headline: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers led by Songping Wang and seven co-authors has introduced MobileInject, a benchmark for testing whether multimodal large language model based mobile agents can be manipulated through malicious content embedded in smartphone applications. The work was posted to arXiv and is listed with a publication date of October 24, 2026. The authors say that such agents can perceive, reason about, and act on smartphone environments, which opens a new security risk in which adversaries hide harmful goals in cross-application content. Prompt injection has been studied on desktop and web platforms, but the authors note that its cross-modal behavior on mobile systems remains poorly understood.

MobileInject is described as the first benchmark designed to evaluate mobile agents against multimodal injection attacks and reasoning-to-action security risks. The framework covers 11 scenarios, 9 security-risk categories, and 108 executable risk instances, and it is presented as a high-fidelity interactive mobile evaluation environment. The authors introduce Cross-Modal Consistency Injection, which exploits agreement across text and visual signals, along with two enhanced attack methods, Multi-Role Collaborative Deception and Reasoning-Camouflage Injection. They also provide a Reasoning Security Diagnosis Framework for fine-grained analysis of failures.

The article states that code release details are given in an appendix section on open science. The authors report that their systematic experiments found mobile agents broadly vulnerable to multimodal injection. They state that many of the failures trace back to reasoning hijacking that occurs at early stages of the agent's process. According to the paper, these findings are meant to establish MobileInject as a systematic cross-modal benchmark for studying and improving the security of mobile agents.

The authors present the benchmark as a tool for researchers rather than as a finished defense against these attacks. The available material does not describe any independent review, any response from developers of commercial mobile agents, or any deployment of defenses based on the benchmark. It also does not say which specific agents or models were tested or how large the observed failure rates were. Based on the abstract alone, the next step would be further study and improvement of mobile agent security using the released benchmark.

Articles.Title: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection

stories.Headline: How Baker Hughes is levering the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA to Accelerate Centrifugal Compressor Simulations with Physics-Informed AI
stories.Summary:
Baker Hughes, working with Dell Technologies and NVIDIA, has reported research into physics-informed artificial intelligence aimed at speeding up engineering simulations of centrifugal compressors. The research, published in an Oil & Gas Journal sponsored asset dated October 23, 2026, describes an AI surrogate model designed to predict complex three-dimensional flow fields. The team used Dell Pro Precision systems with GB300 hardware and AI Physics software to build the model. The article presents the work as a case study rather than a finished product release. According to the article, the approach could reduce computational fluid dynamics simulation times from about 12 hours to roughly 0.1 seconds.

The reported results include inference about 363,000 times faster than conventional CFD simulations and 99.6% median accuracy in predicting 3D flow fields. The research also emphasizes running the models on local infrastructure, which the article says helps protect sensitive design data. The article links these gains to a reduction in the engineering effort needed to process complex models. The companies named in the piece, Baker Hughes, Dell Technologies, and NVIDIA, are the parties behind the research and the sponsored content. The article does not include direct statements from named spokespeople, so the claims about speed, accuracy, and data protection come from the sponsored material itself.

The piece describes the research as exploring a possibility rather than announcing a commercial deployment. The article frames the work as relevant to designing and testing critical industrial equipment as energy demand grows. It invites readers to download the full case study for more detail. The sponsored material does not describe any next steps, timelines, or plans for wider rollout beyond that.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reveals plans for 'an AI factory in a shipping container' to build data centers in weeks, not months
stories.Summary:
Nvidia unveiled the DSX POD at its GTC event in Berlin on Wednesday, October 21, 2026. The DSX POD is a reference design for an AI data center packed into a box about the size of a standard shipping container. Data center construction can take months or years, and costs pile up until the facility starts processing AI tokens. Nvidia wants to cut the time it takes customers to start generating revenue from its AI systems.

The Vera Rubin-powered DSX PODs arrive on site ready to be plugged into power, cooling, and networking infrastructure. Nvidia says this reduces deployment time from six months to 14 days. The container comes with seven Vera Rubin NVL72 racks, along with networking, cabling, and cooling already installed. The design supports liquid cooling, and because it uses dry-cooler designs, Nvidia says it can save up to 54 million liters of water per day versus a standard data center. Nvidia says the pods won't replace traditional data centers but will let companies run AI applications before brick-and-mortar facilities are ready.

CEO Jensen Huang said putting AI factories into service takes months, and reducing that from months to weeks or even a month would be completely game-changing. In a statement, he said the DSX POD brings factory-built precision and speed to AI infrastructure construction, reducing deployment time from months to weeks so customers can scale capacity and bring revenue-generating production online faster. Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, said it is a fully assembled, fully tested, fully pre-plumbed, prebuilt, pre-validated container that is the building block for AI factories, designed to accelerate Europe's infrastructure deployment and shorten the time to first token. Buck said the container is intended for worldwide deployment, and Nvidia chose Berlin because it sees modular infrastructure playing an important role in Europe's AI capacity expansion.

Nvidia said it is working with 17 partners, including Anduril, Armada, Bull, Crusoe, Dell Technologies, Foxconn, HPE, Lenovo, Eaton, Schneider Electric, and Vertiv, to begin delivering the DSX POD in early 2027. IDC analyst Ashish Nadkarni said the pod could appeal to sovereign AI deployments that require physical isolation, smaller-footprint AI deployments, and edge AI environments. Nvidia also said it and its supply chain partners plan to increase substrate capacity by 2.5 times over the next three years, expand advanced packaging capacity by more than 300% by 2028, and increase optical engine capacity for co-packaged optics by 15 times by mid-2027, with a goal of doubling that again by the end of 2028. Nvidia said faster data center deployment should ease one chokepoint in the AI build-out, meaning faster chip sales, though getting electricity to power processors is also a concern, and power plants take far longer to construct than data centers.

Articles.Title: Nvidia puts a Vera Rubin AI factory in a shipping container and says it can go live in 14 days

stories.Headline: Polynomial-Time Cryptanalytic Extraction of Deep Neural Networks in the Hard-Label Setting
stories.Summary:
Researchers have published a paper in the Journal of Cryptology, dated October 1, 2026 and posted online on October 24, 2026, describing a method to extract the parameters of deep neural networks using only hard-label access. In this setting an attacker sees only the final classification, such as "dog" or "car," rather than the numerical output values. The authors report that their approach works in polynomial time with a polynomial number of queries for a broad class of ReLU-based networks. The article's author list is not included in the text provided.

The earlier work this builds on came from Carlini and colleagues (Crypto 2020) and Canales-Martínez and colleagues (Eurocrypt 2024), who showed that all weights and biases of black-box ReLU networks could be recovered when exact output values were available. Chen and colleagues (Asiacrypt 2024) addressed the harder hard-label case, but their method ran in exponential time, applied only to a restricted family of architectures, handled only binary classifiers, and was tested only on networks with at most four neurons across up to two hidden layers. The new paper says it overcomes these limits. It validates the approach on a CIFAR-10 network with 832 neurons in four hidden layers and nearly one million parameters in total.

The authors also present an end-to-end black-box implementation of the attack, evaluated on a smaller artificial network, and extend their methods to leaky-ReLU activations. They conclude that, for the scenarios they studied, all weights of a ReLU-based network can be efficiently recovered by analyzing only the geometric shape of its decision boundaries. The paper treats this as a security concern for valuable model assets exposed through black-box access. The articles do not say what defenses are recommended or how the work has been received beyond its publication venue.

Articles.Title: Polynomial-Time Cryptanalytic Extraction of Deep Neural Networks in the Hard-Label Setting

stories.Headline: Attractor dynamics underlie sequence working memory in data-constrained recurrent neural networks
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to bioRxiv on October 1, 2026, and listed by doi.org on October 24, 2026, reports a study of how monkeys hold sequences of items in working memory. The authors, Matthijs Pals and Jakob H. Macke, both of Tübingen University, examined the question of whether these memories are kept by stable attractor states or by transient sequential dynamics. They built a framework for fitting low-rank recurrent neural networks to recordings of spiking activity from 2,488 units across 30 sessions in two macaques. The fitted networks reproduced population spiking activity that closely resembled the real neural data and recovered the tuning properties of individual units across sessions.

The networks showed that items presented at different sequence positions were represented in separate low-dimensional subspaces, alongside a dominant temporal component. By isolating the temporal and stimulus subspaces, the researchers found that a manifold of fixed points emerged during the memory retention period. Perturbation analyses on the networks were consistent with attractor-like dynamics within that manifold. The authors predict that brief optogenetic perturbations delivered along this attractive manifold could selectively induce persistent shifts in neural activity and in decoded behavior, a prediction that has not yet been tested in the study itself.

According to the abstract, the authors conclude that sequence working memory is organized by position-specific coding subspaces. Within these subspaces, attractor states maintain persistent representations, while activity evolves along time-varying dimensions. The paper is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. The authors declare no competing interests, and the work was supported by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, the European Union, and the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space. Code is available at a public GitHub repository.

Articles.Title: Attractor dynamics underlie sequence working memory in data-constrained recurrent neural networks

stories.Headline: Japan banks prepared to weather AI crash, global rate spike: BOJ stress test
stories.Summary:
The Bank of Japan has said that Japanese banks would keep their capital ratios above regulatory requirements even in a severe scenario. That scenario combines a surge in global interest rates with a collapse in stocks tied to artificial intelligence. The central bank released the findings in its semiannual Financial System Report on Friday, October 23, 2026. The report was published as part of the bank's ongoing review of the country's financial stability. The report's stress test is the basis for its conclusion.

It assumes both a sharp jump in global rates and a steep fall in AI-linked equities, then checks whether institutions would still hold enough capital. According to the report, Japan's financial system would "maintain overall stability" under those conditions. The articles provided do not give specific capital ratio figures, the size of the assumed shocks, or the number of banks tested. The Bank of Japan, the country's central bank, is the body responsible for the report and its findings.

The articles do not include direct quotations from individual officials beyond the report's own wording. They also do not indicate what regulatory or policy steps, if any, the bank plans to take in response. The article places the findings within a wider backdrop of concern about AI-related valuations and global borrowing costs, with related coverage on Asia's AI data center boom facing scrutiny from public markets. Beyond the report itself, the articles do not describe what happens next, and no further timeline or follow-up action is reported.

stories.Headline: Chinese AI startup DeekSeek raises $15 billion ahead of potential IPO
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek, a Chinese artificial-intelligence startup, has raised $15 billion in its second private financing round ahead of a potential public listing, according to people familiar with the matter. The round came in nearly double the company's initial target because of strong investor interest. The company is accelerating its initial public offering timeline and is aiming for a Shanghai listing early next year. If it succeeds, DeepSeek could go public ahead of OpenAI and fellow Chinese AI developer Moonshot AI.

Before the round closed, DeepSeek was valued at around $74 billion, the people said. China's biggest battery maker, Contemporary Amperex Technology, and tech giant Tencent both took part after investing in an earlier fundraise. The round ran from July through October as talks drew in additional investors. Existing shareholders Monolith Management and Shixiang added new capital, while Stony Creek Capital, a semiconductor-focused private-equity firm, joined as a new backer. Legend Capital, which is backed by Lenovo, and carmaker Geely also invested.

DeepSeek has hired the state-owned investment bank Citic Securities to advise on its IPO. In September it also recruited Yan Wentao, a former venture capitalist, as its chief financial officer. According to people familiar with the matter, founder Liang Wenfeng told investors in September that the company's annualized revenue run rate had reached $1 billion. The company has drawn investor interest since impressing Silicon Valley last year with a high-performance, low-cost AI model, which set off a wave of fundraising among Chinese AI labs.

The fundraising comes as some investors scrutinize whether heavy AI spending will produce sustainable profits and whether soaring valuations are justified. DeepSeek is spending on domestic computing infrastructure to reduce its reliance on foreign chips. It still depends on Nvidia chips for the most complex AI training, but it is working with Huawei Technologies to shift more training workloads onto domestic chips. Bloomberg and the Chinese financial magazine Caijing had reported on the latest round earlier.

Articles.Title: Chinese AI startup DeekSeek raises $15 billion ahead of potential IPO

stories.Headline: AgentPerturb: Evaluating LLM Agent Robustness under Controlled Interaction Perturbations
stories.Summary:
The articles report a research paper, posted to arXiv on October 24, 2026, that introduces a benchmark called AgentPerturb for testing how well large language model agents hold up when their inputs are disturbed. The authors are Yuanjian Xu and seven co-authors, including Jinyi Han, Jianing Hao, Yuxuan Sun, Fanyang Lu, Richeng Xuan, Guang Zhang and Zhichao Hu. The work argues that existing evaluations lack a systematic way to characterize both where perturbations are applied and what kind of perturbation is used. The authors describe their approach as a two-dimensional view of perturbation targets and types.

The researchers ran controlled tests on two task environments, APEX-Agents and Toolathlon, to measure the robustness of current frontier models. They found that perturbations consistently degraded performance, though the most damaging kinds of perturbation differed from one task environment to another. A trajectory-level analysis showed that agents rarely noticed altered inputs and often passed corrupted information along without checking it. A separate cost analysis found that perturbed tasks which were completed successfully could require substantially more computation. The authors say these findings point toward training objectives that cover diverse forms of noise, include reward verification, build uncertainty awareness, and support recovery from errors.

The paper is authored by researchers listed on the arXiv preprint, and the articles do not identify any institutional sponsor or funder. The authors state that they provide a rigorous benchmark-construction pipeline and that code and data will be released at a link given in the abstract. The articles do not describe any reaction from outside researchers or companies, and they do not say whether the released models or products are affected beyond the evaluated frontier systems. Because this is a preprint describing a benchmark, the articles offer no information about peer review, adoption, or follow-up work. The stated next step is the planned public release of the code and data.

Articles.Title: AgentPerturb: Evaluating LLM Agent Robustness under Controlled Interaction Perturbations

stories.Headline: How Law Firms Turn AI Efficiency Into Client Value
stories.Summary:
Harvey, the legal AI company, published an article on October 23, 2026 titled in substance as a discussion of how law firms can turn the time AI saves into better results for clients. The piece reports on a panel at Harvey FORUM in Sydney, where Hilary Goodier of Ashurst Perkins Coie, Michelle Mahoney of Mallesons and Michael Griffith, Deputy General Counsel at Telstra, discussed how AI is changing the value firms can deliver and how clients judge it. The article frames the central question as what faster work makes possible for a client, such as an earlier business decision, a wider view of risk, or more time for judgment. It presents the panel's views as a guide for firms thinking about pricing, service and how lawyers spend their time.

Griffith said Telstra, which the article describes as Australia's leading telecommunications and information services company, still judges firms by the same standards it used before AI, but the range of benefits a firm can offer has widened. He suggested clients ask whether AI could lower the cost of the work, bring specialized advice sooner, or allow more documents to be examined and more risks found. The article notes that the right answer depends on the client's goal, since a deadline tied to a business decision may make speed more valuable than a fee reduction. Goodier described an obligations mapping project for a global investment bank that her team finished in five weeks using AI, compared with an estimated six months by conventional methods, and said the client expected to enter a new market five months earlier. She also said that hourly targets and bonuses can discourage lawyers from using time-saving methods, which firms need to address.

Mahoney said her team now spends less time gathering and organizing data and more time examining what it shows, such as checking one clause across thousands of arrangements instead of a small sample. Goodier pointed to contract remediation, portfolio reviews and compliance projects that clients may once have judged too costly to pursue. Griffith cautioned that faster analysis should not compress the time needed for hard decisions, and the article suggests firms can use AI for first-pass review while leaving lawyers time to test findings and weigh tradeoffs with clients. The article closes by saying the most valuable use of AI depends on the matter, and it points readers to an RSGI report, The Accelerating Impact of Legal AI, on how legal organizations measure AI's impact.

Articles.Title: How Law Firms Turn AI Efficiency Into Client Value

stories.Headline: Evidence Accumulation in Synaptic Efficacy: Activity-Silent Decision-Making with Short-Term Plasticity
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to bioRxiv on October 2, 2026, by Tianhao Chu, Yuling Wu, Chenhao Zhang, Fang Fang and Si Wu, all from Peking University in China, proposes how the brain might accumulate evidence during a decision without a visible ramp in neural activity. The authors note that classical models assume evidence builds through ramping neural firing, while recent experiments suggest activity stays largely silent until it abruptly switches into an active decision state. Their study addresses the open question of how evidence is gathered during that silent stretch. The work is listed under neuroscience and carries a copyright notice granting bioRxiv a license to display it.

The team trained excitatory and inhibitory recurrent neural networks that include short-term synaptic plasticity on a reaction-time decision task. After training, the networks learned to use this plasticity to reach decisions while their activity stayed silent. Analyses of the trained networks revealed a functional organization in which choice-selective excitatory and inhibitory groups are coupled. Guided by that architecture, the authors built a minimal circuit model in which evidence accumulates as facilitated synaptic strength, gradually reshaping the circuit until it crosses a stability boundary and rapidly shifts into a choice state. The authors also compared pre-choice activity between their plasticity model and a static model to assess possible energy savings.

The paper is credited to the five named authors, and the abstract states that their results point to short-term plasticity as a mechanism for evidence accumulation in activity-silent decisions. The authors report no competing interests. The abstract also suggests the findings could inform the design of energy-efficient artificial neural networks. The articles provided do not describe any further studies, peer review outcomes or follow-up plans.

Articles.Title: Evidence Accumulation in Synaptic Efficacy: Activity-Silent Decision-Making with Short-Term Plasticity

stories.Headline: AICPA & IRS AI Risk Framework
stories.Summary:
Randy Johnston and Brian Tankersley, hosts of the Accounting Technology Lab Podcast, discussed a proposed AI tax risk framework in an episode published October 24, 2026, by CPA Practice Advisor. The framework is linked to materials associated with former IRS Commissioner Danny Werfel and sorts risks for tax preparers into five categories: technical, practice, legal and regulatory, business, and workforce and strategic. The hosts framed the question of who is responsible when AI gets a tax matter wrong as central to the discussion. They treated the framework as a proposal rather than a binding new IRS rule.

The hosts walked through specific hazards, including AI hallucinations, inaccurate document extraction, client data leakage, and overtrust of AI-generated tax advice. They also described how AI-driven productivity can outpace conventional human review procedures. Additional concerns included shadow AI, professional liability, client disclosure, vendor dependence, erosion of professional expertise, and preservation of institutional knowledge. They distinguished the risks facing practitioners from those facing tax authorities, while noting that hallucinations, overtrust, skill erosion, data leakage, and vendor dependence overlap for both.

The practical message was that faster preparation does not remove professional accountability. According to the discussion, firms need independent verification of AI conclusions, meaningful human oversight, reliable source documentation, and protection of confidential taxpayer information. They also need clear thinking on liability, disclosure, and governance, along with contingency plans in case a vendor fails or changes terms. The episode's summary lists these as the core action items for tax practices. The articles do not name a deadline or indicate when, or whether, the framework would take binding effect.

stories.Headline: CCH Axcess Adds Agentic AI for Tax Preparation
stories.Summary:
Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting has added agentic tax return preparation to its CCH Axcess Tax system, announced October 23, 2026. The feature is built into the cloud-native platform where firms already manage their tax work, and it is meant to reduce repetitive preparation work and increase firm capacity. For individual Form 1040 returns, CCH Axcess Tax powered by Expert AI prepares and calculates the return and then flags exceptions that need attention before professional review begins. Unlike tools that automate a single task, the feature coordinates work across several steps of the return process, using prior-year information and current source documents.

Tax professionals have traditionally spent considerable time gathering documents, entering information and checking work before review can start. Under this approach, firms get a clearer view of which returns are ready for review and which exceptions still need attention. The agentic capabilities are built into the platform rather than sold as separate products, and they work inside CCH Axcess Tax from source documents through preparation, calculation, review and handoff. Expert AI agents use the firm's own data, authoritative CCH content and each firm's permissions and controls to move the work forward.

The company says the agents prepare, check and advance the work, while professionals review, decide and approve the final return. Cathy Rowe, Executive Vice President and Segment Leader for the U.S. Professional Market at Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting, described CCH Axcess as an agentic platform for tax and accounting. She said agentic tax preparation marks a significant shift in how tax work gets done and helps firms add capacity without sacrificing quality or control. Rowe said the goal is to let professionals focus their expertise where it matters most.

The company also states that professionals remain responsible for deciding and approving the final return. The feature is part of a broader push by Wolters Kluwer to extend CCH Axcess beyond tax preparation, since firms already use the platform to collect client documents, extract data, manage workflow and identify advisory opportunities. Wolters Kluwer plans to share more about how CCH Axcess moves work forward across tax, planning and audit at CCH Connections 2026, which begins October 26 in Orlando. More details are available on the CCH Axcess Tax website.

Articles.Title: CCH Axcess Adds Agentic AI for Tax Preparation - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Meta Expects Up To $145 Billion In Capex As AI Investments Expand
stories.Summary:
Meta has said it expects capital expenditure of $135 billion to $145 billion in 2026 as it keeps investing in AI infrastructure and new products. The company released its third-quarter financial results on October 21, 2026, and the figures were reported by Analytics India Magazine. Meta says its AI investments are already producing extra advertising revenue through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetisation. It expects these investments and new product launches to support revenue growth through 2027, even while it keeps spending heavily on infrastructure.

Revenue for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026 came to $64.60 billion, up 26% from a year earlier. Advertising revenue rose to $63.06 billion from $50.08 billion in the same quarter last year. Ad impressions across Meta's family of apps increased 10%, while the average price per ad rose 14%. The company also pointed to the launch of Muse and Muse Wonder, which it described as its first frontier model. Meta expects total expenses for 2026 to range from $175 billion to $179 billion.

Those expense projections include a $9.9 billion charge tied to legal proceedings recognized in the third quarter. The charge relates to an August agreement with 52 US state attorneys general to resolve litigation over teen mental health and social media. Total costs and expenses reached $51.61 billion in the quarter, up 68% year-on-year. Excluding the legal charge, Meta's third-quarter operating income would have been $22.88 billion, compared with the reported $12.99 billion. The reported operating margin was 20%, down from 40% a year earlier.

Meta also expects Reality Labs losses of $18 billion to $19 billion in 2026, and it anticipates those losses narrowing to around $15 billion in 2027 as it redirects investment toward other priorities, primarily AI. The company's infrastructure capacity and planned additions, it said, will let it allocate resources across model training, core business growth, and new product development and support. The results show a company spending heavily on AI while its advertising business continues to expand. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Meta Expects Up To $145 Billion In Capex As AI Investments Expand - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: AI is unearthing internet’s hidden flaws – and more outages may follow
stories.Summary:
Advances in artificial intelligence have uncovered a growing stream of software vulnerabilities, and cybersecurity professionals warn this will bring more disruption like the outages that spread across government websites in Europe and elsewhere beginning on October 21. Those outages followed the discovery of weaknesses in PHP, a long-established programming language that powers a large share of the internet. VulnCheck, a Massachusetts-based threat intelligence firm, says AI helped double the number of flaws discovered year-on-year, with research due to be published in the coming days. The same week also brought disclosures involving Node.js, Plex, LiteLLM, Railway and the Indian certificate authority eMudhra.

Operators rushed to fix their software before attackers could exploit it, and some who felt they could not patch in time simply took their sites offline until they were safe. VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity said the scramble over PHP came during an already busy week, and he expects many more urgent fixes for internet-exposed software. Experts say AI has shortened the time needed to find bugs and turn them into working attacks, which once took weeks or months of skilled effort and now can take hours. Shane Fry of RunSafe Security said the change is in how quickly both discovery and weaponisation now happen. The article notes that the timescale defenders once relied on has effectively collapsed.

Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince says he knows of several other severe vulnerabilities in critical software and predicts that "every single week" may feel alarming for a couple of years. Daniel Stenberg, lead developer of the file transfer tool curl, argues that AI-found bugs tend to be exotic and hard for attackers to exploit, and Ramy Rahman of ArmorCode says more disclosed flaws do not automatically mean more successful attacks. Threat intelligence firm Hunt.io has seen aggressive attempts to exploit the PHP bug, though its research head Esteban Borges says the criminals it tracks appear not to have built a working tool yet. Prince has seen anecdotal evidence of compromises tied to the PHP flaw, but he argues the wave of discoveries will ultimately be a net positive, since the flaws are being cleaned up rather than left hidden.

Articles.Title: AI is unearthing internet’s hidden flaws – and more outages may follow - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: China defends DeepSeek after US ban of its AI from government systems
stories.Summary:
The US Department of Homeland Security has ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products, along with third-party products and services built using DeepSeek, from their IT systems. The notice was made public on Monday, October 19, 2026, and the order itself dates back to late July. It also bars those agencies from buying DeepSeek products and services. China responded on Tuesday, October 20, by pushing back against the restriction and warning of retaliatory measures. Beijing's stance is that the move uses national security as a cover for suppressing Chinese companies.

According to the notice in the Federal Register, DeepSeek's models present several threat vectors. The concern centers on DeepSeek's servers being located in China, which could allow Chinese authorities to reach private company infrastructure and sensitive US data. DHS also said use of the product could transfer sensitive data to China if US government employees or vendors used it. DeepSeek's open-source models are widely available in the United States and elsewhere, and they are mostly free to use. The ban applies only to civilian agencies, and the articles do not describe any broader restrictions on private use.

China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said Beijing would firmly protect the lawful rights and interests of Chinese companies. She added that China opposes stretching the concept of national security too far. The Ministry of Commerce voiced strong dissatisfaction and firm opposition, saying the US disregarded an understanding reached between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. It also accused Washington of using discriminatory restrictions to contain China and said Beijing would take all necessary measures to defend its interests. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The dispute comes as the two countries remain at odds over many issues despite some recent progress on AI governance, including a US proposal for a notification system for national security incidents. AI is expected to be on the agenda when Trump and Xi meet again in mid-November on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. US-led restrictions still block China from some of the most advanced AI chips and chipmaking machines. Washington has also accused Chinese AI startups, including DeepSeek, of large-scale distillation of capabilities from American models, a charge Beijing has dismissed. Last week, Beijing proposed its own restrictions on exports of certain advanced AI models.

Articles.Title: US banning Chinese AI DeepSeek from government agency IT systems - CNA

stories.Headline: Mass Weighting Algorithm Optimizes Fourier-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network in Adhesive Contact Mechanics
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers has published a paper in Tribology Letters describing a mass weighting algorithm that speeds up a Fourier-based physics-informed neural network used to model adhesive contact mechanics. The paper, titled "Mass Weighting Algorithm Optimizes Fourier-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network in Adhesive Contact Mechanics," appeared online on 30 September 2026 as article 112 in Volume 74. The authors address a known problem in these networks, in which the elastic kernel grows with wave number so that short-wavelength modes dominate the updates and convergence stalls. Their method reweights loss gradients in Fourier space before back-propagation, boosting low-wavenumber components and filtering out sub-grid noise.

Applied to adhesive line contact problems, the authors report that the weighted network reaches machine-zero residual loss within 400 Adam iterations for a specified benchmark. The reference benchmark, by comparison, stalls at a loss three orders of magnitude higher. The authors say the converged displacement and contact stress fields agree quantitatively with Green's function molecular dynamics solutions for both smooth Hertz contact, across pressures from tension to compression, and rough surfaces with roughness spanning several decades of wavelength. The method runs on a uniform real-space grid and needs no explicit Green's function integration or quadrature rules, and the authors say it extends directly to two-dimensional rough surfaces.

The paper is authored by researchers whose names appear on the Springer Nature Link page, and the article cites its source code and data files at a public repository on GitHub. The reference list draws on prior work in contact mechanics by researchers including B.N.J. Persson, M.H. Müser and others. The article page does not describe a timeline for further validation or any next steps beyond the extension to two-dimensional surfaces that the authors already identify. Readers can consult the full PDF through an institutional subscription or purchase.

Articles.Title: Mass Weighting Algorithm Optimizes Fourier-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network in Adhesive Contact Mechanics

stories.Headline: Recursive Releases Flint, an Open-Weight 40B MoE Local Coding Model for Agents with 2.5B Active Params
stories.Summary:
Recursive Superintelligence has released Flint, its first model, a coding model built for local use by software agents. Flint is a mixture-of-experts system with about 39.8B total parameters and roughly 2.5B active per token, and the company says its Eureka Machine, an automated research system, helped build nearly every part of the stack. The weights were published on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. A second article, dated two days later, reports that Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro, a mixture-of-experts model with 2.8T total and 104B active parameters and a 1M context window, though the text supplied for it cuts off before any further detail.

Flint is a text-only, decoder-only Transformer that supports reasoning and OpenAI-compatible tool calls. Its model card documents a context of 262,144 tokens, while the company's blog cites up to 512k. It has 49 layers, two dense and 47 mixture-of-experts, each with 256 routed experts, of which a router picks six per token alongside one always-active shared expert. Thirty-five layers use a 513-token sliding window and 14 use full attention, with 32 query heads and 4 key/value heads. The 4-bit weights take about 23 GB, so the model runs on 48 GB Apple Silicon Macs (M4 Pro, M5 Pro, M5 Max) or 48 GB NVIDIA GPUs, and Recursive claims up to twice the speed of comparable models, over 125 tokens per second on a MacBook Pro and over 150 on RTX Spark.

All benchmark scores are self-reported by Recursive. The 16-bit version scores 54.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 89.7% on SWE-bench Pro v2, 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified, 80.3% on LiveCodeBench v6, 89.2% on IFBench and 95.1% on IFEval. The 4-bit NVFP4 version stays close at 53.7%, 88.5%, 74.1%, 80.8%, 88.1% and 94.6% on the same tests, within 0.7 points of the 16-bit model overall. Recursive's chart puts Flint ahead of other mixture-of-experts models under 50B on agentic coding, including Qwen 3.6, which scores 73.4% on SWE-bench Verified. Flint trails the strongest dense models, with dense Qwen 3.8 reaching 73.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 75.6% on SWE-bench Verified.

Recursive attributes much of the design to the Eureka Machine, which proposes ideas, implements and tests them, and chooses what to try next. Starting from a baseline of 35B total and 3B active parameters, it searched expert configurations and widths and arrived at the final 40B and 2.5B figures. It also quantized the output layer to 4 bits, against common practice, and used offline distillation with the 16-bit model as teacher to recover accuracy, nearly halving training steps compared with a quantization-aware training baseline. It wrote specialized kernels as well, including a Metal megakernel that fuses the whole decode forward pass on M4 and M5 chips. The supplied articles do not describe any planned next steps for either release.

stories.Headline: Exact Representation of Piecewise Polynomial Finite Element Functions by Two-Hidden-Layer Multilayer Perceptrons
stories.Summary:
A research preprint posted to arXiv under the number 2609.39856 describes a method for building neural networks that exactly reproduce finite element functions. The authors are Jun Hu, Pengzhan Jin and Shengyang Xu, and the paper was submitted on 30 September 2026 and listed under Numerical Analysis. The work covers finite element functions of any polynomial degree on simplicial meshes in any spatial dimension. Its central claim is that such functions can be represented exactly by a multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers.

The construction uses a specific activation in each hidden layer. The first hidden layer uses a combination of ReLU-zero and ReLU, while the second uses a degree-dependent activation written as ReLU to the power k. The network can represent both zero-skeleton versions of discontinuous finite element functions, which vanish on the mesh skeleton, and prescribed-skeleton versions, which carry independently chosen polynomial data on each lower-dimensional subsimplex. For continuous functions, the authors use a half-open decomposition that reduces the width of the second hidden layer by assigning each subsimplex to a single incident element. The number of nonzero parameters grows linearly with the number of elements for fixed dimension, degree and output dimension, and in the continuous case it is of the same order as the number of global degrees of freedom, provided the mesh is shape-regular.

The article credits the work to the three named authors, and the paper states that all network parameters can be computed explicitly from the mesh and the finite element function, without any training. The abstract does not describe any external review, funding or institutional statement beyond the general acknowledgment of major funding support shown on the page. The paper is a version 1 submission, and the articles give no further information on revisions, publication in a journal, or reactions from other researchers. Readers wanting the full technical details would need to consult the PDF or HTML version of the paper.

Articles.Title: Exact Representation of Piecewise Polynomial Finite Element Functions by Two-Hidden-Layer Multilayer Perceptrons

stories.Headline: AI's Dark Cash, the Oregon Massacre, Erin's Law & a Kid With a Camera
stories.Summary:
Pro-AI super PACs are spending heavily to influence 36 House and Senate races, mostly in Georgia, New York and Texas, according to Scripps News reporting featured in this episode. The reporting describes the spending as aimed at each candidate's perceived weak spot rather than at artificial intelligence itself. The reporting follows the money behind these campaigns, which are tied to regions where data center construction is concentrated. The episode is hosted by Jon Leiberman, with national investigative reporter Patrick Terpstra following the funding.

The same episode features Erin Merryn, who was abused as a child and kept quiet because her abuser told her no one would believe her. Her advocacy led to Erin's Law, which the episode says is now on the books in 38 states. The law requires schools to teach children body safety once a year. Merryn's story is presented as an example of breaking that kind of silence after abuse.

The episode also covers a range of other news items, including a count of protesters marching across France, President Trump's endorsement of Benjamin Netanyahu, a Supreme Court decision declining to revive the 9/11 plea deal, and Trump's call for New Mexico to rename itself. Andrew Rafferty offers a midterm update with under two weeks to go, and a panel discusses the push to bring back the Redskins name, newly unsealed records in the O.J. Simpson case, and the New Mexico proposal. Viewers can text the word Scripps to 202-968-2449 to comment or join an upcoming panel discussion. The episode is a roundup format rather than a single breaking event, and the articles do not indicate further developments on the AI spending story beyond the episode itself.

stories.Headline: Autocata: Reaction-network-guided autonomous catalyst screening via capability-centric AI
stories.Summary:
On September 30, 2026, a team of six researchers led by Ruili Li and Yi Gao posted a preprint to arXiv describing Autocata, a software agent designed to screen catalysts for chemical reactions with little human intervention. The paper, arXiv:2609.39060, was categorized under chemical physics and later indexed by its DOI on the doi.org record dated October 24, 2026. The authors say the agent is built around a Transformer model pretrained on two million catalyst-adsorbate structures. It works from a registry of 79 generative models that each specialize in adsorbate chemistry involving carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen intermediates.

According to the abstract, a user gives Autocata a high-level prompt in natural language, and the system breaks the target reaction into its network of steps. It then selects and configures matching generative models, produces candidate surface configurations, and filters them for physical and geometric validity. Machine-learning potentials are then used to evaluate and rank the most promising materials. The authors state that the agent can adjust its own workflow when it reaches the limits of a given model or hits a bottleneck in the task.

The authors describe the work as a shift from fixed toolkits toward an adaptive, language-driven computational infrastructure. They present it as a way to lower the barrier to expert-level catalyst discovery, and they test it on three reaction pathways: methane activation, the nitrogen reduction reaction, and conversion of carbon dioxide to methanol. The paper runs to 21 pages with four figures. The abstract frames the approach as a scalable model for self-driving catalytic research, though the preprint's own claims rest on the authors' testing and have not been independently reviewed in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Autocata: Reaction-network-guided autonomous catalyst screening via capability-centric AI

stories.Headline: Bipartisan Bill Would Task NIST With AI Cyber Defense Standards
stories.Summary:
Reps. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., and George Whitesides, D-Calif., introduced the bipartisan AI Cyber Defense Act on Oct. 22, 2026. The bill would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to develop voluntary standards for protecting artificial intelligence models from foreign exploitation and for using AI to strengthen cybersecurity defenses for critical infrastructure. It would give NIST 180 days after enactment to begin engaging private-sector AI stakeholders and to set up an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable.

That roundtable would include AI companies and critical infrastructure owners and operators, and it would develop voluntary standards and best practices for defensive uses of AI. Harrigan said the companies building this technology need to work directly with those responsible for defending power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. NIST would also work with industry to define distillation attacks, which let outside actors extract valuable capabilities from advanced AI models. Together with industry, the agency would develop voluntary standards and best practices for detecting and preventing those attacks.

NIST would have to publish these standards on its website within one year after they are established, though the bill sets no separate deadline for their development. Within one year of creating the roundtable, NIST would also have to publish its voluntary standards and best practices for defensive AI use. The bill defines eligible private-sector stakeholders broadly, covering businesses that develop, train, deploy, offer, sell, or license AI systems, along with providers of substantial computing infrastructure, data, or technical services. It excludes entities of concern, including foreign businesses headquartered in China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, or Cuba, or whose parent companies are based in those countries.

Whitesides said the proposal would help protect American AI development while supporting infrastructure operators facing evolving cyber threats. He argued that every month that keeps China and other adversaries from stealing American progress is a month gained to build needed safeguards. The bill has been referred to the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology. The article does not say when the committee will take it up or whether a companion bill is planned in the Senate.

Articles.Title: Bipartisan Bill Would Task NIST With AI Cyber Defense Standards

stories.Headline: When Safety Fails Collectively: Robust Alignment Against Harmful Fine-Tuning via Joint Weight Perturbations
stories.Summary:
Researchers Zhiyuan Wang, Yuezhi Zhou, Zhu Zhang and Zhixing Tan have published a paper on arXiv, dated October 24, 2026, describing a new way to protect large language models against harmful fine-tuning. Their work starts from the observation that harmful fine-tuning can quickly erode the safety alignment of these models, which creates real risk when aligned models are adapted for downstream tasks. The authors note that existing defenses prepare models during safety alignment by using harmful examples and simulated harmful weight perturbations, but they say the combined effects of such perturbations have been little studied. Their central finding is a collective failure pattern in which parts of a harmful perturbation have limited effect on their own, yet applied together they raise the model's harmfulness beyond the sum of the individual effects.

Based on this finding, the authors propose Joint Weight Perturbations, or JWP, an alignment-stage defense. The method estimates a harmful perturbation from the current model, masks different parts of it, and trains the model to respond safely in each resulting state. According to the paper, this exposes the model to many combinations of harmful perturbations, which reduces its sensitivity to their accumulation during later harmful fine-tuning. The abstract says the approach was tested across downstream tasks and several model families, and that it offered stronger resistance to harmful fine-tuning than prior defenses while largely preserving task performance. The articles do not give specific numerical results, benchmark names, or the exact models used in those experiments.

The paper is authored by the four named researchers, and the articles do not indicate any institutional affiliation, funding source, or statement from outside parties. The paper is listed on arXiv, which hosts preprints that have not necessarily been peer reviewed, and the articles do not say whether it has been accepted at a conference or journal. stories.Headline: FRACTION: Fraud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context Navigation
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a research paper, not a news event, and it was posted to the arXiv preprint server with an October 24, 2026 date. The paper, titled FRACTION, was written by Cecelia Soh and eight co-authors, including Bryan Hooi and Bingsheng He. It addresses how to generate human-readable explanations for why a graph of linked records, such as financial transactions, has been flagged as fraud. The authors say existing graph-enhanced large language models are not well suited to this job for two reasons, and the paper is their proposed fix.

The first reason given is that current methods lack evaluation protocols designed for explanation quality. The second is that these methods supply graph information at a granularity that does not match what an explanation needs. To address this, the authors built a framework that gives a language model graph tools so it can progressively reveal the records of relevant neighbors instead of reading an entire neighborhood at once. They also introduced a rubric that scores explanations on faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency and conciseness, and say they checked the rubric against human judgments. The agent is trained through a rubric-guided trajectory distillation strategy, which the authors say teaches it both how to use the tools and how to write structured explanations.

According to the paper, experiments on three fraud datasets showed consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines when judged by the human-aligned rubric. stories.Headline: Does This Action Still Explain the Task? Reverse Scoring for Diffusion Language Model Agents
stories.Summary:
The article is an arXiv preprint posted on 29 September 2026, with the page dated 24 October 2026, titled "Does This Action Still Explain the Task? Reverse Scoring for Diffusion Language Model Agents." Its authors are Jiacheng Qiu, Christopher E. Mower, Jan Peters, Haitham Bou-Ammar and Matthieu Zimmer, and it is filed under machine learning and artificial intelligence. The paper addresses diffusion-based large language models, which can decode in parallel to avoid the sequential delays of autoregressive agents. Recent evaluations found that this speed does not carry over to embodied agents, which often get stuck in retry loops and reissue actions that have already failed.

The authors trace the loops to the way masked decoding works: the sampler commits the positions it is most confident about and defers the uncertain ones. At a failure, the surrounding context already offers a confident fill for the deferred decision, namely the failed action, so the retry gets committed before any failure feedback is taken into account. They model this as a task-blind corruption that inflates the probability of contextually salient actions, such as the one just taken, by a factor that depends on the state and action but not on the task. Under that model they prove an invariance: the factor cancels from the reverse conditional, the likelihood of the task given the state and a candidate action, which matches the task posterior of an idealized uncorrupted model.

Their remedy requires no retraining. Masked diffusion models can evaluate the reverse conditional directly by masking the task tokens and denoising, at the cost of a few parallel passes per candidate action. The authors implement this as a rule they call Reflect Reverse and evaluate it on four multi-turn embodied benchmarks. According to the paper, it improves task success and progression rates over forward-scoring baselines. The article does not name a publication venue, funding details beyond a general acknowledgment, or any follow-up work, and it notes only that the paper is a version 1 submission.

stories.Headline: APEX: Active Protection at Execution Boundaries for LLM Agents
stories.Summary:
A team of ten researchers posted a preprint on arXiv describing APEX, a defense against indirect prompt injection in large language model agents. The paper, arXiv:2610.06966, was first submitted on 3 October 2026 and revised on 7 October 2026, and the DOI record shows an update dated 24 October 2026. The authors include Xinran Zheng, Xin Fan Guo, Zhiqiang Hao, Fan Yang, Xingzhi Qian, Jiawei Du, Jinfeng Xu, Zheng Xing, Shuo Yang and Xingjun Wang. The paper is listed under Cryptography and Security, with a secondary category in Artificial Intelligence.

The authors argue that existing defenses, which try to recognize specific attack patterns, fall behind as agents combine more kinds of tools, servers and skills that can carry hidden instructions. APEX instead enforces two checks at the point where an agent turns its internal state into an external action or output: whether the action is authorized, and whether the information behind it is endorsed by the trusted task. Both are drawn from a single authorization contract compiled before the agent handles untrusted content. The method combines evidence-gated prevention, which allows an action only when the contract justifies it, with deception-based exposure, which is meant to make unendorsed use reveal itself before the action commits. According to the abstract, the approach needs no attack-specific policies or taint tracking.

The authors report results against 13 baseline defenses. APEX reached 0% attack success on five of six benchmarks and 0.56% on the sixth, and stayed at 0% under adaptive attacks across three types of capability units. The abstract also says it remained effective across different defender backbones. The authors have made the code available, and the paper is a preprint that has not been described in the articles as peer reviewed. The articles do not say how the results compare with the methods in the broader research community, nor do they describe any deployment or any planned next steps beyond the code release.

Articles.Title: APEX: Active Protection at Execution Boundaries for LLM Agents

stories.Headline: How the Audit Rule Shapes Faithful Factor Explanations in LLMs
stories.Summary:
A new arXiv preprint, titled "How the Audit Rule Shapes Faithful Factor Explanations in LLMs," was posted on October 1, 2026, by Taolin Zhang, Hanyu Wang, Jiuheng Wan, Tingyuan Hu and Chengyu Wang, and its record appeared on doi.org on October 24, 2026. The paper studies how large language models report which input factors influenced their outputs. For structured inputs, such reports can be checked by counterfactual perturbation, but each factor must be queried several times to estimate its effect, so checking is usually limited by budget. The authors examine how that limit changes whether a model has an incentive to report factor influence truthfully.

The authors formalize the interaction as a verification game and argue that proper scoring alone is not enough when auditing depends on the report. Under report-dependent auditing, factors reported as important are more likely to be checked and penalized for estimation noise, which creates a suppression incentive. Report-independent auditing, or a mixed rule with a small report-independent floor, removes this channel and makes truthful reporting preferable to full suppression. The paper instantiates the framework with the Counterfactual Brier Score and evaluates its predictions on four NLP benchmarks. The main design implication, according to the paper, is that factor-level explanation systems under partial verification should include a report-independent audit component.

The paper's results are reported as follows: a synthetic rational agent matches the theoretical prediction exactly, and real LLMs follow the same incentives when those incentives are made explicit. The authors state that the aim is to prevent under-reporting from being used to avoid scrutiny. The preprint is listed under the Computation and Language category and is marked as version 1, submitted by Chengyu Wang. The articles do not describe any reaction from outside researchers, any peer review outcome, or planned follow-up work.

Articles.Title: How the Audit Rule Shapes Faithful Factor Explanations in LLMs

stories.Headline: Correcting to Predict: Pseudo-Value Correction for Multimodal Attribute Value Extraction
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on 28 September 2026, titled "Correcting to Predict," describes a new method for product attribute value extraction, the task of identifying specific attribute values, such as a product's color or material, from its text and images. The paper was written by Junhao Zhang, Feiran Hu, Xiao Hu, Baoliang Cui and Xiaoyi Zeng, and the arXiv record shows a version 1 submission dated that day. The authors describe their approach, called Correcting to Predict (C2P), as a framework that treats extraction as a process of fixing an initial placeholder or candidate value rather than predicting from scratch. The paper is listed as accepted for the CIKM 2026 conference as an oral full paper.

The method works by giving the model an initial pseudo-value, such as a retrieved candidate or a placeholder, and training it to correct that value using visual and textual evidence. During training, a range of different pseudo-values is used, and a self-consistency refinement stage is added to reduce the model's sensitivity to those starting values. At inference time, a fixed placeholder is enough to trigger the learned correction, so the system can produce a prediction in a single pass without online retrieval or repeated refinement. The authors say this is aimed at implicit attributes, where the correct value depends on subtle combinations of image and text and where similar-sounding values are easily confused.

The authors report that C2P outperforms strong baselines on a public benchmark and on a large-scale industrial dataset, with notable gains on ambiguous attributes. They also say online A/B tests on the AliExpress e-commerce platform showed consistent improvements in seller adoption, attribute completeness and user engagement. The paper's abstract presents these results as validation of the method's effectiveness and efficiency in real-world deployment. The abstract does not describe any further deployment plans, and the articles provided do not say what follows beyond the conference presentation.

stories.Headline: How Far Are We from Removing the Visual Encoder? Scaling Laws for Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv on September 28, 2026, asks how far multimodal AI systems are from dropping the separate visual encoder that most of them rely on. The paper, titled "How Far Are We from Removing the Visual Encoder? Scaling Laws for Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining," was written by Lin Chen and eight co-authors, and a DOI-linked version appeared on October 24, 2026. Most modern multimodal large language models currently build on a pretrained visual encoder that supplies a strong visual prior. The authors compare how these encoder-free and encoder-based models scale, with the aim of filling a gap in what has been systematically characterized.

The study reports three main findings. Removing the visual encoder shifts the compute-optimal allocation for the multimodal objective toward larger models, while the allocation for text stays nearly unchanged. On the text objective the two architectures have nearly overlapping loss-compute frontiers, but on the multimodal objective encoder-free models trail at small scales and are predicted to catch up at around 10^22 FLOPs. Without an encoder, the language model takes over the visual role through vision-specific adaptation, including more useful bidirectional interactions among visual tokens and visual processing moving toward earlier layers.

Expert routing for visual tokens also becomes more concentrated as training compute grows. The lead author, Lin Chen, is listed on the paper with eight co-authors, and the paper was submitted under the computer vision category. The authors conclude that the advantage a pretrained encoder gives diminishes with scale. They present encoder-free architectures as a promising direction for multimodal pretraining.

The abstract does not describe any further experiments or follow-up work beyond these findings. The results sit within an ongoing effort to simplify how AI systems handle images alongside text. The reported crossover point of around 10^22 FLOPs is described as within practical pretraining budgets, which the authors use to argue that the approach is realistic. Beyond the preprint itself, the available material does not say what comes next for the research or for the field.

Articles.Title: How Far Are We from Removing the Visual Encoder? Scaling Laws for Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining

SEMARNAT, Mexico's environment ministry, published a regulation barring environmental permits for mining exploration and extraction inside federally protected natural areas. The rule applies retroactively, reaching concessions granted before 2023. Backed by Supreme Court rulings, the decree makes the technical assessments of CONANP, the national protected areas commission, binding. Legacy concession holders inside protected zones must submit mine restoration and closure plans within 15 business days.

The article also reports that SEMARNAT has resolved 85% of pending permit applications while updating core rules, including NOM-157 on mine waste management, and that a proposed overhaul would replace the General Law on Ecological Equilibrium and Environmental Protection, known as LGEEPA. That draft would remove automatic administrative approval, expand protected territorial categories, and strengthen state enforcement powers. The article does not name a single official who made these decisions beyond the agencies themselves, but it credits SEMARNAT with the permit clearances and the protected-areas ban, and it describes CONANP's assessments as binding under the new decree. Legal analyst Santiago Suárez Sevilla is quoted in the piece on the proposed LGEEPA overhaul, and he is described as arguing that mining firms will need proactive preventive compliance strategies.

Elio Céspedes Bravo of Datamine is cited as arguing that successful AI adoption in mining depends more on data quality, system integration, and governance than on advanced algorithms, since mining data sits in separate silos. The same roundup also covers Capitan Silver, which reported a carbonate replacement deposit discovery at its Cruz de Plata project in Durango, with high-grade assays and a fourth drill rig added to its 60,000-meter drilling campaign.
