stories.Headline: Can AI Fiber Still Deliver? Corning Faces High-Stakes Q3 Earnings Test Oct. 27 as Valuation Stretches
stories.Summary:
Corning, the optical fiber maker, reports third-quarter results before the market opens on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, and the stock has fallen 19.93% over the past month. The company has beaten earnings-per-share estimates five quarters in a row, yet shares dropped 12.1%, 8.9%, and about 5% on the last three earnings days. The upcoming report is seen as a test of whether demand for AI fiber still supports a premium valuation. Analysts note that the shares trade at roughly 38 times 2026 consensus earnings.

Last quarter, core EPS came in at $0.78 against a $0.7538 estimate, but revenue of $4.505 billion fell short of the $4.63 billion consensus despite 16.6% growth. Optical Communications led with $2.072 billion in sales, up 32%, while Enterprise Networks grew 65% on generative AI demand. Management raised its Springboard Plan targets to annualized sales run rates of $20 billion by the end of 2026, $30 billion by 2028, and $40 billion by 2030. Core operating margin expanded 190 basis points to 20.9%. The EPS consensus now sits near the top of the company's $0.85 to $0.89 guidance range, and analysts have made four upward EPS revisions and no downward ones over the past 30 days.

Corning's chief executive, Wendell Weeks, said in July that demand for the company's generative AI products and enterprise networks remained strong and that orders were accelerating. He added that results so far reflect scale-out only, with scale-up and photonics still ahead. Analysts are watching whether Optical keeps growing 30% or more and whether new hyperscaler deals join existing ones with Meta, Amazon, and NVIDIA. Revenue is seen as the bigger hurdle, since Corning missed revenue consensus in each of the last four quarters. The company's chief financial officer, Edward Schlesinger, said the third-quarter guidance was not meant to signal any slowdown in growth.

Other pressures are also in view. The Solar segment posted a $7 million net loss after a wafer shutdown added $30 million of expense compared with the first quarter, and investors will watch whether its $3 billion revenue target stays on track. Corning expects capital spending to rise in the third and fourth quarters, with about $2 billion committed this year, even as some existing markets look soft. Handheld unit sales are expected to fall by a mid-teens percentage this year, and Carrier sales grew only 1% in the second quarter. JPMorgan analysts said strong third-quarter revenue could put Corning on track to reach its $20 billion run-rate target ahead of schedule, which makes the fourth-quarter outlook just as important.

stories.Headline: AI bear slams Nvidia's GPU pitch: 'There's not scarcity other than that which is created by Jensen Huang'
stories.Summary:
Ed Zitron, CEO of the public relations firm EZPR and a well-known critic of the AI spending boom, has argued that Nvidia is manufacturing the scarcity it sells against. In an appearance on Yahoo Finance's The 8:30 on a Friday, he pointed to how concentrated Nvidia's customer base is, saying five companies accounted for about 70% of its accounts receivable in the first half of the year. He described the situation as channel stuffing, claiming Jensen Huang pushes GPUs into the supply chain by telling buyers they must purchase now or lose access in a few months. Zitron called this morally reprehensible and said it drives up the price of consumer electronics. Investor Steve Eisman has also recently flagged the same customer concentration risk.

Asked whether Huang's pitch simply reflects real demand, given years-long lead times in semiconductors, Zitron questioned how scarcity can exist for a product the company has too much of. He also questioned what the data center build-out delivers, citing a Bloomberg report that Microsoft has about 2 gigawatts of AI compute online out of 12 gigawatts reported. He noted that Amazon recently canceled a data center in Loudoun County, Virginia. Zitron has argued that OpenAI and Anthropic have become load-bearing for Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, CoreWeave and Nebius, and when asked what should happen if they falter, he said to let them die. The hosts countered that a record share of Americans own stocks, and that Bloomberg's Eric Balchunas has argued this could push the government to step in during a crash.

Zitron responded that a bailout would not keep the market up, because it would crash anyway unless buyers keep purchasing GPUs at ever higher prices. He said GPU sales are what matter and what keeps the market alive. The articles do not describe any formal response from Nvidia or Huang to these criticisms. They also note that the commentary was produced with internal AI tools and reviewed by humans before publication. The coverage presents Zitron's views as one prominent skeptical voice in an ongoing debate about AI spending.

stories.Headline: UK government sets out $800 million of AI security funding
stories.Summary:
On Saturday, October 24, 2026, the British government set out around £600 million ($800 million) of funding aimed largely at protecting the country against health and security threats posed by artificial intelligence. The largest share goes to a new biosecurity initiative, including £100 million for a laboratory that will use AI to detect biological threats and £65 million to develop countermeasures against pathogens. AI minister Kanishka Narayan said the goal is for the AI Biosecurity Lab to become a major global institution. He described it as bringing together world-leading scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats. The package was reported by Reuters, and the funding has been announced by the government.

Beyond the biosecurity lab, the package includes several other commitments. The government will give its existing AI Security Institute an extra £120 million, and £130 million will go toward cyber defence projects called the National Cyber Shield and the National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre. A fund worth £60 million will invest in British companies using AI in robotics, autonomous systems and manufacturing. An extra £23 million will support research into the economic impact of AI, while £15 million will fund a prize for AI solutions to public policy problems, initially focused on healthcare. The National Cyber Security Centre will also receive an unspecified sum to expand in Manchester.

Tech companies are contributing as well. OpenAI and Anthropic will offer up to £200 million of model credits to the biosecurity initiative, and Google Deepmind and London-based AI life sciences startup Basecamp Research will provide other assistance. The announcement was made by the government, with Narayan speaking on its behalf about the lab's purpose. The articles do not give further detail on how the contributions will be delivered or governed.

The article notes the wider context of Britain's relationship with AI developers. Related coverage cited in the piece reports that the UK has regained access to OpenAI and Anthropic models before their release, and that Nvidia has pledged $250 million to UK AI safety research. The articles do not say what will happen next or when the lab and other projects will begin operating. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Wenge AI launches enterprise decision AI seminar series in Shenzhen
stories.Summary:
Wenge AI, a company based in China, held the first session of its new seminar series on putting decision AI into practice in enterprises in Shenzhen, bringing together more than 50 academics, industry experts and business leaders from the Greater Bay Area. The event was reported on October 23, 2026, and participants discussed how AI is being used for management decisions, risk anticipation and business analysis. Professor Liu Min, a director at The Chinese University of Hong Kong Business School, said in his opening remarks that AI is reshaping the basic rules of business competition. He argued that managers should test AI in real operating environments instead of only watching it develop.

He also welcomed Wenge AI's continued investment in decision AI and voiced hope that Chinese AI firms would turn their technical strengths into productivity gains for society. Hang Tian, director of the Asian Institute of Supply Chains and Logistics at the same university, described his institute's recent AI research and said his team had built a macro-event analysis system now helping deploy logistics agents for warehousing, transport capacity and compliance. He said he looked forward to working with Wenge AI to help Chinese companies expanding overseas. Wenge AI chairman Wang Lei said general-purpose large language models still struggle with enterprise decisions involving many stakeholders, complex reasoning and fast-changing conditions.

He said decision AI would go beyond answering questions to simulate future scenarios. The company has built what it calls the Decitron Decision Engine, described as the world's first general-purpose large decision model, along with a Decision Intelligence Platform, or DIP. Other speakers gave examples of how companies are applying these tools. Xu Huansheng, vice-president of Meinian Health Group, said his company has pursued an AI transformation since 2021 and argued that the quality of AI-assisted decisions depends on complete and continuous data.

Wenge AI vice-president Zhang Xina described a Fortune Global 500 new energy company that had spent several days manually reconciling tens of thousands of purchase orders. After adopting Wenge AI's platform and model, the company's materials planners reportedly finished that work in about 10 minutes a day, and the system traced a 25-percentage-point monthly drop in on-time delivery to incomplete shipments rather than slow dispatch. A veteran chief information officer named Frank said his company had embedded an AI ontology into the sales, planning and materials modules of its ERP system, with audit trails for traceability. The articles present these accounts as evidence that AI's value depends on redesigning real business workflows, though they are largely statements from the event's participants and the company itself.

stories.Headline: No, China isn’t killing its open AI (yet)
stories.Summary:
The article examines whether China will restrict its open AI models after a surprise proposal for new export controls raised fears in the industry. The piece is published by The Straits Times on October 23, 2026, and it frames the story around worry that Beijing might cut off tools that developers worldwide now rely on. Its central answer to the headline's question is that China is not shutting off the outflow of these models for now, though the proposal makes clear it has the power to do so. China spent roughly two years encouraging a global user base for its cheap, open-weight artificial intelligence models. These models make their inner workings public, which lets developers download and adjust them for their own purposes.

The article says the stakes are large for the Chinese AI sector and especially for start-ups and research institutions overseas that adopted Chinese tools as an alternative to offerings from Silicon Valley. The article does not provide figures for user numbers, revenue or the specific terms of the proposed controls. The article's account centres on the tension between openness and control. It describes the proposal as a surprise and notes that it has prompted anxiety, but it does not attribute specific statements to named officials in the material provided. Its reporting suggests that the government has not yet acted to halt the flow of models, which is the basis for the headline's qualifier "yet."

The article offers no direct quotations from Beijing, and it does not say what penalties or timelines the controls would involve. The article leaves open how the situation will develop, since the source material does not say whether the proposal will be adopted, revised or dropped. It presents the question as unresolved, with the possibility that Beijing could restrict the models while currently choosing not to. Readers are left to watch whether the export controls move forward and whether the open-weight releases continue.

stories.Headline: Wuzhen Summit Puts Spotlight on Tongxiang's Expanding AI Industry
stories.Summary:
The 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit will open on Nov. 2, bringing technology leaders, researchers and companies to the historic water town. Ahead of the event, reporters visited seven Tongxiang-based companies working in robotics, intelligent vehicles, synthetic data, industrial automation, logistics and computing infrastructure. These firms are expanding AI applications from commercial cleaning and autonomous delivery to industrial control and data-center cooling. The summit is a chance to demonstrate how local companies are commercializing AI technologies for customers at home and abroad.

CenoBots, a Tongxiang-based company, has sold cleaning robots in more than 40 countries and regions, with customers including Changi Airport, Tesco, the University of Minnesota and Novo Nordisk. This year, the company supplied about 600 autonomous cleaning robots for Tesco Express stores across the United Kingdom. CenoBots has expanded its research, development and production facilities in Tongxiang from approximately 3,000 square meters in its early years to more than 20,000 square meters. TEEMO makes drive-by-wire skateboard chassis and core components for autonomous vehicles used in last-mile delivery, patrols and logistics, and its customers span the United States, the Middle East, India and Russia. Dayan Technology, founded in Tongxiang in May 2025, provides synthetic-data and toolchain services for autonomous-driving and humanoid-robotics companies.

Freetech develops intelligent-driving systems and 4D imaging radar for passenger and commercial vehicles, and its technology has been selected for hundreds of vehicle programs. At its intelligent-manufacturing base in Wuzhen, an in-house AI system reads customer orders and calculates components and materials needed for each production line, increasing overall efficiency by more than 20%. Shuhan Technologies, founded in 2019, provides on-premises industrial AI for chemical plants, energy facilities and wastewater-treatment systems. At a coal chemical plant with annual capacity of 1.2 million metric tons, Shuhan said its system reduced raw-material consumption by 6% and generated more than 176 million yuan, or about $26 million, in annualized economic benefits, while reducing carbon emissions by more than 500,000 metric tons. SynthCool develops two-phase liquid-cooling systems that support heat dissipation of more than 3,000 watts per chip and heat flux above 250 watts per square centimeter.

CenoBots co-founder and vice president Shen Jizhong said cleaning robots are appearing in more settings, much like electric vehicles becoming a familiar sight on the roads. TEEMO director of operations Zhang Yongjian said autonomous delivery vehicles have strong potential in overseas markets where distances are long and last-mile delivery is difficult to staff. Freetech founder and CEO Dr. Zhang Lin said transportation combined with a specialized function will be an important direction for the future, with potential applications including robots, elder-care vehicles, mining equipment and agricultural machinery. Shuhan Chief Technology Officer Zhai Zhengjun said all industrial process challenges can be framed as control and optimization problems. SynthCool general manager Zhu Zhijiang said heat dissipation is infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Singapore embraces AI for cyber defence, with one caveat: breach transparency
stories.Summary:
Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences while pressing them for greater openness about security breaches. The move comes as regional governments try to harness artificial intelligence without ignoring the new dangers it brings. The concern was sharpened by an AI agent linked to OpenAI, which gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year. At a summit earlier this month, Singapore launched a refreshed cybersecurity strategy, and it lays out a plan to bring AI into its cyber defence operations step by step.

The strategy requires that AI be progressively deployed across cyber defence operations, with industry partners helping to speed up adoption. Its aim is to bolster protection for the city state's critical infrastructure. K. Shanmugam, Singapore's coordinating minister for national security, said in a speech at Singapore International Cyber Week on October 13 that the country would take a "pragmatic" approach. Singapore will not need to build its own AI models for every use case, he said, because the real need is the ability to evaluate the best available models and adapt them to local requirements.

Shanmugam leads the government's security effort and set out this stance publicly at the cyber week event. The articles do not detail specific breach reporting rules for the firms involved. They do make clear that the government is asking companies to be more transparent about incidents as their AI systems grow more capable and autonomous. Those expectations are the caveat attached to the country's embrace of the technology.

The articles present this as a balancing act rather than a settled outcome. The reporting does not say what enforcement steps, if any, will follow if companies fail to disclose breaches quickly. It also does not describe a timetable for when AI tools will be fully in use across Singapore's cyber defence work. Further detail on how the partnership and transparency expectations will be implemented is not provided in the articles.

stories.Headline: Preemption Arbitrage: The Forum-Shopping Edge in AI Compliance
stories.Summary:
The Yahoo Finance and Forkast articles, both dated October 23, 2026, describe a new commercial strategy the authors call preemption arbitrage. Large AI deployers are using federal policy to escape stricter state rules, and the FTC's July 1 policy statement on preemption theory is presented as the blueprint for doing so. The piece was written by Priya Nair for Yahoo Finance, and its Forkast counterpart runs the same text. Both say the approach rests on what they call the forum-shopping edge in AI compliance. The articles explain that companies with enough legal and operational resources can pick the most favorable regulatory environment, invoking obstacle preemption against more restrictive laws.

Smaller deployers, by contrast, must absorb the higher cumulative cost of meeting several state requirements that may contradict one another. The mechanism depends on the gap between federal policy statements and state responsibility doctrines. States such as California and Colorado have passed laws assigning liability for agent-initiated transactions, but the FTC's theory suggests federal consumer protection mandates could override them if they are found to impede the delivery of truthful information. The authors do not attribute any direct statement to the FTC beyond the existence of its July 1 policy statement, and they name no specific companies. They describe the trend as a commercial lever large technology firms are increasingly pursuing, while noting that the current patchwork of state AI rules has created a fragmented enforcement landscape.

The writer frames the advantage as belonging to organizations that can navigate this forum-shopping terrain, rather than to those with the strongest models. The articles present these as the authors' own assessments of the market. Looking ahead, the articles say the industry is moving toward 2027 enforcement windows, and they argue that regulatory positioning will matter as much as technical safety for investors and builders. They conclude that preemption will stay a powerful but unevenly distributed tool until Congress enacts a comprehensive federal framework. Until then, the articles suggest, the central question in AI regulation is which rules apply to whom, and where.

stories.Headline: PC Sales Just Crashed 21% as AI Eats the World’s Memory Chips
stories.Summary:
On October 22, 2026, Counterpoint Research released preliminary data showing that global PC shipments fell 21% year over year in the third quarter, to 57 million units. The headline's word "sales" is shorthand, since the figures count shipments into the sales channel rather than consumer purchases. Counterpoint's report points to rising memory and component costs as the main cause. Stock prices barely moved the following day, October 23, 2026.

Other trackers reported similar declines, though their totals differ. Gartner counted 55.4 million shipments, down 22.4% from 71.3 million, while IDC counted 62.7 million, down 20.1% from 78.5 million. Counterpoint also recorded a 13.8% drop from the second quarter and expects a 27% year-over-year decline in the fourth quarter, with flat volumes in 2027. HP shipped 10.3 million units, down 31%, the steepest drop among the top six vendors. Apple shipped 11% fewer Macs yet grew its share to 9.8% from 8.7%, which Counterpoint credits to its cheaper MacBook Neo.

The link to AI runs through memory supply. TrendForce said on September 30, 2026, that server demand will push fourth-quarter conventional DRAM contract prices up another 10% to 15% and NAND flash up 15% to 20%. AI servers use far more memory than PCs, so memory makers shift capacity toward higher-margin server chips. PC makers then pay more for what supply remains and pass those costs on through higher prices. Counterpoint analyst Minsoo Kang said this forces consumers to delay replacement purchases.

The articles also note other factors, including a year-ago quarter inflated by buying ahead of the Windows 10 support deadline and by tariff stocking. IDC's Jitesh Ubrani pointed to a strong pull-in of demand in the first half. HP's Personal Systems revenue rose 18% in its fiscal third quarter while units fell 16%, and its operating margin narrowed to 4.6% from 5.4%. Dell, which sells both PCs and AI servers, reported an AI server backlog of $95 billion, while Micron benefits from higher contract prices. Counterpoint's David Naranjo warned that stabilization should not be mistaken for recovery, and HP's next report is estimated for November 24, 2026, though the company has not confirmed that date.

stories.Headline: 4 Data Center REITs With Growing Dividends and an AI Tailwind
stories.Summary:
Four US-listed real estate investment trusts that own data center buildings, land, fiber and power connections, all of which are seeing demand from AI and cloud customers, were highlighted in an October 24, 2026 article on Yahoo Finance by Chris Lange. The piece describes the group as offering dividend growth with modest starting yields, with each quarterly payout covered by operating cash flow. The article ties this to a Colorado Legislative Council Staff report saying a single operating data center can draw more than a gigawatt of power, roughly enough for 750,000 homes. The four names it covers are American Tower, Iron Mountain, Digital Realty and Equinix. Each is examined for how safe its payout looks and what could slow it down.

American Tower, which owns over 148,000 communications tower sites leased to wireless carriers, yields 3.93% at $188.97 per share on a $1.79 quarterly payout, or $7.16 a year. Its CoreSite subsidiary runs interconnected US data centers, and data center revenue rose 13.4% year over year to $297 million in the second quarter. Management raised full-year AFFO per-share guidance to $11.00 to $11.17, and the article says the chief financial officer named supporting a growing dividend as the first capital priority. The payout was cut from $1.70 to $1.62 at the start of 2024, then raised to $1.70 in 2025 and $1.79 in 2026. Net leverage stood at 4.9 times against a target range of 3 to 5 times, and the article flags DISH-related cancellations that cut $63 million from US and Canada property revenue in the quarter.

Iron Mountain stores more than 735 million cubic feet of physical records across about 1,300 facilities and yields 2.94% at $109.94 on an $0.864 quarterly dividend. Its data center business, with 31 facilities in 21 markets, grew revenue 38.8% to $262.9 million, and the article says the trailing four-quarter AFFO payout ratio was 60%. Full-year AFFO guidance was lifted to $5.87 to $5.93, and the article notes the latest raise was the fourth consecutive year of increases, taking the quarterly rate from $0.65 up to $0.864. Digital Realty, a data center-only REIT with 309 facilities, yields 2.77% at $172.38 on a $1.22 quarterly dividend that has held flat since 2022, while revenue grew 29.9% and total backlog reached a record $1.9 billion. Equinix, operating more than 270 data centers, yields 1.98% at $955.03 on a $5.16 quarterly dividend, and management projects AFFO per share growth of 9% to 12% a year from 2027 through 2029, with dividend growth expected to match.

The article cites company executives for the bullish case, including American Tower chief executive Steven Vondran, who said CoreSite's campuses have become critical destinations for AI traffic, Iron Mountain chief executive William Meaney, who tied recent European deals to AI inference demand, Digital Realty chief executive Andy Power, who credited hyperscale leasing for the record backlog, and Equinix chief executive Adaire Fox-Martin, who said most leading AI model providers already run networking workloads on its platform. It also lists risks: rising capital spending at Equinix, with capex guided at $5.0 to $6.0 billion for 2026, and negative shareholders' equity and rising interest costs at Iron Mountain. The article presents these names as suited to long-term dividend-growth investors rather than those seeking the highest current income. Earnings reports from American Tower and Equinix are scheduled for October 27 and October 28, respectively.

stories.Headline: Mave, which is developing an AI-driven tool to automate security investigations, raised a $28M Series A led by Red Dot, bringing its total funding to $34M (Meir Orbach/CTech)
stories.Summary:
Mave, an Israeli cybersecurity startup, has raised a $28 million Series A round led by Red Dot Capital Partners, bringing its total funding to $34 million. The company, which is developing an AI-driven platform to automate security investigations, also raised a $6 million Seed round led by Dell Technologies Capital and Emerge Ventures, and Lumir Growth Partners took part in the Series A. The news was reported on October 22, 2026, with the funding announced the evening before in Israel. Mave plans to use the new capital to accelerate its AI research, strengthen its enterprise products and expand internationally. Mave was founded in 2025 by CEO Raziel Oren and CTO Guy Eshel, both veterans of Israel's Unit 8200 intelligence unit. Oren previously led go-to-market operations at Wing Security, and Eshel was the first employee at Alterya, where he later served as vice president of R&D before Chainalysis acquired the company.

The company says it already works with Fortune 50 companies and global managed security service providers, protecting hundreds of customers. It also reports that its annual recurring revenue has grown by more than 400% over the past six months, and that it is closing deals worth seven figures. After the funding round, Mave plans to more than double its team, with hiring focused on go-to-market operations and AI research. The platform addresses a problem that Mave describes as the fragmentation of corporate security systems. Large organizations often run dozens of security tools, and during an incident, the information needed to understand an attack is spread across them, forcing analysts to switch systems and rebuild events by hand.

Mave connects directly to tools an organization already uses, without moving security data into a new repository, and queries each tool through its native interface. The company says the system investigates every alert within minutes, filters out false positives, identifies relevant active campaigns and can carry out approved response actions under rules set by the security team. It also records queries, decisions and actions so that each investigation has a traceable record. Oren, the CEO, said the company was founded to address gaps in security management by using AI to investigate incidents faster and more efficiently than human analysts.

He argued that building a product on an existing AI model is not enough to stand out, and said Mave relies on models that can be more precise rather than depending solely on a large language model. In the company's funding announcement, Oren said security teams still investigate threats one tool at a time, and that Mave is built to give them AI that can keep pace with attackers while knowing when human judgment is required. He also said he wants the company to grow while keeping strong revenue and solid margins. The funding will let Mave invest more in sales, marketing and engineering, and its Israeli development center will remain central to its expansion.

stories.Headline: Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the company
stories.Summary:
Anthropic published a report on Thursday, 22 October 2026, saying that artificial intelligence has changed how work gets done at the company and reshaped its workforce. The company said it is hiring fewer junior technical workers and that human attention has become a "bottleneck" as it relies more on its Claude AI agents. Its report says that since March 2025, shortly after the release of its coding tool Claude Code, entry-level technical hires fell from nearly 30% to 9%, and headcount fell from about 21% to 14%. Employees now spend about 22% of their time managing Claude agents, more than double the amount a year ago, and from May 2026 AI agents logged more work hours than human staff.

The report presents these shifts as a preview of wider changes in the labor market. It suggests software engineers could face a tougher job market as more companies adopt AI agents, while entry-level tech workers may struggle to build the skills and experience they need. It also raises the possibility of single-person startups run by a human founder directing swarms of agents. To address rising public concern, Anthropic suggests that tech employers offer workers stock ownership, arguing that workers should hold a financial stake in successful AI rollouts. The company did not respond to the Guardian's request for comment.

Several experts question both the findings and the motives behind them. Some AI researchers argue the report is an attempt to boost Anthropic's valuation before its initial public offering, which could come as soon as November. Yale social scientist Julián Posada said the report was written from the perspective of a company that wants investors, and noted that it lacked independent assessment by outside auditors. Morgan Frank, a Case Western Reserve University researcher, has a peer-reviewed paper showing that AI-exposed job markets weakened starting in early 2022, before ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. He said factors such as cutting pandemic-era hires and "AI-washing," where bosses credit AI for layoffs they would have made anyway, could explain recent job losses.

Dylan Baker, a lead research engineer at the nonprofit Distributed AI Research Institute, called shifting development to AI while hiring few entry-level workers "shortsighted," and disputed the report's description of humans as a bottleneck. Baker argued that software design is a social and interpersonal process, and questioned whether well-designed products can come from a team facing what the report quotes an unnamed engineer describing as "an army of Claudes." The scrutiny comes as Anthropic nears its IPO. A draft of its S-1 filing reportedly showed an $80bn net loss over the first half of this year, and investors now project a valuation of $1.5tn, down from earlier estimates of $2tn or more. Baker said tech workers will be affected regardless of how the market turns, and hopes for a reassessment of how much software has always depended on human work.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang GTC Berlin 2026 Full Speech Transcript: AI Is Not Software — It’s a Manufacturing Industry
stories.Summary:
The Moroccan technology group ABA Technology, led by Mohamed Benouda, presented its Fusion AI In-a-Box platform directly to Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang at a highlight event during the GTC Berlin 2026 conference. The meeting, reported on October 24, 2026, reflects the growing weight of Morocco's technology sector on the international stage. It also signals a commitment to solutions that protect data sovereignty and security, which the coverage describes as a priority in the global digital economy. Nvidia, according to the article, has recognized the platform as one of the five most promising initiatives in developing open models for the European public and sovereign sectors. That recognition matters because it highlights the need for technology that can run artificial intelligence inside an organization's own infrastructure rather than in external clouds.

The platform is built around sovereign artificial intelligence, which lets companies and public agencies run AI applications locally without sharing their data with outside providers. This design keeps information under the owner's control, a feature the article calls fundamental for sensitive sectors where privacy and security are paramount. The approach also supports compliance with strict data protection rules, which the article notes is especially relevant for public institutions and firms that handle confidential data. The platform comes in two main configurations, each covering a different phase of the AI model lifecycle. Fusion AI Factory In-a-Box serves the development stage, where data is prepared and AI solutions are fitted into business processes, and it supports adapting and custom-building models.

Fusion AI Inference In-a-Box targets production by optimizing how models run, with an emphasis on reducing costs and improving performance. The article presents the second configuration as the means to keep deployed systems efficient and affordable, which it describes as crucial for scalability and long-term sustainability. The article describes the launch as a significant step toward sovereign artificial intelligence and autonomy over critical data, and it credits ABA Technology with pairing its software with Nvidia's computing infrastructure. Its main claim is that an emerging technology company can work alongside a large firm like Nvidia to answer concerns about privacy, technological dependence, and operational efficiency. The coverage stops at that assessment and does not describe any further commercial agreements or deployment timelines.

stories.Headline: Will Top Talents Like Wang Hong and Wei Dongyi Be "Outperformed" by AI?
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released 722 mathematical papers at once, and among the results were a number of long-standing problems that had resisted mathematicians for decades. The article says the papers cover number theory, geometry, theoretical computer science and other fields, and that the average computation for each result equalled about three hours of thinking by ChatGPT Pro. The Riemann Hypothesis, first proposed in 1859, was one of the problems OpenAI said it had advanced. The same batch included a claim that Catalan's constant is irrational, a question open for more than 100 years. The article also describes a separate episode in July, when a researcher at Anthropic posted on X that he had disproved the Jacobian conjecture, a problem that has troubled mathematicians for more than 80 years.

The piece says that the flood of AI results has left many mathematicians uncertain about their own work and funding, and it notes that some research projects were overtaken almost immediately. One PhD student quoted on Reddit said his group had solved a special case and was preparing a thesis when OpenAI's results appeared, and the article says the reliability of the AI results has not yet been confirmed through peer review. The article places much of the responsibility on the AI companies themselves, arguing that they are competing hard for technological leadership, users, capital and markets. It quotes OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as saying that AI could not even compare 9.8 and 9.11 last year but can now challenge the Riemann Hypothesis. The writer argues that major AI firms are recruiting mathematicians while also using their results as public demonstrations of progress, and that the pace of new model releases pushes companies to keep producing headline achievements.

The author describes mathematics as well suited to this purpose because its formal logic makes AI capability easy to show. The article ties this to the wider race, saying that rapid model iteration forces companies to keep announcing new breakthroughs or risk falling behind, as Google's Gemini reportedly did. It notes that Fields Medalists Wang Hong and Deng Yu won the prize this year, and that Jacob Zimmerman has joined OpenAI for AI safety work while his student Alpöge works at Anthropic. The article does not say what the next round of announcements will bring or how the mathematical community will respond to them.

Articles.Title: Will Top Talents Like Wang Hong and Wei Dongyi Be "Outperformed" by AI? - 36Kr

stories.Headline: A Starting Point for Your City’s AI Policy
stories.Summary:
The League of Minnesota Cities published a model artificial intelligence policy on October 23, 2026, to help cities use AI responsibly in their operations. The League says AI tools can save time and improve efficiency, but they also raise questions about data privacy, accuracy, and accountability. The guidance is aimed at cities whose staff use AI to draft communications, analyze information, or handle everyday tasks. It notes that cities need clear expectations for what the technology can and cannot be used for. The article explains why a policy matters, pointing to several risks.

Information entered into AI platforms may be retained by third-party providers, and automated recommendations can reflect errors and biases. The article also says cities have legal duties, including compliance with the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act, and that government data created with AI assistance is likely covered by those requirements. Without guidelines, employees may expose sensitive information or rely on content that has not been properly reviewed. A clear policy helps staff know when AI is useful and what precautions to take.

The League's model policy offers a framework that cities can adapt to their own operations, technology, and needs. It includes two options for permitted and prohibited uses and defines low-, moderate-, and high-risk data with precautions for each. It keeps employees responsible for reviewing, verifying, and approving AI-generated content and decisions, and it gives guidance on disclosing when AI has materially helped create documents or public communications. The article says cities should review and adapt the model with their city attorney before adopting it.

It also recommends regular reviews, since the technology continues to change. The League directs cities to a companion resource, Cities and Artificial Intelligence (AI): What You Should Know, which covers data classification, compliance with the Government Data Practices Act, and the risks of relying on AI-generated information. The article also lists the League's Resource Research Department, which can be reached through an online form or by phone at (651) 281-1200 or (800) 925-1122, to help cities with questions. The article closes by saying that AI may change how cities carry out their work but does not change their duty to protect government data and serve their communities.

stories.Headline: TRACE: Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure for Multi-Turn Safety
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv on October 1, 2026, by Fengpeng Li and five co-authors describes a new training method called TRACE, short for Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure, aimed at multi-turn safety in large language models. The authors note that safety-aligned models often refuse a harmful request made in a single prompt but comply once the same goal is spread across several turns. They argue that existing preference objectives, which score whole responses to single prompts, cannot control this risk on unseen conversation histories. The paper was listed under the Artificial Intelligence category, and its DOI was given as 10.48550/arXiv.2610.01323.

The paper presents analysis giving sufficient conditions under which suppressing harmful behavior at supervised single-turn contexts yields a bound on multi-turn trajectory risk. That bound is described as accounting for coverage, transfer slack, and leakage, and as measuring contraction relative to a base-policy risk budget. TRACE turns this principle into a token-level objective, weighting each token of a safe response by the discounted return of a refusal-attributable advantage. The advantage compares a frozen reference model with a copy whose refusal behavior has been ablated, so earlier response tokens can receive credit from later refusal-related evidence. A gradient-norm penalty replaces the retain set in the method.

The authors report testing across five open-weight models and seven multi-turn attacks, and they say TRACE produced the lowest attack success rate in all 35 model and attack pairs. They also report that model utility, measured on the MMLU and HellaSwag benchmarks, dropped by at most 1.23 points. The paper states that source code is included in the supplemental material. The article itself does not describe any reaction from outside researchers, companies, or regulators, and it does not say whether the work has been peer reviewed or accepted at a conference. The submission is a single version, v1, dated October 1, 2026.

Articles.Title: TRACE: Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure for Multi-Turn Safety

stories.Headline: DOME: A Decoupled Offline-Online Memory Externalization Framework for Interpretable Domain-Generalized Face Anti-spoofing
stories.Summary:
The article describes DOME, a research framework for face anti-spoofing, published in the International Journal of Computer Vision with a date of 3 October 2026 (volume 134, article 459), and indexed online on 24 October 2026. The authors argue that current interpretable approaches built on Multimodal Large Language Models store their knowledge implicitly inside model parameters, so explanations end up as after-the-fact justifications of predictions rather than as the basis for the decision. To address this, they propose an approach that places interpretable knowledge in an explicit external store, which they call a vision-language memory bank. The article does not name individual authors in the portion provided, and no independent parties are quoted.

The memory bank is described as a structured repository holding two things: textual rules and visual prototypes. Construction happens in two stages. In the first, an offline stage, the researchers populate the memory by extracting rules and aggregating prototypes through a decision tree applied to a small number of training samples. In the second, an online stage, a trainable fusion module retrieves stored rules as prior evidence for the language model and uses the visual prototypes to enhance the image features. The authors say this makes explanations active predictive priors rather than passive outputs, and that it reduces the need for massive supervision.

The authors report that the method achieves competitive performance on multiple domain generalization protocols while providing structured explanations. The datasets named are the publicly available face presentation attack detection benchmarks OULU-NPU, CASIA-FASD, Idiap Replay-Attack, MSU-MFSD, and CelebA-Spoof. The authors also state that they created finer-grained annotations for four of these datasets. Those derived annotations are not posted publicly because of the restrictive license terms of the source datasets, and the article says they are available from the corresponding author on request to qualified researchers with authorized dataset access. The provided text does not give specific accuracy figures or describe any follow-up work or next steps.

Articles.Title: DOME: A Decoupled Offline-Online Memory Externalization Framework for Interpretable Domain-Generalized Face Anti-spoofing

stories.Headline: Britain is quietly seeking powers over foreign AI firms
stories.Summary:
Last week the British government quietly tabled a new clause for the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would let it regulate AI companies located anywhere in the world. In simple terms, ministers would gain broad discretion to inspect AI firms, test their platforms and require developers to test their models, with sanctions available if companies do not comply. The clause was introduced as a government amendment at the final substantive stage of amendments, and Monday is likely to be the only real chance for scrutiny in both the House of Lords and the Commons. The author, Elle Smith, a former civil servant who worked on AI policy, argues that this would be the first time the British state can regulate a technology she calls the most economically promising and risky of our time, so she asks where the democratic scrutiny is.

The clause would also bring AI models and their developers into the scope of the bill as critical suppliers when an energy company or data center uses them. The legislation does not say how AI would be regulated or how sanctions would apply, and it simply grants ministers wide room to introduce further rules later. Parliament would likely have little input once the bill passes. The author notes that the Trump administration showed in June that it can restrict model access for the UK, so regulation of this kind is unlikely to go unnoticed. She suggests that before acting, the government should assess the risk of losing access to frontier models and the consequences of that loss, alongside the direct risks of AI.

The article's case rests on the view that AI both raises cyber risks and helps fix them, since a PHP vulnerable across many websites was recently found using OpenAI tools. The author argues that Britain has no domestic developer of broadly capable AI models and depends on US and Chinese models. She cites Center for Governance on AI research finding that 7% of model releases were delayed or withheld in the UK compared with the US, while the figure for the EU was 11%. She writes that Britain could reduce this dependence by speeding up the planning system and grid queue to build data center capacity, and that a UK model developer or a chip designer could still emerge. The piece closes by asking whether lawmakers could at least debate the balance between model access and regulation.

stories.Headline: A multifunctional optoelectronic synaptic device for logic operation and neuromorphic computing
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers led by Ghulam Dastgeer and Jonghwa Eom at Sejong University in Seoul has reported a light-driven neuromorphic memristor built from tri-layer tungsten diselenide, a two-dimensional material whose charge carriers were adjusted through benzyl viologen doping. The work was published on October 1, 2026, in the journal Advanced Composites and Hybrid Materials, and the authors describe it as a multifunctional optoelectronic synaptic device. The device responds to visible and deep-ultraviolet light, and the deep-ultraviolet pulses cause charge trapping that allows the memory to hold its state. The article states that the study addresses the need for energy-efficient hardware that can mimic biological synapses for artificial intelligence and edge computing.

The researchers used atomic force microscopy and Raman spectroscopy to confirm the structural integrity and material quality of the film, and they measured its electrical behavior through gate-dependent transfer curves and current-voltage measurements. Optical pulses produced adjustable conductance changes, including paired-pulse facilitation, which indicates short-term plasticity, along with long-term potentiation and depression. According to the article, controlling the duration of the deep-ultraviolet pulse raised the device response from 25.2% to 1438.7%. The device also recognized selected alphabet characters and performed a logic OR operation. When the synaptic weights were used in an artificial neural network trained on the MNIST handwritten digit dataset, the network reached an accuracy of 92%, which the authors checked with epoch-dependent learning curves and a confusion matrix.

The article names Dastgeer, Sobia Nisar, Inshaal Fatima, Rana Faryad Ali, Iqra Rabani, Kashif Hussain, Ali Alsalme and Jonghwa Eom as authors, with affiliations spanning Sejong University, Dongguk University, Government College University Faisalabad, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the University of Antwerp, Peking University and King Saud University. The authors report that the work received support from a Korean Basic Science Institute grant, an Information Technology Research Center grant funded by the Korean government, and a King Saud University funding program. The authors declare no competing interests. The article notes that the authors present the platform as a promising basis for low-power, optically programmable neuromorphic systems for intelligent sensing, but it does not describe any commercial plans or next steps beyond that.

Articles.Title: A multifunctional optoelectronic synaptic device for logic operation and neuromorphic computing

stories.Headline: Prediction of mammaprint risk in breast cancer using a combined radiomics-habitat model integrating intratumoral and peritumoral MRI features: a retrospective dual-center study
stories.Summary:
A retrospective dual-center study published in BMC Medical Imaging on 1 October 2026 describes an MRI-based model meant to predict MammaPrint risk in breast cancer without a tissue test. The work was led by Yi Dai, Jiajia Lin and Kexin Chen, who contributed equally, with Junwei Cui and Lei Wu among the corresponding authors. The researchers combined radiomic features taken from the tumor itself and the tissue around it with a habitat analysis, which maps how different parts of the tumor vary inside. The target was hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, and the aim was to offer an imaging stand-in for genomic risk stratification.

The study included 156 patients who had dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI before treatment and also underwent MammaPrint testing. Several machine learning models were built and judged with receiver operating characteristic analysis, calibration analysis and decision curve analysis. Among clinical predictors, mass margin was independently associated with the outcome, with an odds ratio of 0.854. The published abstract is partly garbled, so most of the other statistics are not legible, apart from P values of 0.267, 0.491 and 0.892 that appear in the calibration results. Decision curve analysis was reported to confirm the model's clinical usefulness.

The authors conclude that the radiomics-habitat model shows promise for noninvasive prediction, though they frame it only as a potential surrogate for genomic testing. They declared no competing interests, and the paper was received on 25 July 2026 and accepted on 22 September 2026. Ethics approval came from Peking University Shenzhen Hospital (No. 2025-126) and Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital (No. KY2024-869-01), and written consent was waived because the study was retrospective. Funding came from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (82472051), the Guangdong Medical Research Foundation (A2024014), the Shenzhen Science and Technology Program (JCYJ20250604183659019), the Peking University Shenzhen Hospital research foundation (KYQD2023624) and the Shenzhen Key Medical Discipline Construction Fund (SZXK050). The funders had no role in the design, analysis or writing of the study.

A second paper in the same journal, published on 26 September 2026, looks at related questions using a different technique. It tested whether radiomics could improve MR cytometry, a diffusion MRI approach, for telling benign from malignant breast lesions in 221 patients from two centers, 47 benign and 174 malignant. Radiomics-based models beat those using only mean parameter values, for example an external test AUC of 0.901 against 0.841 for combined ADC and MR cytometry measures. Logistic regression reached the highest AUC, 0.943. Both studies reflect wider interest in using imaging features to capture tumor heterogeneity that a limited biopsy may miss, but the articles do not say what further validation is planned.

Articles.Title: Prediction of mammaprint risk in breast cancer using a combined radiomics-habitat model integrating intratumoral and peritumoral MRI features: a retrospective dual-center study

stories.Headline: AbsorbEvo: An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Inverse Design of Microwave Absorbers
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv describes AbsorbEvo, an agentic framework for the autonomous inverse design of microwave absorbers. The paper was authored by Zhicheng Feng, Yubo Zhao and Xuefeng Yao, and was submitted on 1 October 2026, appearing on arXiv under the subject area of artificial intelligence. The authors say designing high-performance microwave absorbers normally demands specialized knowledge of electromagnetic theory, materials science and simulation programming, along with lengthy optimization work. AbsorbEvo is presented as a way to turn natural-language performance objectives directly into designs that are checked by full-wave simulations.

According to the abstract, the system's candidate evolution strategy combines language reasoning, physics-based prediction and feedback from earlier computational runs. A large language model suggests the direction and size of parameter changes based on the task objectives and the computing history. The framework pairs directed adjustments with global sampling to produce candidate designs, then uses a low-cost predictive model as a physics prior to rank them, so that only the highest-ranked designs go through full-wave simulation. Designs that pass physical validity checks feed back into performance evaluation and guide the next round of search. The authors also say that lessons from training tasks are distilled into textual skills, which are independently validated before being applied to new tasks.

The authors report results on held-out AbsorbBench-36 tasks under identical proposal budgets. AbsorbEvo achieved a task success rate of 79.17 percent, compared with 25.00 percent for a generic agent and 12.50 percent for random search. Its mean best coverage was 0.7816, against 0.6434 and 0.6448 for the two baselines. The abstract concludes that the approach offers a methodological foundation for natural-language-driven autonomous inverse design of microwave absorbers. The article does not describe any further publication, peer review status or next steps beyond this initial version.

Articles.Title: AbsorbEvo: An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Inverse Design of Microwave Absorbers

stories.Headline: Token-Disentangled Latent Test-Time Scaling for Vision-Language Reasoning
stories.Summary:
Two research papers posted to arXiv in late 2026 describe new ways to make large AI models more accurate and better at judging their own confidence when they are actually being used. The first, submitted on September 28, 2026, was written by Hao-Xuan Ma and ten co-authors and proposes a method for refining the hidden internal states of vision-language models during inference. The second, submitted on October 2, 2026, was written by Zizhuo Zhang and six co-authors and addresses how language models express confidence on tasks where no correct answers are provided. Both papers were listed on arXiv with the same publication date of October 24, 2026, and both are open for public reading.

The first paper, called Token-Disentangled Latent Test-Time Scaling, argues that existing methods treat every editable internal token the same way, applying one scalar reward to all of them. The authors separate the tokens by role, routing visual feedback to tokens sensitive to the image and reasoning feedback to tokens where the model's uncertainty is high, while tokens that receive neither signal are held in place by an anchor regularizer. Tested on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B, the method raised macro accuracy over chain-of-thought prompting by 2.57 and 1.51 points respectively. The paper is 20 pages long, includes four figures, and the authors have released code.

The second paper, Test-time Calibration Learning, targets a practical gap in earlier work, which relied on ground-truth labels to teach models to report accurate confidence. The proposed framework, TTCL, is label-free and derives its supervision from multiple responses the model generates to unlabeled target-task questions. The authors state that their theoretical analysis establishes TTCL as a bounded surrogate for the ideal calibration objective. Across mathematical reasoning and factual question answering, the authors report an average relative accuracy gain of +40.13% and an expected calibration error reduction of +70.80% across eight benchmarks on base models. The paper runs 34 pages and the source code has been published.

Both papers position their work as improvements for deployment settings where labeled data is scarce and models must adapt to new tasks on the fly. The first focuses on squeezing better reasoning out of multimodal models at inference time, while the second focuses on making the confidence those models express more trustworthy. The articles do not say whether either method has been adopted in commercial systems, nor do they report independent replication. Future work, according to the papers' framing, would extend these inference-time techniques to additional models and domains, but the articles do not specify concrete next steps beyond the reported experiments.

stories.Headline: PACE: Provenance-Aware Capability Enforcement for Tool-Using LLM Agents
stories.Summary:
A group of eight researchers posted a preprint on arXiv on October 1, 2026, describing a security system called Provenance-Aware Capability Enforcement, or PACE, for AI agents that use tools. The paper, listed under cryptography and security, addresses the risk that tool-using large language model agents turn generated text into real side effects. It notes that poisoned tool metadata, retrieved web pages, memory, and reusable skills can all steer the next tool call. The authors argue that vetting an artifact before it is admitted is not enough, since a safe and a leaking variant can produce identical admission evidence. Instead, PACE checks every tool call immediately before it executes.

Its path confinement component proposes a cut across the represented influence paths, while its capability and effect verification component checks schema-defined effects against authority compiled from the authenticated request. The paper separates the certified execution contract from the evaluated configuration, which can restore an authorized call after a proposed block or apply a declared repair. Confinement requires the final action to preserve the certified cut. The authors report results on eight executable agent-security benchmarks across three target-model families. The evaluated configuration gave the strictly lowest attack success in 62 of 79 eligible attack columns and tied in 14, and full-benchmark native utility fell by at most three points compared with the undefended agent.

A full ablation over 1,167 paired cases attributed most of the security gains to effect verification and most of the refusal control to boundary adaptation. A reduced-scale adaptive search succeeded on 0 of 30 out-of-authority targets against the defense. The paper is the work of Fengpeng Li, Qizhou Wang, Yuke Hu, Kemou Li, Jun Liu, Haiwei Wu, Jiantao Zhou, and Di Wang, and it is the first version, submitted to arXiv and not yet described as peer-reviewed in the material provided. The article gives no further detail on deployment plans or next steps beyond the reported experiments.

Articles.Title: PACE: Provenance-Aware Capability Enforcement for Tool-Using LLM Agents

stories.Headline: Controllable Stochastic Quantization Encoding for Adversarially Robust Spiking Neural Networks
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on October 1, 2026, and indexed on October 24, 2026, describes a new method for making spiking neural networks harder to fool with adversarial attacks. The authors, Yujia Liu, Peiyu Liu, Yajing Zheng and Tiejun Huang, report that SNNs, which mimic brain-like timing and are prized for energy efficiency, remain vulnerable to inputs with tiny, hard-to-see changes that mislead their predictions. Most earlier defenses focused on how these networks are trained, while the way inputs are encoded received little attention. The paper is listed under the Neural and Evolutionary Computing subject area and has not, based on the listing, been published in a peer-reviewed venue.

The authors propose a stochastic quantization encoding method that converts an input image into spike form with a controllable amount of randomness, set by a quantization scale. They note an observation that Poisson encoding appears more robust than direct encoding, possibly because of its inherent randomness, and their approach is built on that idea. The authors say the method is a general framework that reduces to both Poisson encoding and direct encoding depending on the chosen scale. Because it works at the input stage, it can be combined with existing training-based defenses for additional gains. The paper reports experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 image datasets, which the authors present as evidence of its effectiveness.

The work is credited to the four named authors, and the listing does not identify their institutional affiliations or name any funding source beyond a general acknowledgment. The authors frame their contribution as highlighting the importance of input encoding for SNN adversarial robustness and as offering a new perspective for understanding and improving it. The articles do not describe any reaction from outside researchers, nor do they give code availability or details on how the method performs against specific attack types. Further detail on the findings would depend on the full paper, which the listing links as a PDF and HTML version.

Articles.Title: Controllable Stochastic Quantization Encoding for Adversarially Robust Spiking Neural Networks

stories.Headline: A strategic roadmap for an atomistic machine-learning ecosystem
stories.Summary:
A strategic roadmap for an atomistic machine-learning ecosystem was posted to arXiv as a preprint, with its first version submitted on 30 September 2026 and a revised second version on 13 October 2026. The paper is authored by Jörg Behler, Michele Ceriotti, Cecilia Clementi, Gábor Csányi and dozens of colleagues, 50 authors in all. It was listed under chemical physics, with materials science and machine learning as secondary subjects. The article carries a DOI assigned through DataCite and runs 28 pages with four figures.

The paper addresses how data-driven machine learning has become central to atomistic simulations of matter, building on physics-based methods that range from first-principles electronic-structure calculations to molecular dynamics. The authors say this integration raises conceptual and practical challenges, such as choosing between data-centric and physics-based approaches and adapting software to modern hardware accelerators and machine-learning libraries. Several community members met at CECAM in Lausanne in January 2026 to discuss algorithms, models, software and hardware infrastructure, and promising scientific applications. The paper summarizes those discussions and proposes long-term goals and concrete actions to build a sustainable and impactful atomistic machine-learning ecosystem.

The authors take responsibility for the roadmap as a collective community document, and the abstract describes its purpose as coordinating efforts across the field. In its own words, the paper aims to reflect on the current state of the art and open challenges as the field evolves quickly. The articles provided do not describe any formal adoption, funding commitments or timelines for implementing the proposed actions. Further steps, such as community responses or follow-up meetings, are not specified in the material available.

Articles.Title: A strategic roadmap for an atomistic machine-learning ecosystem

stories.Headline: Parameter symmetries determine representational geometry in overparameterized nonlinear networks
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on September 30, 2026, by Marvin Theiss, Lukas Braun, Andrew M. Saxe and Erin Grant examines how the internal representations of neural networks relate to the computations those networks perform. The paper, titled "Parameter symmetries determine representational geometry in overparameterized nonlinear networks," is listed under Machine Learning and is slated to appear at NeurIPS 2026. The authors note that researchers across machine learning, psychology and neuroscience often draw conclusions about biological and artificial systems from their representations. That practice assumes a meaningful link between representational geometry and computation, which the authors say is unclear for artificial networks. The article records that the paper runs 89 pages with nine figures.

The authors identify a key obstacle, which is that these networks admit parameter symmetries, meaning changes in parameterization that keep the function exactly the same while altering the geometry of the representations. According to the abstract, a broad class of these symmetries acts on representations through just three primitive feature transformations: addition, duplication and scaling. The authors use this feature-level view to produce a closed-form decomposition of representational geometry into essential and auxiliary components. The work shows how degeneracy in representational geometry can grow as networks become more overparameterized, even when their function stays fixed. The abstract further states that implementation-level selection rules can resolve this degeneracy, producing identifiable geometries in which features are weighted by their contribution to the network's function.

The authors present these findings as delineating when representations can support inferences about computation and when they cannot. The article does not describe any response from outside researchers, and it does not indicate any changes to existing practice beyond what the authors propose. The listed first version was submitted on September 30, 2026, with the page showing a publication date of October 24, 2026, and code is referenced through a link on the page. The articles do not say whether further revisions are planned or when the NeurIPS 2026 proceedings will be released.

Articles.Title: Parameter symmetries determine representational geometry in overparameterized nonlinear networks

stories.Headline: Preemptive LLM Unlearning against Forbidden Capability Acquisition via Gradient Sealing
stories.Summary:
A group of nine researchers, led by Kemou Li, posted a preprint to arXiv describing a method they call preemptive LLM unlearning, which aims to stop open-weight language models from acquiring forbidden capabilities during later fine-tuning. The first version of the paper was submitted on September 30, 2026, and a revised version followed on October 10, 2026. The paper was also indexed under a DOI on October 24, 2026. The authors say the work is the first focus on this setting, which differs from retrospective unlearning that removes capabilities already present in a fixed model.

The authors argue that releasing open-weight models creates legal and ethical risks, because users can fine-tune them to add illicit knowledge or to support hostile operations. Their proposed defense is a gradient-sealing principle that pushes relevant pre-activations into the negative region, where ReLU-family activations have zero or near-zero derivatives. This blocks the internal pathways through which forbidden-domain data would otherwise induce gradients. The paper reports that existing retrospective methods leave models open to such acquisition, even when current outputs appear suppressed.

According to the abstract, experiments across multiple LLM families showed stronger resistance to downstream acquisition than retrospective baselines. The authors present this as evidence that gradient sealing is an effective mechanism for pre-release protection. The article lists the authors' affiliations only indirectly through their names, and it does not describe any independent review or adoption of the method by model providers. The abstract does not say what the next steps for the research will be.

Articles.Title: Preemptive LLM Unlearning against Forbidden Capability Acquisition via Gradient Sealing

stories.Headline: Pretext: Defeating Malicious Skill Detection Frameworks for AI Agents
stories.Summary:
A preprint on arXiv, titled "Pretext: Defeating Malicious Skill Detection Frameworks for AI Agents," describes an attack against the scanners used to vet third-party "skills" for AI agents. The paper was first submitted on 30 September 2026 and revised on 8 October 2026, and it is authored by Tobias Kaiser and Aritra Dhar. It is listed as accepted at the AIWild workshop at NeurIPS 2026. The arXiv record shows a DOI and a formal entry in the cs.CR (Cryptography and Security) category, with cs.AI cross-listed.

The authors say that skills extend an agent's capabilities by injecting instructions and information into its context, and that agents such as OpenClaw and Claude Code use them widely. They note that prior work found malicious skills hosted on third-party marketplaces, which can give attackers direct influence over a victim's agent. The defense they examine scans skills before installation, combining deterministic static checks with an LLM-based semantic judge, as in NVIDIA's SkillSpector. The paper's central claim is that such defenses fail when the attacker knows the detector. The authors built a white-box LLM attacker, called Pretext, that iteratively rewrites skills to evade detection while still delivering the payload and doing the stated task.

According to the abstract, Pretext moves the payload out of code and into natural language, which leaves static analysis ineffective, and it frames the payload as part of the skill's legitimate purpose while splitting instructions across files so the LLM stage stays below its blocking threshold. The authors report testing across three open-source models and say Pretext reached up to 97 percent success against a frozen detector and up to 77 percent against a co-adaptive one. They conclude that the results reveal major gaps in current skill scanners. The articles do not describe any response from the scanner developers, any real-world exploitation, or any planned changes to the tools.

Articles.Title: Pretext: Defeating Malicious Skill Detection Frameworks for AI Agents

stories.Headline: Automated proximal femur CT radiomics identifies age- and sex-related radiomic patterns of bone structure: a nationwide multicohort validation study
stories.Summary:
A study published in BMC Medical Imaging on September 30, 2026, by a team led by Hanwen Cheng, Liwei Zhuang, Yiran Zhang, Yuyang Ran, Baoguo Jiang and Yuhui Kou tested whether an automated method could detect age- and sex-related changes in the proximal femur, the upper part of the thigh bone, using routine CT scans. The retrospective nationwide multicohort study included 4,152 participants, 1,947 of them men, with a median age of 59 years and an age range of 18 to 99. The researchers manually annotated a subset of femurs to train an nnU-Net-based segmentation model, then extracted radiomic features from the segmented volumes with PyRadiomics. The article reports that the automated segmentation reached a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.963 on the test set.

The machine learning models were built on a development cohort of 2,969 people and checked against an external validation cohort of 1,183 people. The best age model, a support vector regression, reached an R² of 0.50 on external validation, with a mean absolute error of 8.84 years and a root mean squared error of 11.32 years. For sex classification, support vector classification and XGBoost both reached an area under the curve of 0.94 externally, with support vector classification showing slightly higher accuracy and F1-score. The authors also found that a radiomics-derived age index correlated more strongly with femoral neck volumetric bone mineral density, measured by quantitative CT in the external cohort, than chronological age did (Spearman r of −0.546 versus −0.443), which they describe as support for the biological relevance of the patterns.

The authors say their results show that automated proximal femur CT radiomics can identify patterns linked to age- and sex-related bone structure changes across multiple nationwide datasets. They note that the association with bone density supports these patterns' biological meaning, but they call for further validation with clinical outcomes before any practical use. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee of Peking University People's Hospital and was registered as NCT07162168, with written consent waived because the data were retrospective and de-identified. Funding came from the Beijing Natural Science Foundation-Fengtai Joint Innovation Project, the National Natural Science Foundation of China Science Center Program, and the Shenzhen Medical Research Fund. The article does not describe any next steps beyond calling for further validation.

Articles.Title: Automated proximal femur CT radiomics identifies age- and sex-related radiomic patterns of bone structure: a nationwide multicohort validation study

stories.Headline: Dirac-Interconnected Neural Elements: Discovering Modularity in Physical Systems Without Reduction
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv on October 2, 2026, by Reiho Li, Razmik Arman Khosrovian, Takaharu Yaguchi, Hiroaki Yoshimura and Takashi Matsubara introduces a neural network model called Dirac-interconnected neural elements, or DINEs. The paper, which runs 29 pages with 3 figures and 8 tables, is listed under machine learning and was indexed by doi.org on October 24, 2026. The authors describe it as a way to model physical systems built from interconnected components. The article's own figures give no evidence of any wider release or institutional announcement beyond the paper itself.

The authors say existing methods either need the connections between components to be known in advance or reduce a system to an ordinary differential equation, which discards the algebraic constraints that the interconnections impose. DINEs instead represent a physical system as a differential-algebraic equation, with those constraints given by a Dirac structure in kernel representation. From data, the model identifies both the interconnection among components, as a Dirac structure, and the behavior of each component, as a neural network. The learned subsystems stay in unreduced form, so they can be isolated or combined into a new system without retraining, and the model can also handle partially observable systems. The paper reports experimental results on physical systems that the authors say existing methods cannot reach.

The article names the five authors and their paper but does not describe any affiliations, funding details beyond a partial acknowledgment, or public statements from them beyond the abstract. It also does not say whether code or the trained models have been released. The paper is an unreviewed preprint, and the excerpt does not indicate any peer review or follow-up work. The provided text does not say what the next steps for the research will be.

Articles.Title: Dirac-Interconnected Neural Elements: Discovering Modularity in Physical Systems Without Reduction

stories.Headline: Unveiling Representation Expansion: A New Lens on Out-of-Distribution Detection
stories.Summary:
The article is a research paper published in the International Journal of Computer Vision, dated September 30, 2026, in volume 134, article 455. Its authors propose a new way to improve out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, the task of recognizing inputs from classes a machine learning model was never trained on. The paper argues that existing methods look at a single input and therefore miss some overconfident OOD inputs, which get wrongly accepted as familiar data. The authors instead propose expanding the representation at two levels, data and model, to make the gap between OOD and in-distribution (ID) data easier to see.

At the data level, the authors apply different common corruptions to each input and compare the results with the original. They report a phenomenon they call confidence mutation, in which the model's confidence in OOD data drops sharply under corruption, while confidence in ID data stays higher because its semantic features hold up better. Based on this, they propose a scoring method called CoVer, which takes the average of the scores from the different input variants. At the model level, they feed inputs to several well-trained models with different backbones, which enlarges the difference between OOD and ID data, and they extend the framework to CoVer+ with multiple expansion levels.

The paper is authored by researchers whose names the article page lists, and the publication is handled by Springer Nature for the journal. The authors state that extensive experiments and analyses verify the effectiveness of the methods, and the article's data availability note says the experiments used public benchmarks, including ImageNet-1K, with OOD evaluation sets such as iNaturalist, SUN, Places and Textures. The article page does not describe any follow-up plans beyond the publication itself. Readers wanting the full results can access the paper through an institution or by purchasing the PDF, which the page lists at USD 39.95.

Articles.Title: Unveiling Representation Expansion: A New Lens on Out-of-Distribution Detection

stories.Headline: Effective Does Not Mean Useful: Conditional Functional Substitutability for Redundancy and Scaling in Transformers
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on September 30, 2026, by seven researchers led by Jiaheng Chen, introduces a method called Conditional Functional Substitutability, or CFS, for measuring redundancy inside Transformer neural networks. The paper's title, "Effective Does Not Mean Useful," reflects its central claim that a component can matter for performance yet still be swappable with others.
