stories.Headline: Same Bytes, Different Authority: Reserved-Token Representations in Chat-Template Prompt Injection
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on September 28, 2026, by six authors led by Yan Zhan, examines a weakness in how large language model agents handle injected instructions. The paper, titled "Same Bytes, Different Authority," studies forged chat-template markers that can reach a model either as a single reserved control token or as a run of ordinary subword tokens. The two forms decode to identical text, but the server performs tokenization, so the defender, not the attacker, determines which form the model sees. The authors report that the reserved form makes injected instructions markedly more effective.

Encoding the forged markers as subwords, while holding the text fixed and controlling for the extra tokens this adds, lowered attack success on the InjecAgent benchmark by 39 to 66 percentage points on three of four open-weight model families. The authors say the gap carries over to multi-turn agent tasks in AgentDojo. On Qwen3-8B the gap was 8 points, which the paper attributes to the model recognizing the forged turn from its text through reasoning; suppressing that reasoning block widened the gap to 50. The paper also finds that the authority resides in the single learned vector at the marker position, since averaging the marker's subword vectors does not reproduce it. The authors further report that instruction tuning strengthens the model's preference for reserved markers in every base and instruction-tuned pair they tested.

The paper points to a standard mitigation, a tokenizer option that encodes special tokens as ordinary subwords, and says it has limits. According to the authors, it applies only to tokens a configuration declares special, so in 33 of 67 distinct tokenizer configurations, covering 255 of the 400 most-downloaded chat models on Hugging Face, it leaves intact the tool-protocol tokens through which agents read untrusted tool output. The gap persists on that channel. The article describes the work as a preprint of 28 pages with six figures, with code and a dataset linked from the arXiv listing, and it does not describe any response from the model developers or any outside review.

Articles.Title: Same Bytes, Different Authority: Reserved-Token Representations in Chat-Template Prompt Injection

stories.Headline: Machine learning empowered compositional design of multiple rare-earth principal component disilicates
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Institute of Metal Research of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Shenyang, working with partners including the Liaoning Academy of Materials and AECC Shenyang Liming Aero-Engine Science and Technology, have published a study in the Journal of Advanced Ceramics on the design of rare-earth disilicates for environmental barrier coatings. The article was made available online on 28 September 2026, after being received on 22 June 2026 and revised on 24 September 2026. The materials in question are multi-rare-earth-principal-component disilicates, written as (nREx)2Si2O7, which are candidates for protecting components from high-temperature service conditions. The authors say that a key requirement for these coatings is that they keep a stable β or γ crystal phase under high temperatures, which is difficult because the phase structure changes with the properties of the rare-earth elements occupying the cation sites.

To address this, the team built a random forest machine learning model that sorts compositions into four phase categories: single-β, single-γ, single-δ or mixed δ+γ, and separate phase. The model identifies the average rare-earth 3+ cationic radius and the deviation of that radius as the most influential factors in predicting the phase. The authors tested the trained model by predicting phase compositions for (GdHoYbLu) and (NdHoYbLu) systems, and they supported these predictions with experimental characterization of representative compositions. High-throughput density functional theory calculations suggest that phase formation is linked to the low energy cost of accommodating configurational randomness in the multicomponent system, which shows up as a rapid convergence of the configurational entropy of mixing as excitation energy rises.

From this work the authors set out quantitative criteria for single-phase β and γ disilicates. For β polymorphs, the average radius should be below 0.885 Å, and for γ polymorphs it should fall between 0.885 Å and 0.900 Å. The deviation of the radius must also be sufficiently small, and its permitted upper bound rises monotonically with the average radius, reaching about 0.04 near the 0.885 Å and 0.900 Å thresholds. The authors describe the study as providing a paradigm for the targeted design of candidate environmental barrier coating materials. The article is open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license, and the journal's peer review status for it is listed as under review.

Articles.Title: Machine learning empowered compositional design of multiple rare-earth principal component disilicates

stories.Headline: Decoding natural scenes from patterned optogenetic responses in mouse visual cortex
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to bioRxiv on September 28, 2026, by a team led by Ya-tang Li and including Zhaofei Yu and Jian K. Liu, reports work on whether artificial stimulation of the mouse brain can carry the same visual information as natural sight. The researchers worked in awake mice and co-expressed a calcium indicator, GCaMP6s, and a red-shifted light-sensitive protein, rsChRmine-oScarlet, in the primary visual cortex, the region that first processes visual input. This setup let them convert frames from natural movies into patterns of optogenetic stimulation and compare the resulting brain activity with activity produced by real light exposure. The article is described as a proof of concept, and its data are not yet peer reviewed.

The central finding is that patterned optogenetic stimulation evoked cortical states that the authors describe as highly comparable to those driven by actual visual photostimulation. To test this, the team built a deep learning model called STAR, which uses spatial and temporal attention mechanisms, and used it to reconstruct the frames of natural movies from primary visual cortex signals under both forms of input. The authors conclude that complex sensory information can be both naturally encoded and synthetically injected into these circuits with high decoding fidelity. The article does not give specific numerical accuracy figures in the portion provided.

The authors present the work as groundwork for cortical visual prostheses and bidirectional brain-machine interfaces. They describe it as an empirical and computational proof of concept for intelligent, closed-loop biomimetic encoders, meaning systems that would translate visual input into stimulation patterns and adjust in real time. The authors declared no competing interests, and the research was supported by funders including China's STI 2030 Major Projects program, the National Natural Science Foundation of China, and the Natural Science Foundation of Beijing Municipality. The article itself does not describe next steps such as animal trials in other settings or human testing.

Articles.Title: Decoding natural scenes from patterned optogenetic responses in mouse visual cortex

stories.Headline: Certified Selective Automation of LLM Agent Evaluation
stories.Summary:
A research preprint posted to arXiv on September 28, 2026, by Chengguang Gan and three co-authors, titled "Certified Selective Automation of LLM Agent Evaluation," asks how much of the evaluation of large language model agents an automatic judge can take over while guaranteeing a bounded error rate. The authors note that agent evaluation still usually ends with a human reading agent trajectories, since automatic judges come with no guarantee of how often they are wrong. The paper is listed under Computation and Language and carries the arXiv identifier 2609.34320, with a DOI assigned through DataCite. The study was submitted in its first version on September 28, 2026, and the article metadata shows a timestamp of October 24, 2026.

The authors argue that existing methods can overstate how much is safe to automate, because many agents attempt the same tasks and their trajectories arrive in correlated clusters. A naive certificate could claim 98 percent automation while its realized error exceeded the budget in 17.5 percent of task resamples. To address this, they introduce a task-level bootstrap certificate that they say holds in every regime tested while matching the naive certificate's coverage, and they report that finite-sample cluster-valid alternatives certify nothing at realistic task counts. Under this certificate, a 4-billion-parameter judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reject-weighted GRPO certifies between 0.30 and 0.59 of evaluation on tool-use and web corpora at an error budget of alpha equals 0.1. The authors state that this judge is the only one among strongly elicited frontier models that certifies on both headline corpora.

The paper's authors are Chengguang Gan, Yunhao Liang, Qinghao Zhang and Shiwen Ni, and the work is presented as their own research. According to the abstract, they report that certified coverage can be predicted before training from base rate and discrimination alone, with a leave-one-corpus-out R-squared of 0.96. They also describe the certificate as doubling as a self-training filter, with pseudo-labels harvested inside certified regions showing contamination between 0.000 and 0.041 across six harvests. This, they say, lets a judge enter an unseen domain at in-domain strength with zero target training labels. The articles do not describe any independent review or external reaction to these claims.

Articles.Title: Certified Selective Automation of LLM Agent Evaluation

stories.Headline: When Words Fall Short: Iterative Synergy Between Verbalized Reasoning and Hidden Features for LLM Confidence Estimation
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on September 28, 2026, by Yekun Xu and five co-authors presents a method for estimating how confident large language models are in their answers. The paper, titled "When Words Fall Short," challenges the view that asking a model to verbalize its confidence works better than using a separate confidence estimator. The authors report that a dedicated estimator can substantially outperform verbalized confidence, which they take to mean that a model's internal representations hold richer confidence signals than its own stated reports reveal. Their empirical study rests on this finding. On that basis, the authors propose a framework they call Iterative Policy-Estimator Training, or IPoET.

The method alternates between optimizing the model's policy and updating the estimator, feeding the estimator's confidence feedback into policy learning and refreshing the estimator on new policy rollouts. The authors say this lets the approach exploit richer hidden features while adapting to the changing policy distribution. The article does not give specific figures for the gains beyond describing the results as consistent improvements. The results, according to the abstract, were tested across diverse datasets and on Qwen and Llama backbone models. IPoET consistently outperformed both estimator-based and verbalization-based baselines on in-domain tasks.

On out-of-domain metrics, the authors report superior or comparable results. The paper is listed under the Computation and Language category, and the abstract does not name a funder or a publishing venue beyond arXiv. The work sits within a broader effort to make large language models more trustworthy by knowing when their answers may be wrong. The article provides no information on next steps, peer review, or any adoption by developers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: When Words Fall Short: Iterative Synergy Between Verbalized Reasoning and Hidden Features for LLM Confidence Estimation

stories.Headline: As news traffic collapses, Nevada outlet puts AI to work without handing over editorial control
stories.Summary:
Nevada News & Views, a smaller outlet in Nevada, has said it is using artificial intelligence to help its reporters work faster while keeping human journalists in charge of sourcing, judgement and final copy. The move comes as major publishers face a steep fall in traffic. According to Similarweb data reported by Axios, U.S. traffic to around 100 major news sites dropped sharply in July compared with the previous year. Media Copilot separately reported that traffic to the top 50 US news websites fell by 37% between July 2024 and July 2026, and that generative AI still accounted for only a small share of visits.

The collapse is linked to changes in how people find information, since search engines now answer more questions on the results page and AI assistants can offer quick summaries that reduce clicks to publisher sites. The articles describe a familiar squeeze of fewer clicks, weaker advertising revenue and newsroom cutbacks that can reduce the depth and pace of coverage. Against that background, the outlet presents AI as a research aid that sifts public records, checks figures and speeds up document-heavy work. It insists that reporters still chase leads, question filings and decide what matters.

A survey by the Associated Press found that most journalists and newsroom leaders have used generative AI in some form, even as they call for clearer rules, training and oversight. The outlet points to its coverage of Republican congressional candidate David Flippo as an example of this approach in practice. It says senior political writer Brittany Sheehan used federal election filings, supported by AI-assisted research, to examine campaign loans and donor refunds, including repeated contributions from some of the same names. The publication argues that such tools speed up the routine parts of reporting without replacing human verification.

The articles do not describe any penalty, regulation or formal change tied to this coverage. Industry groups and trade outlets describe a broader shift from testing to wider deployment of AI across newsroom production and audience strategy, including faster service journalism and routine updates. Critics continue to warn that speed alone cannot substitute for judgement, verification and trust. The tension now runs between legacy brands losing traffic and leaner outlets trying to use the same technology to work efficiently and build direct readership.

Articles.Title: As news traffic collapses, Nevada outlet puts AI to work without handing over editorial control

stories.Headline: ReSight-SMC: Two-Stage Power Sampling via Island SMC with Visual Scouts
stories.Summary:
A new arXiv preprint, titled "ReSight-SMC: Two-Stage Power Sampling via Island SMC with Visual Scouts," was submitted on September 28, 2026, by Yaowen Zhang, Xiangyu Qiu, Junyi Hu, Zhi Lu, Wenwen Tian, Aoqin Wang, Junhai Luo, and Zhenming Peng. The paper, filed under computer vision and pattern recognition, describes a training-free method for improving reasoning in large vision-language models. The authors say the method builds on a power sampling approach that has already been used to elicit reasoning from text-only language models, and that this approach had not been widely explored for vision-language models. The preprint was listed on the arXiv site with a timestamp of October 24, 2026.

The authors transfer an existing method called Power-SMC to vision-language decoding by defining a target that depends on both the image and the prompt. They identify two weaknesses in that direct transfer: global resampling can collapse the lineages of candidate trajectories, and sequence-level sharpening makes different reasoning paths compete even when they reach the same answer. To address these, they propose ReSight-SMC, a verifier-free, two-stage sampler. In the first stage, ancestry-isolated particle groups keep separate trajectory families independent, while a bounded set of visual scouts directs attention toward image regions relevant to each partial response and discourages redundant overlap. In the second stage, the method combines the importance weight of all trajectories that give the same canonical answer, sharpens that answer distribution, and samples an answer along with a supporting trajectory.

According to the abstract, the authors tested ReSight-SMC on four vision-language model backbones and five benchmarks, and it achieved stronger overall performance than Power-SMC on both reasoning and perception benchmark groups. The authors also report that, without any post-training, the method remains competitive overall with backbone-matched models that were trained using reinforcement learning. The paper has not been peer reviewed, and the abstract does not state specific benchmark scores. The authors have posted an HTML and PDF version along with a TeX source, and the preprint is a first version, so the abstract does not describe any follow-up plans.

Articles.Title: ReSight-SMC: Two-Stage Power Sampling via Island SMC with Visual Scouts

stories.Headline: Composable Decoding on the Probability Simplex: Theory and Implementation
stories.Summary:
Researchers Xiaotong Ji, Ahmed Khaled Khamis, Rasul Tutunov, Matthieu Zimmer and Haitham Bou-Ammar posted a paper to arXiv on 28 September 2026 describing a new way to think about decoding for large language models. Decoding, the process that picks each next token a model outputs, has usually been treated as a set of separate sampling strategies with little theory tying them together. The authors instead frame decoding as an optimisation problem over next-token distributions on the probability simplex, weighing the model's expected score against a regularisation term under support constraints. The paper was first submitted as version 1 and carries a DOI issued through DataCite.

The framing matters because it lets familiar decoding methods be recovered by choosing particular regularisers and support constraints, and it lets new decoders be built by combining distributional preferences inside one optimisation problem. According to the abstract, this needs no external rewards, no learned critics and no updates to model parameters. The authors also introduce CompoSimplex, a library offering configurable support rules, regularisation primitives and simplex solvers for building and evaluating these compositional decoders. They tested standard samplers, individual regularisers and combinations across several models and reasoning tasks.

The authors state that their results show compositions can reach trade-offs between single-sample quality, multi-sample quality and diversity that no single decoding objective achieves on its own. The abstract gives no figures for these gains, and the listed authors are the only people the article names as responsible for the work. The paper is listed under Machine Learning (cs.LG) and Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) on arXiv, and the record shows no peer review or publication in a journal or conference beyond that posting. The articles do not describe any next steps for the work.

Articles.Title: Composable Decoding on the Probability Simplex: Theory and Implementation

stories.Headline: Distillation Defenses Easily Break After Reinforcement Learning
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv on September 28, 2026, by Shidan Javaheri, Alexander Panfilov, Oliver Britton, Yarin Gal, and Yonatan Gideoni, argues that certain defenses against distillation attacks fail once attackers add reinforcement learning. Distillation attacks copy the reasoning abilities of closed-source large language models by collecting large volumes of reasoning traces from a frontier model and training another model on them. The authors note that existing defenses are usually tested only right after distillation, which assumes attackers stop there. The article describing the work appeared on doi.org on October 24, 2026.

The authors say a more realistic threat model should include further training with reinforcement learning after distillation. In their account, some defenses that look effective after distillation can be broken by that additional step, which gives a false sense of security. They also say reinforcement learning makes a distillation attack more likely to succeed. They show that simple attacks, using data that is easily obtained from current APIs, can steal reasoning capabilities and produce gains comparable to more sophisticated attacks that extract full hidden traces. The paper concludes that any defense leaking enough information to reconstruct approximate reasoning traces is likely ineffective.

The responsibility for the findings rests with the five named authors, who are affiliated with research work on machine learning and security, and the paper is categorized under machine learning, artificial intelligence, and cryptography and security. The abstract does not name any company or model whose defenses were broken, and it does not describe any response from API providers. The authors state that they discuss broader implications and suggest batch-level distillation defenses as a possibly more effective approach. The articles do not say whether those batch-level defenses have been tested or adopted.

Articles.Title: Distillation Defenses Easily Break After Reinforcement Learning

stories.Headline: Learning Multimodal Embeddings with Evidence-Aligned Readout
stories.Summary:
Researchers Zirong Chen and ten co-authors posted a paper on arXiv on September 27, 2026, describing a method called EviAlign for learning multimodal embeddings. The work addresses a gap in how multimodal large language models use the evidence they generate: producing useful evidence does not by itself determine where that evidence should be read for a retrieval embedding. The authors ask whether the semantic organization of that evidence can also specify where representations are read, and they answer it with a system built on a shared multimodal large language model. The paper was indexed under the computer vision category, with information retrieval as a secondary subject.

EviAlign couples Semantic Evidence Generation with Boundary Readout, organizing evidence into five semantic units. It reads the contextualized state at each unit boundary and combines those states into a single normalized embedding. Generation and contrastive retrieval objectives train this structure jointly. In a controlled study comparing consistent and permuted evidence organization across three readout strategies, the advantage of consistent semantic organization grew from 0.65 points at length-based training positions to 2.39 points at evidence boundaries, a 1.74-point co-design interaction. Across 12 MMEB retrieval tasks, the method reached an average Recall@1 of 76.9 using 500K training pairs while keeping single-vector indexing and scoring.

The paper's authors are the ones responsible for the work, and they report that with the same trailing readout, semantic evidence and free-form chain-of-thought produced nearly identical retrieval performance. They conclude that evidence organization alone does not explain the full gain, and that the placement of the readout matters alongside it. The authors describe the results as coming from a controlled comparison and a benchmark evaluation. The articles do not name any outside reviewers, funders beyond a partial note, or a publishing venue, and the preprint is listed as version 1 with no later revisions shown. The articles do not say whether code or model weights have been released, nor do they indicate any independent replication of the reported figures.

Articles.Title: Learning Multimodal Embeddings with Evidence-Aligned Readout

stories.Headline: When Consent Outlives Context: Residual Authority Replay in Long-Lived Agents
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on 27 September 2026 by six researchers, led by Zhihao Zhang, describes a security weakness in long-lived AI agents that keep user approvals active across tasks and sessions. The paper, titled "When Consent Outlives Context," reports that a user's approval for a sensitive action, granted for one specific task, can persist after the circumstances that justified it have ended. The authors show that this leftover authority can be reused later without asking the user again. The work was indexed under a DOI and classified in artificial intelligence, and the arXiv listing shows it as a single version, v1.

The authors describe an attack in which a bad actor first identifies the authority needed to carry out a target sensitive action, then induces harmless-looking interactions that legitimately grant that authority, and finally replays the leftover authority during an adversarial run. Testing covered 508 AgentDojo attack cases across six LLM families using production-derived authorization rules. Compared with a fresh authorization state, residual authority raised the attack success rate by as much as 35.1 percentage points. In live context-rebinding attacks on 55 Terminal-Bench cases across three real-world production coding agents, the increase averaged 24.9 percentage points.

The paper's central claim is that persistent authorization does not match the contextual nature of user consent, and it implies that agent developers need to rethink how approvals are scoped and expired. The listing does not name any company or product owner responding to the findings, and it does not mention any remediation, patch, or formal response from the agent vendors involved. The abstract also does not say whether the live coding agents were disclosed to their makers before publication. Beyond the preprint itself, the available information does not describe any follow-up steps or peer review status.

Articles.Title: When Consent Outlives Context: Residual Authority Replay in Long-Lived Agents

stories.Headline: How Synthetic Labels Improve Conformal Prediction: A Perspective on Conditional Coverage
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on September 27, 2026, by Qianyi Chen and Bo Li, titled "How Synthetic Labels Improve Conformal Prediction: A Perspective on Conditional Coverage," reports a method for improving uncertainty estimates when trusted labeled data is scarce. Conformal prediction gives finite-sample marginal coverage without distributional assumptions, but its calibration step may not contain enough examples to learn how uncertainty changes across different inputs. The authors ask whether cheaply obtained synthetic labels, produced by domain models or general-purpose language models, can help when only a small trusted sample exists. They answer that question with a proposed approach they call prediction-powered quantile learning.

The method works in three steps: a pool of synthetic-labeled data estimates pinball risk, paired trusted and synthetic outcomes correct the bias in that estimate, and an independent trusted split carries out the final conformalization. The authors show that conditional-coverage error corresponds to the functional gradient of pinball risk over scalar corrections, and that the Hessian removes global shifts and weights remaining shape error by boundary density. Combining this geometry with prediction-powered learning yields what they describe as a three-resource expansion and a rule for judging when synthetic labels are worth their cost. The paper says the approach is tested across eight regression benchmarks. The abstract does not state exact coverage figures or set sizes.

According to the abstract, the results show substantially better downstream conditional coverage while marginal validity is preserved and the prediction sets become more compact. A separate human-rating study finds that labels from external language models produce similar gains and reveals a tradeoff between label quality, label quantity, and cost. The authors are the sole source of these claims, and the article is a preprint that has not been described as peer reviewed. The abstract does not describe any next steps, such as publication, code release, or follow-up work, beyond the listed PDF and HTML versions and the arXiv DOI.

Articles.Title: How Synthetic Labels Improve Conformal Prediction: A Perspective on Conditional Coverage

stories.Headline: EPFL Machine Learning for Biomedicine Lab Opens Research Opportunities for Postdoctoral Fellows, PhD Students and Interns in Switzerland (Fully Funded)
stories.Summary:
The Machine Learning for Biomedicine Lab at EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, has opened applications for postdoctoral fellows, PhD students, summer research interns, and bachelor's and master's students. The announcement was published on 25 October 2026 by Global South Opportunities. The lab works on artificial intelligence methods that help researchers understand biological systems and make new scientific discoveries from complex biological data. Applicants can pursue research projects or thesis work, depending on their qualifications and interests.

Postdoctoral candidates should hold, or be close to completing, a PhD in computer science, computational biology, statistics, applied mathematics, or a closely related field. Those applying must email a CV with a publication list, a one-to-two-page research statement, the names and contact details of two references, and a preferred start date to mlbio.postdoc@epfl.ch, using the subject line "Postdoctoral application." Prior experience with biomedical data is preferred but not required for candidates with a strong AI background. PhD applicants must apply through EPFL's doctoral programmes in computer and communication sciences or computational and quantitative biology, where admission is managed centrally. Bachelor's and master's students may apply for research projects through a designated form, and EPFL master's students can contact the lab directly about theses.

The lab's research areas include single-cell foundation models, multimodal learning, generative models of biology, cell engineering, and agentic AI for scientific discovery. Lab leaders named in the listings include Yist Yu, Siba Smarak Panigrahi, and Yulun Jiang, each a contact for a specific student project. The lab also has access to substantial GPU computing resources through the Swiss AI Initiative and collaborates with programmes such as the CIFAR Multiscale Human Program. The listed project descriptions were last updated on 15 November 2025, so applicants must confirm that projects remain open for the relevant period.

The announcement does not give a universal application deadline, salary, stipend, or funding package, and the article notes that these vary by programme and opportunity. Candidates are advised to check the official application pages and the lab's Join Us page before applying. The article also points to external fellowships such as the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral Fellowships and the EPFL AI Center Postdoctoral Fellowship. The source states that Global South Opportunities does not own or verify the opportunities it shares.

Articles.Title: EPFL Machine Learning for Biomedicine Lab Opens Research Opportunities for Postdoctoral Fellows, PhD Students and Interns in Switzerland (Fully Funded)

stories.Headline: ZeroGAR: Benchmarking the Adversarial Robustness of Zero-Shot Graph Models
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted to arXiv on September 27, 2026, by Zhongjian Zhang and six co-authors introduces ZeroGAR, a benchmark for testing how well zero-shot graph models hold up against adversarial manipulation. Zero-shot graph models learn knowledge from source graphs and apply it directly to unseen target graphs without any further adaptation. The authors note that these models have grown in popularity, yet they are mostly evaluated on clean graphs, while earlier robustness benchmarks focused on supervised settings. The paper was listed under Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence, and its DOI was shown as pending registration on the arXiv page.

ZeroGAR evaluates 13 representative zero-shot graph models drawn from three paradigms, using 8 graph datasets across 4 domains. The tests cover both in-domain and cross-domain transfer and apply structural, textual, and node injection attacks at multiple perturbation budgets. The benchmark also checks whether existing graph defenses still work when a model is applied in a zero-shot setting. The authors describe the work as the first systematic benchmark of this kind for zero-shot graph models. Their stated aim is to support rapid and equitable evaluation and to encourage further research into the security of these models.

According to the paper, the experiments show that strong clean zero-shot performance does not guarantee adversarial robustness. The authors report that graph neural network based methods are especially vulnerable to structural and node injection attacks, while methods built on large language models are more vulnerable to textual attacks. They also say that stronger language model backbones bring a trade-off between structural and textual robustness. Finally, they find that existing graph defense methods do not consistently improve zero-shot robustness and may reduce clean performance. The article does not describe any response from outside researchers or organizations, and it does not say what follow-up work the authors plan.

Articles.Title: ZeroGAR: Benchmarking the Adversarial Robustness of Zero-Shot Graph Models

stories.Headline: Progressive-View On-Policy Distillation for Regional-to-Global Transfer in Multimodal LLMs
stories.Summary:
A new arXiv preprint, posted on September 26, 2026 by Shanfeng Huang, Zhou Fang, Song Xiao and Hai Du, describes a training method called progressive-view on-policy distillation, or PVD, for multimodal large language models. The work addresses regional-to-global distillation, in which a teacher model that sees a cropped part of an image guides a student model that must understand the full image. The authors say the central problem is carrying the teacher's advantage from cropped views over to the student's full-image inference. The paper was listed on doi.org with a timestamp of October 24, 2026, and its DOI is still marked as pending registration.

The method works in stages rather than all at once. It moves the student's view distribution from the crop toward the full image through an intermediate aspect-preserving padded crop, which keeps regional content while matching the full image's visual-token grid. Across stages, the mixture gives increasing probability to the full image. A lightweight regional-advantage weighting then reallocates token-level supervision based on the gap between the crop-conditioned teacher's and the student's log-probabilities, applying mild reweighting when the gap is small and emphasizing tokens when it widens. The authors interpret this schedule through a Jensen-Shannon metric decomposition as a shift from matched-input imitation toward the deployment objective.

The authors report results across benchmarks covering perception, visual mathematics and general multimodal question answering. Their full variant, PVD-full, reaches an average accuracy of 77.51 over three seeds, which they say improves on the reward-free distillation baseline by 2.01 points and on its reward-matched variant by 1.00 point. In the reward-free setting, the PVD-distill variant still gains 1.16 points. The paper lists Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence as its subject areas, and the version posted is v1. The articles do not describe any follow-up work or peer review beyond this preprint.

Articles.Title: Progressive-View On-Policy Distillation for Regional-to-Global Transfer in Multimodal LLMs

stories.Headline: MM-OPD: Towards One More Bottleneck Between Perception and Reasoning
stories.Summary:
A preprint describing a new training method, titled "MM-OPD: Towards One More Bottleneck Between Perception and Reasoning," was posted to arXiv on September 26, 2026, under identifier 2609.32690. Its nine authors, led by Jintao Tong, report that multimodal large language models perform better when images are replaced with captions or code-based symbolic descriptions, even though the images seem to carry more information. The authors measured performance gains of 10.2% to 23.6% across model scales and datasets, and they call this difference the Symbolic Visual Gap. The paper was listed under computer vision and artificial intelligence categories and carries a DOI issued through DataCite.

According to the abstract, the authors' experiments found that image-input models do contain the correct visual evidence in their reasoning traces, but they attend to it less than symbolic-input models do. They conclude that a separate bottleneck exists between perception and reasoning, located in selecting perceived visual information as appropriate evidence for later reasoning. To address it, they propose MM-OPD, a multimodal on-policy self-distillation framework. The method uses symbolic-conditioned behavior as a source of guidance, transferring it to the image-conditioned model through residual token-level targets so that it moves toward correct visual evidence. The symbolic views can be generated at scale without manually labeled evidence.

The abstract reports that MM-OPD improves a range of multimodal abilities, including visual perception, chart and document understanding, mathematical reasoning, and general visual question answering. The authors state these results hold across benchmarks and model scales. The submission history shows a single version, v1, of 5,739 KB, and the paper links to a project page. The abstract does not describe any further publication or peer review steps, so the paper's status beyond this preprint is not stated in the source material.

Articles.Title: MM-OPD: Towards One More Bottleneck Between Perception and Reasoning

stories.Headline: Function Over Form: Distributional Orthogonalization in Mixture-of-Experts with Replica Expert Mechanism
stories.Summary:
On September 26, 2026, researchers Jinfan He, Yunzhuo Liu, Kai Zhang, Weidong Han, and two other authors posted a paper on arXiv describing a new training method for mixture-of-experts language models. The paper, titled "Function Over Form: Distributional Orthogonalization in Mixture-of-Experts with Replica Expert Mechanism," was listed under artificial intelligence and was marked as accepted to COLM 2026. The authors wrote that the method addresses two problems that waste model capacity: expert collapse and representation redundancy. They described the work as an early version of the paper, first submitted that same day.

The authors propose an auxiliary regularization they call the Distributional Orthogonalization Loss, or DO-loss, which shifts attention from static weight diversity to how experts are actually used during routing. Each expert's history of token assignments is represented as a high-dimensional binary load signature, and the loss penalizes overlap between these signatures. The paper also introduces a Replica Expert Mechanism, or REM, which balances load in two stages: adjusting where replica experts are placed across a global batch and dispatching tokens in real time within each micro-batch. According to the abstract, the method outperformed the routing algorithms tested on downstream tasks for both a 4.8BA0.5B model and a 30BA3B model, while keeping training efficiency comparable.

The abstract does not name any organization that funded or sponsored the work, and the listing shows only the authors and their endorsers. The paper frames its contribution as an improvement to how mixture-of-experts models are scaled, since those architectures separate active computation from total parameter count. The articles provided do not say whether the results have been independently reproduced or how the method compares with routing approaches beyond those tested. Nothing in the materials indicates further announcements, releases of code, or follow-up work.

Articles.Title: Function Over Form: Distributional Orthogonalization in Mixture-of-Experts with Replica Expert Mechanism

stories.Headline: Radiomic analysis of MR cytometry mappings for breast tumor diagnosis
stories.Summary:
A research team from Tsinghua University, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region People's Hospital, Qinghai University Affiliated Hospital, Fudan University Cancer Center and other institutions has published a prospective study on using radiomics to improve how MR cytometry, a non-invasive MRI-based method, distinguishes benign from malignant breast lesions. The study enrolled 221 patients with pathologically confirmed breast lesions from two centers, 47 with benign lesions and 174 with malignant ones. All patients were scanned on a 3T MRI using pulsed gradient spin-echo and oscillating gradient spin-echo sequences, and radiologists manually outlined the lesions. The article was published online on September 26, 2026, in BMC Medical Imaging, and it was received June 3, 2026 and accepted September 21, 2026.

The researchers compared two approaches: models built on mean values of intratumoral parameters, which is the current standard, and models that also use radiomic features extracted from multiple parameter maps to capture tumor heterogeneity. Six machine learning models were trained with five-fold cross-validation on a training cohort and then tested on an external cohort. On the training set, radiomics-based models outperformed mean-value models in every category, with the combined ADC and MR cytometry approach reaching a mean AUC of 0.935 against 0.879. On the external test set, the combination reached 0.901 against 0.841, and the logistic regression model achieved the highest single AUC at 0.943. The authors state that MR cytometry adds clinical value beyond conventional apparent diffusion coefficient measurements, and that combining the two further improves diagnosis.

The study was approved by the institutional review board of Tsinghua University and the ethics committee of Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center, and all patients gave written informed consent. The authors declare no competing interests and receive funding from China's National Natural Science Foundation and China Postdoctoral Science Foundation. The authors conclude that radiomics can improve machine learning diagnostic performance over mean-value analysis, and that MR cytometry is a promising non-invasive alternative that reflects intratumoral heterogeneity better than limited biopsy sampling. The article does not describe any planned clinical rollout or next steps beyond the reported findings.

Articles.Title: Radiomic analysis of MR cytometry mappings for breast tumor diagnosis

stories.Headline: G$^2$PTQ: Improving LLM Post-Training Quantization with Generalized Gradient Compensation
stories.Summary:
Researchers Ruikang Liu and ten co-authors posted a preprint on arXiv describing G$^2$PTQ, a new method for post-training quantization of large language models. The paper was submitted on September 25, 2026, and the listed DOI date is October 24, 2026. The work is categorized under Computation and Language and Artificial Intelligence. Its aim is to shrink the memory and computing demands of large language models without retraining them.

The authors say existing GPTQ-based methods have two complementary weaknesses. Methods with local, layer-wise objectives lack global supervision, while methods with global objectives fix their Hessian estimates at the start and ignore first-order gradients, so their guidance becomes stale as quantization proceeds. G$^2$PTQ combines first- and second-order information under a globally supervised, block-wise objective. Before quantizing each Transformer block, it refreshes gradient and Hessian estimates, and it adds a trust-region scaling mechanism that bounds the gradient step to prevent exploding weight updates. The authors also describe efficient implementations for block-wise Hessian approximation and exact gradient compensation.

The abstract reports that experiments on various model families and bit-widths show G$^2$PTQ aligns better with the full-precision model than state-of-the-art baselines. The authors have made the code publicly available. The paper lists the work as a version 1 submission, and the articles do not describe any peer review, journal acceptance, or further revisions. The funding acknowledgments are present on the page but their details are not given in the text provided.

Articles.Title: G$^2$PTQ: Improving LLM Post-Training Quantization with Generalized Gradient Compensation

stories.Headline: ConsultMind:Towards Automated Diagnostic Consultation via Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning
stories.Summary:
On September 25, 2026, a team of twelve researchers led by Xiao Sun posted a preprint on arXiv titled "ConsultMind: Towards Automated Diagnostic Consultation via Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning." The paper describes a way to automate the back-and-forth questioning a clinician uses to reach a diagnosis. The authors frame this as an online, sequential decision process in which evidence accumulates through patient interaction until a diagnosis is sufficiently supported. The work was posted to the cs.AI section of the site and has not, according to the listing, been peer reviewed.

The paper introduces two pieces. The first, AutoDisym, is a pipeline that combines diagnostic knowledge with diagnosis-labeled clinical narratives to build a Disorder-Symptom Bayesian Network, which the authors call a DSBN. The second, ConsultMind, updates the probability of each disorder after every patient response and uses the remaining uncertainty to decide what to ask next and when to make a diagnosis. The authors tested the methods across psychiatry, respiratory medicine, fever clinics, and three public datasets. They report macro-averaged F1 scores of 81.37 for canonical symptoms and 72.19 for manifestations using GPT-5.6-Sol.

According to the abstract, ConsultMind raised Top-1 diagnostic accuracy by up to 22.15 percentage points and Top-3 accuracy by up to 37.89 percentage points. The authors also say physician evaluation found better ranking explanations, differential diagnoses, and diagnosis rationales across language models of different sizes. The paper is credited to Xiao Sun, Yuming Yang, Yun Chen, Jiang Zhong, Junnan Zhu, Xinyi Jiang, Haoyang Zeng, Ruirui Chen, Yining Wang, Xinyu Zhou, Rong Tang, and Kaiwen Wei. The authors describe their approach as promising for automatic diagnostic consultation, though the articles provide no clinical deployment data.

Articles.Title: ConsultMind:Towards Automated Diagnostic Consultation via Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning

stories.Headline: Bit-sliced quantization for robust memristor-based compute-in-memory
stories.Summary:
Researchers have published a paper describing bit-sliced quantization (BSQ), a framework for running AI models on memristor-based compute-in-memory hardware. The article appeared on October 24, 2026, in the journal npj Unconventional Computing. The work addresses a problem with analog memristor arrays, which offer limited conductance resolution and random device fluctuations that degrade accuracy when standard quantization is applied directly. The authors say BSQ combines distribution-aware non-uniform post-training quantization, hardware-aligned noise injection, and mapping of weights onto stable binary device states. The framework stores each weight group as a small number of binary slices paired with learned scaling coefficients, which are then combined during computation to recover higher precision.

Because it is applied after training, the method avoids costly retraining of the model. The noise used in testing is calibrated from measured device and array statistics, so the robustness results are meant to reflect realistic hardware conditions rather than abstract assumptions. The authors state that the model architecture itself remains unchanged. The authors report accuracy gains under programming noise compared with conventional quantization. They say BSQ improves accuracy by 16.0 percent on 2-bit handwritten digit classification, by 0.5 percent on 3-bit SST-2 sentiment classification, and by as much as 20.08 percent on 3-bit large language model reasoning benchmarks.

The paper presents these tasks as increasing in complexity, with the language model test serving as a check on scalability. The authors conclude that aligning quantization with device physics matters for dependable analog inference. The study is framed as a step toward energy-efficient edge AI on memristor hardware, where moving data between memory and processors is a major source of power use. The articles do not describe any commercial deployment, hardware demonstration beyond the calibration statistics, or next steps the authors plan to take.

Articles.Title: Bit-sliced quantization for robust memristor-based compute-in-memory

stories.Headline: Causal-chain-aligned lightweight LLM for interpretable early sepsis warning
stories.Summary:
A research team from the Chongqing Institute of Green and Intelligent Technology, Southwest Hospital of the Army Medical University and the Chongqing Perioperative Medical Big Data Laboratory has published a study describing a new early warning system for sepsis, a life-threatening response to infection. The paper appeared in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making, with an online publication date of 25 September 2026, and its authors are Yuwen Chen, Yang Yang, Peng Wang and Bin Yi. The researchers say sepsis is hard to catch early because its symptoms are nonspecific, and that existing machine learning tools often have many missing data points and are difficult to interpret. The authors describe their approach as a way to pair clinical cause-and-effect relationships with a language model.

The framework converts clinical time-series data into plain-language descriptions using predefined rules, then builds a structural causal model to capture the timing and cause-and-effect links among clinical variables. These causal chains are fed into chain-of-thought prompts that guide a lightweight 7-billion-parameter language model, which was adjusted using Low-Rank Adaptation for early sepsis risk assessment. The study reports that the model reached an area under the curve of 0.8118 on the PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2019 dataset and 0.7780 on the MIMIC-IV dataset. According to the article, these results beat traditional machine learning baselines and larger language models, and the authors also report clearer causal reasoning and closer agreement with expert clinical reasoning.

The article lists Yuwen Chen and Bin Yi as corresponding authors. It states that the study used only publicly available, de-identified datasets, so no institutional review board approval or informed consent was needed, and it reports no competing interests. The work was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Chongqing Municipal Natural Science Foundation, the Chongqing Technology Innovation and Application Development Program, and the Southwest Hospital Cultivation Project of Clinical Innovative Technologies. The authors conclude that the approach could support real-time clinical decision making in critical care, though the article describes this as a potential solution rather than a deployed one.

Articles.Title: Causal-chain-aligned lightweight LLM for interpretable early sepsis warning

stories.Headline: AI for Mathematics: Progress, Challenges, and Prospects
stories.Summary:
The article is an academic review titled "AI for Mathematics: Progress, Challenges, and Prospects," published online on October 24, 2026, with authors Haocheng Ju of Peking University's School of Mathematical Sciences and Bin Dong of several Peking University and affiliated research centers. It appears in the SuperIntelligence journal, volume 3, issue 3, and it surveys the field of AI for Mathematics, which uses machine learning to tackle mathematical problems that early symbolic systems could not handle. The review explains that mid-twentieth-century symbolic methods automated formal logic but struggled because the search space grew too large to manage. The authors argue that data-driven approaches have revitalized the field, and they describe mathematics as a demanding testbed for building stronger general reasoning in AI systems.

The review sorts existing work into two complementary directions. The first is problem-specific modeling, which designs specialized architectures for particular mathematical tasks, and the second is general-purpose modeling, which focuses on foundation models able to handle broader reasoning, retrieval and exploratory workflows. The authors say they will discuss key challenges and prospects, and they call for AI systems that go beyond checking formal correctness to help discover meaningful results and unified theories. Their stated view is that the real value of a proof lies in the insights and tools it offers the wider mathematical community. The reference list, which runs to dozens of entries, cites work on theorem proving in systems such as Lean, automated geometry, machine learning applied to knot theory and Calabi-Yau manifolds, and large language models trained on mathematics.

The authors are researchers at Peking University, and the review presents its positions as their own assessment of the field rather than as a policy or regulatory matter. The articles provided do not describe any specific deadline, requirement or formal change arising from the review, and they do not report on any follow-up plans beyond the review's own call for future systems. Because the document is a scholarly survey, its impact is expected to be felt through how researchers in the field frame future work, not through any mandated action. The provided material gives no further information on subsequent developments.

Articles.Title: AI for Mathematics: Progress, Challenges, and Prospects

stories.Headline: Good news, photographers: Two-thirds of content buyers believe human-made is better than GenAI
stories.Summary:
Surveys by the stock platform Storyblocks, published by Digital Camera World on October 24, 2026, found that around two-thirds of content buyers believe human-made works are better than AI-generated content. The buyers surveyed are people who license photos, videos, graphics, audio and other content through stock platforms. The company ran four surveys over the summer, covering more than 1,400 people who regularly license content for their jobs. Although a large majority favored human-made work, 87 percent of respondents said they had used AI-generated visual or audio content in the past year.

The findings point to a split between what buyers prefer and what they actually do. About half of respondents said they had rejected a piece of stock content because it was AI-generated. Across the four surveys, between 74 and 94 percent called for AI-generated content to be labeled, a demand Storyblocks described as near-universal, and even respondents open to AI reportedly agreed on labeling. About 63 percent said their organizations now have policies on AI-generated content. When asked what mattered most in a stock platform, the availability of AI-generated content ranked last in every survey.

Storyblocks, a stock platform for photos, videos and audio, conducted the surveys and reported the results, which the article presents as the company's own findings. The article notes that content made by computers, unlike content made by humans, cannot be copyrighted in the United States. Between 33 and 37 percent of all respondents believed AI content may be of better quality, but among those who already use a non-AI platform for their content, that figure fell to between 5 and 8 percent. The article does not say what further steps the company or the industry plans to take.

Articles.Title: Good news, photographers: Two-thirds of content buyers believe human-made is better than GenAI

stories.Headline: rea enables local app analysis with uncensored llms
stories.Summary:
REA (Reverse Engineer Anything), an MIT-licensed MCP server, now gives an AI agent tools to examine applications and files on a local machine. According to TechGig, which published the report on October 23, 2026, this local analysis means findings do not automatically move to cloud models. The approach is aimed at developers and auditors who worry about privacy when handling sensitive material. Coverage describes the setup as a way to keep the whole process on the user's own hardware.

REA works as a plugin inside Locally Uncensored, an open-source desktop application released under the AGPL-3.0 license, which lets users run models on their own machines. Since version 3.0.7, the plugin lets the agent operate with a local model while all data stays on the machine. The article says REA needs roughly a 27B model with a 64K context for good results, because smaller models can run out of context during analysis. In one test, a stock Qwen 3.8 27B model on Ollama, set to a 64K context, reverse-engineered a four-file Electron test application in 3 minutes 15 seconds. The setup requires Node.js 22.19 or later, 24.11 or later, or 26 or later.

The report says uncensored model builds are preferred for this work, since terms such as "decompile" or "bypass" can trigger refusals in standard models and interrupt an analysis. It also reports that performance improved when the tooling offered fewer tools per turn, passed references instead of full copies of earlier results, and supplied the model with facts rather than provenance. The article does not name a separate party responsible for the release beyond the project and application themselves. It does not describe any further plans, timelines, or next steps for the project.

Articles.Title: rea enables local app analysis with uncensored llms

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence: AI boom brings new wealth to Bay Area, and new worries about growing affordability crisis
stories.Summary:
The Bay Area is facing a sharp split as the artificial intelligence boom brings new wealth to the region, and some residents worry it will deepen an already severe affordability crisis. ABC7 News reporter Monica Madden reported on the story from San Francisco, where the trend was visible during Dreamforce, Salesforce's annual conference, held in the city this month. Redfin estimates that current and former employees of OpenAI and Anthropic hold nearly $200 billion in after-tax equity at the valuations modeled in its analysis. That figure equals roughly 29% of the value of all residential real estate in the San Francisco metro area, though Redfin says the comparison is illustrative rather than a prediction of how much of that housing will be bought. Some buyers are already using pre-IPO stock to purchase homes, a trend the article links to growing interest in the market.

Workers interviewed for the report described mixed feelings about the boom. Jennifer Lum, a senior account executive at Slack Salesforce with a two-year-old child, said she has a housing arrangement that lets her stay in the region but could see her family having to move if it fell through. Jesus Oroseo, a Bay Area native and longtime Salesforce software developer, said he bought his Fremont home about 25 years ago and feels lucky compared with younger workers. He said some friends have left the area because costs became too high, though he does not describe himself as financially struggling. Nakul Srikanth, a Salesforce software engineer in his 20s, said he is optimistic about the technology but believes someone in his position could still be priced out.

The reporting places these local worries inside a wider debate about California's economy. A Public Policy Institute of California survey found that 70% of likely voters believe the state is divided into two economic groups, the "haves" and the "have-nots," and affordability is a central issue ahead of the November election. The article says the Bay Area's past technology booms produced a similar pattern of new wealth arriving where housing was already scarce and expensive. Lum said that while the technology has potential benefits for humanity, she is concerned about how it will be deployed and who might be left out. The article does not describe any specific policy response or set out a timeline for what comes next.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence: AI boom brings new wealth to Bay Area, and new worries about growing affordability crisis

stories.Headline: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
stories.Summary:
Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation into their own tools, the five-year-old company struggled to justify staying independent. Chatbot platform Character.ai has also filed for bankruptcy, just five years after launching. Beyond these two, the article notes that about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence.

The article cites several reasons for these failures, including insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, and weak user demand. OpenAI has had its own setbacks, including a redesign that folded several modes into ChatGPT and drew user criticism before it was rolled back. The company has also shut down or folded stand-alone products into ChatGPT, such as the ChatGPT Atlas browser, which was discontinued on August 9. Its video-sharing platform, Sora, shut down in March 2026 after struggling with high operating costs and user retention.

Apple and Microsoft have faced their own problems with AI features. Apple repeatedly delayed an improved Siri that it had highlighted with Apple Intelligence in 2024, and that delay contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims about how it marketed the iPhone 16's AI capabilities. Microsoft's Recall feature, which took periodic screenshots of user activity, drew privacy and security criticism and was delayed for nearly a year. Notion Mail, launched in April 2025, is scheduled to shut down on September 22 after the company noticed users were relying on separate AI agents for their email instead.

Hardware and app startups have also struggled. Humane raised $230 million for its AI Pin, but the device faced performance problems and a battery fire warning, and the company shut down the business in February 2025 with its assets acquired by HP for $116 million. The Rabbit R1 sold 100,000 units shortly after its 2024 launch, but early reviews were unflattering. Character.ai filed for bankruptcy in early October, and Disney is now the opening bidder with an offer of $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property, with the sale expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

Articles.Title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it

stories.Headline: Will Generative AI do more harm than good?
stories.Summary:
Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime AI critic, published an opinion post on his Substack on October 24, 2026, revisiting a question he said he thinks about nearly every day: whether generative AI does more harm than good. He recalled a March 2023 debate he held with Keith Teare, hosted by Open to Debate, on whether ChatGPT would do more harm than good. In the new post, he argues that the case against generative AI is now serious, pointing to nonconsensual deepfake pornography, a rise in phishing scams, large-scale disinformation, and the use of the technology for surveillance. He also cited threats to democracy from governments subtly influencing large language models and harms to artists and writers from what he called intellectual property theft.

Marcus described a recent wave of security incidents that some have called "Black October," which Paul Kedrosky dubbed "The Hackening." Salesforce chief executive Marc Benioff called the situation a "code red," echoing a post by Jason Clinton of Anthropic, who warned that conditions were likely to worsen before improving. Clinton urged security leaders to ask their boards for help with basic security measures, and reportedly suggested the difficult period could last roughly 18 months, though Marcus noted Clinton thought it might last only a year or two. Marcus framed these developments as part of the reason the balance of harms now looks troubling.

On the positive side, Marcus pointed to Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, who has been fairly positive about the technology but recently argued that many of the expected benefits are not materializing. Marcus acknowledged that some people, particularly friends using generative AI for coding, have gained a great deal from it, and that employment effects have so far been more modest than some expected. Still, he concluded that it is not hard to argue the technology has been a net detriment to society, and he warned that it could pull down the broader economy. He also said he would return to Open to Debate in Baltimore the following Tuesday, partnered with Cathy O'Neil, with edited versions expected to appear later on YouTube and NPR affiliates including WNYC.

Articles.Title: Will Generative AI do more harm than good?

stories.Headline: AI in life sciences: 6 takeaways for strategy, risk and real-world use
stories.Summary:
Business leaders in the life sciences sector are still working out how to approach artificial intelligence, according to a set of takeaways published by RSM US on March 2, 2026, drawn from a recent RSM-hosted roundtable. Executives and decision makers from a range of life sciences organizations shared their experiences, challenges and goals for AI adoption. The discussion surfaced six main themes that the article presents as the current view of the industry. Together, they describe a sector that is interested in AI but has not yet settled on how to use it well.

The first theme is a strategy gap. Most organizations have basic policies on acceptable AI use, but few have a full strategy that ties AI projects to business goals. Even among larger, well-resourced companies, only a small minority reported a defined roadmap for AI development, adoption or governance. Leaders in the article say they need to move past compliance and toward value-driven plans with measurable goals. Hesitation also plays a part, as many leaders prefer to watch how the technology and their peers develop before acting.

The article attributes that hesitation to limited internal expertise, unclear business cases and concern about risk, especially for sensitive data such as clinical trial results and proprietary research. Early adoption has focused on personal productivity and back-office work, with tools such as Copilot used to handle routine tasks and documents. Leaders are beginning to see that the larger value lies in sector-specific uses, such as speeding drug discovery, improving clinical trial recruitment or automating complex regulatory work. On the build-versus-buy question, most organizations are buying third-party platforms, but the article notes that many underestimate the work needed to prepare their own data for those platforms. Risk and governance are also major concerns, including data breaches and questions about who owns the AI strategy and who is accountable.

Peer learning emerged as one of the most useful parts of the roundtable, with leaders saying they found generic consultant advice unhelpful. Examples shared included using AI agents to automate contract analysis during acquisitions, which the article says saved months of manual effort, and using AI to detect anomalies in financial audits. To address these themes, the article suggests developing a formal AI strategy with governance and risk management, starting with targeted pilots in areas of clear business value, investing in data management, linking AI projects to key performance indicators and fostering communities of practice. The article presents these steps as a way for life sciences organizations to move past uncertainty and begin realizing AI's potential.

Articles.Title: AI in life sciences: 6 takeaways for strategy, risk and real-world use

stories.Headline: Managing AI’s Human, Cyber, and Legal Challenges
stories.Summary:
The New Jersey Business & Industry Association (NJBIA) has announced a virtual Business Growth Roundtable called "Managing AI's Human, Cyber, and Legal Challenges," scheduled for November 10 from 12:00 pm to 1:00 pm. The event is free and aimed at solo professionals, small business owners, and mid-sized company leaders who are already using or exploring AI tools, often before formal policies exist. The organizers say business leaders do not need to slow innovation but do need practical guardrails to protect data, support employees, and keep AI adoption tied to business goals. Anthony Arena, reachable at aarena@njbia.org, is the contact for the event. The roundtable is designed to cover where informal AI use can create cybersecurity, privacy, compliance, and data protection risks.

Sessions will address what leaders should weigh before employees use AI tools in their daily work, and how policies, employee training, technical controls, and clear communication can fit together. Attendees will also get a starting point for steps they can take within 30 days to move AI adoption forward responsibly. The audience includes operations, HR, legal, IT, and cybersecurity decision-makers, along with leaders responsible for training, vendor management, or data protection. The speakers are Darek Hahn, CEO of AffinIT, who helps leaders connect IT strategy, cybersecurity, and technology adoption to growth goals; Marie Pryor, Community Manager for Microsoft's TechSpark initiative in New Jersey, who works on AI workforce and skilling programs; and Michelle Schaap, chair of the Tech, Privacy & Data Innovations group at Chiesa Shahinian & Giantomasi PC, who advises clients on cybersecurity preparedness, privacy obligations, and incident response.

Hahn brings more than 20 years of experience modernizing technology and reducing risk, Pryor focuses on digital skills and public-private partnerships, and Schaap concentrates on cyber and privacy risk along with generative AI issues. The articles do not describe any regulatory requirement or mandated change that the event itself imposes on businesses. The context is that many small and mid-sized businesses are already experimenting with AI tools faster than they can write formal rules for them. The articles do not report on any outcome, follow-up program, or further action beyond the roundtable itself.

Articles.Title: Managing AI’s Human, Cyber, and Legal Challenges

stories.Headline: If we compare the robot industry to artificial intelligence (AI), we are now in the GPT-3 phase. It'..
stories.Summary:
The article reports an interview with Andrew Kang, CEO of RoboStrategy, a robot-focused investment company listed on Nasdaq in May under the stock code BOT. Kang told Maeil Business Newspaper that the robot industry is now in a phase comparable to GPT-3 in artificial intelligence, and that robots with capabilities similar to later AI models are only a matter of time. The interview was published on October 24, 2026. RoboStrategy invests mainly in unlisted robot companies such as Figure AI, Dynamic Robotics, and Standard Bots, allowing individuals to gain indirect exposure through the BOT shares.

Kang described rapid progress in the general-purpose AI models that serve as the "brain" of robots, saying a robot can now follow similar movements after being shown a demonstration. He noted that these changes are happening mostly in research institutes and factories and are not yet easily visible to the public. He also said U.S. venture capital firms are shifting money from software toward physical AI because investors are pressing them to change strategy. Commercialization is already under way in manufacturing and logistics, with a welding-only AI model from Pass Robotics cited as having been used in the field for more than two years.

Kang singled out Figure AI, a humanoid robot developer founded in 2022, which was valued at $39 billion (about 55 trillion won) in a funding round last year with participation from Nvidia and Intel. He said the company is already producing hundreds of robots a month. On Korea, he pointed to large affiliates such as Samsung and LG, which are working with U.S. robot companies as distribution partners and developing robots themselves. He praised Korean engineering and robot AI talent, but said RoboStrategy has not yet invested in Korean unlisted robot companies, though it is reviewing early-stage firms.

Kang also warned that Chinese humanoid robot companies look less attractive to him because of excessive competition, citing roughly four to five serious humanoid companies in the United States against hundreds in China. He argued that such crowding would push down selling prices and profits, and he noted that in July the U.S. Federal Communications Commission banned the sale of new Chinese humanoid and quadruped robots in the United States. He estimated the combined value of unlisted physical AI companies worldwide at only about $200 billion, and cautioned individual investors that failure rates among early companies are significant, so they should study deeply or invest through experienced operators. More to follow.

Articles.Title: If we compare the robot industry to artificial intelligence (AI), we are now in the GPT-3 phase. It'..

stories.Headline: Minuttia Study Finds Vendors Write Up to Half of AI-Cited Best Tools Lists
stories.Summary:
On October 24, 2026, Minuttia, an SEO and AEO agency for software companies, published the Self-Promotional Content Data Study, its second large-scale look at how Google and AI assistants answer questions about software. The team asked 18,084 software questions across Google Search, AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity in August 2026, then read every cited page, 311,766 in total, and labelled who had published it. Its central finding is that between a third and a half of the "best alternatives" listicles these platforms cite are written by a vendor in the category they sell in. For "X vs Y" comparison questions, the share rises to between 56% and 65%.

The study shows that vendors' own lists are almost always built to favor the vendor. Across the platforms, 93% of these lists highlight the vendor's product, 87% rank it first, 90% criticize competitors, and only 16% clearly disclose that the vendor wrote the page. The shares by platform range from 34% for ChatGPT to 47% for Google and Gemini on alternatives questions. Minuttia notes these figures are a floor, since pages the team could not read were counted as not self-promotional. The study also found that the level varies widely by category, from 12% in Audio Production to 76% in AI Security Operations Center, while the 20 most-cited vendors account for only 6% of citations.

Minuttia attributes the pattern to how each platform selects its sources. According to the study, ChatGPT searches the vendor's own website before answering, with 92% of its "site:" searches targeting that site, and vendors' own sites make up 42% of its alternatives citations. Perplexity, by contrast, cites pages that rank well in its search results and offer useful features such as a comparison table or a stated selection method, not promotional language. Zacharias Xiroudakis, Managing Director at Minuttia, said that each platform picks its sources differently and that the company published its data so software teams can check the work for their own categories.

The study carries stated limits. It is a snapshot taken in August 2026, and when Minuttia re-asked Perplexity 2,000 of the questions in September, only 28% of the pages it listed had appeared in the August answer. The findings describe shares of page types and sites rather than which individual page wins. The full study, methodology and CSV data are available at self-promotional-content-data-study.minuttia.com. Minuttia conducted the study with Convex Works, and the release lists Xiroudakis as the media contact.

Articles.Title: Minuttia Study Finds Vendors Write Up to Half of AI-Cited Best Tools Lists

stories.Headline: Will AI expose the rickety infrastructure of the internet?
stories.Summary:
Earlier this week, researchers disclosed vulnerabilities in PHP, the open source programming language that powers a large share of the web, prompting website owners to patch their sites immediately or take them offline if they could not update in time. The flaws had existed for decades without anyone knowing about them. Human researchers taking part in OpenAI and Wiz's "Hack the Planet" initiative found the bugs, though AI was used to exploit them. Because of the disclosure, governments and some popular websites temporarily went down while fixes were rolled out.

The episode is being treated as a warning about how fragile core internet infrastructure can be. Hosts Anthony Ha, Kirsten Korosec, and Sean O'Kane discussed the incident on TechCrunch's Equity podcast, with O'Kane calling it a real reckoning moment. He argued that the internet's foundations are held together by improvised fixes, and that widespread access to large language models and AI agents will make finding similar flaws far easier. Korosec pointed out that many site owners do not realize their sites run on PHP, a language behind content management systems such as WordPress and Drupal, which she said account for roughly 70 percent of websites.

The panel also raised concerns about how the disclosure was handled. O'Kane said some people appeared to get ahead of the embargo, which set off a race among hackers, and Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince reported seeing attempted attacks climb into the millions. Korosec noted that Amazon said its decoy network saw attempts to exploit the flaw before it was publicly announced. The hosts also expressed worry that smaller organizations, including some government sites, lack the resources of large companies to respond quickly. Korosec also expected link rot as sites are shut down rather than patched, and wondered whether new security startups or open source tools might emerge in response.

Articles.Title: Will AI expose the rickety infrastructure of the internet?

stories.Headline: Kenya plans artificial intelligence deployment in national water management
stories.Summary:
Kenya's government officials have put forward plans to bring artificial intelligence into the country's national infrastructure for water management, as reported by Nation.Africa and carried by Mjengo Hub on October 24, 2026. The proposals were shown during the Kenya Water and Irrigation Conference 2026, where officials explored AI tools aimed at curbing distribution losses and dealing with a falling water supply. The plan is meant to strengthen monitoring across urban and rural supply networks. Delegates also looked at interactive architectural models and infrastructure mapping systems that illustrate planned utility network expansions.
