Lee chose the site, a $1.35 billion project won by Samsung C&T in a consortium with UAE builder Trojan General Contracting, which is scheduled to begin operating next year and will supply about one gigawatt of electricity to AI data centers. During his visit he also held an on-site strategy meeting and shared a meal with employees who stayed at the site despite the unstable situation.

The article says Samsung plans to move beyond supplying individual products and equipment and to target the UAE market with a combined offer spanning AI and energy infrastructure. It describes the opportunity as covering power generation and transmission, semiconductors, cooling equipment, data center operations and direct investment. Samsung Electronics is cited for advanced chips, its subsidiary FläktGroup for cooling, Samsung SDS for data center operations and Samsung SDI for energy storage systems. Samsung C&T's past work includes the Barakah nuclear plant and the Al Dhafra plant, and it signed a memorandum of understanding with Emirates Nuclear Energy Corp. in July of last year. Samsung E&A won the TAZIZ methanol project in the UAE last year.

The article attributes the strategy to the group's own conclusions and to industry watchers, and it quotes an unnamed business community official saying the scope for cooperation with Samsung affiliates is widening as the UAE moves toward advanced manufacturing. It also notes that Lee has built solid networks with senior UAE figures and discussed cooperation with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in November of last year. Against the backdrop of UAE plans to move away from an oil-centered economy, the article lists large projects, including roughly $150 billion in energy infrastructure by 2030 from Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. and the Stargate UAE AI computing cluster, whose first 200-megawatt facility is targeted to begin operating this year. It also reports that six Samsung companies invested $1 billion last month in Helix Digital Infrastructure, a firm set up by KKR. The article does not say what orders or investments, if any, will result from the visit.

Articles.Title: Samsung Chairman Visits UAE to Pitch AI Infrastructure - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Meta Lifts Capital Spending Floor, Citing Muse AI Agent Momentum
stories.Summary:
Meta raised the bottom of its annual capital spending forecast, signaling that it will keep pouring money into artificial intelligence, according to a filing the company made on the 21st. The move follows strong demand for Muse, the AI agent Meta launched on September 8 and linked to Facebook, Instagram and Threads. Meta said it had raised the lower end of its annual capital spending range by $5 billion, to between $135 billion and $145 billion. Free cash flow turned negative at $2.12 billion in the third quarter, the first deficit since the company went public in May 2012.

Third-quarter revenue from July through September rose 26% from a year earlier to $64.6 billion, beating the $63.4 billion consensus estimate compiled by the London Stock Exchange Group. Quarterly net income jumped 264% to $9.86 billion but fell short of the $17.2 billion analysts had expected. Earnings per share came in at $3.83, below the $5.75 market estimate, which Meta said reflected $9.9 billion in costs booked for a settlement of social media lawsuits. Muse passed 10 million users within 40 days of its first release in North America, and about 25% of users who installed the app use it daily. Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg said shopping is the most popular use case.

Zuckerberg said on a conference call that running Muse requires substantial computing, but he expects cost efficiency to improve more than tenfold next year, which he believes will secure profitability as revenue scales. He also said he expects revenue per user from Muse to exceed that of the company's existing app family, which earns a few hundred dollars a year. Meta said it would issue non-voting common shares in January to raise money for AI investment, distributing one new share for each share held, which works out to a two-for-one split. The company said the goal is to fund growth and maintain its leading position. Meta is trying to shift from a business that draws 97% of revenue from social media advertising toward becoming an AI company.

Articles.Title: Meta Lifts Capital Spending Floor, Citing Muse AI Agent Momentum - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Jay Y. Lee Visits UAE to Expand Samsung's Middle East AI Data Center Push
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Jay Y. Lee traveled to the United Arab Emirates, where he visited the construction site of the Al Dhafra gas-fired power plant in Abu Dhabi on November 21, local time, as the company reported on October 22. The trip was his first to the Middle East since he accompanied President Lee Jae-myung to the UAE last November. He toured major facilities at the plant, reviewed the construction schedule and safety management, and met with employees. At the site, he also held a meeting with executives from Samsung C&T and Samsung E&A on business strategy and new market entry.

Samsung said it is expanding its existing nuclear power and combined-cycle gas power businesses in line with the UAE's industrial development. The company is also looking for chances to join future projects in AI data centers and energy infrastructure. The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar are moving quickly to build data centers and power plants as AI adoption spreads across the region. Samsung Electronics, Samsung C&T and Samsung SDS plan to take part in designing, building and operating AI data centers. They also plan to supply advanced semiconductors and cooling equipment and to help construct power plants.

The company framed the visit as part of a push to move the group into new local businesses in a region the articles describe as still unsettled by war. Lee's presence at the site and his talks with the affiliate executives signal that the group is directing senior attention to the effort. The articles do not give investment amounts, contract values or timelines for any new AI data center or energy project. They also do not report any agreement signed during the visit. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Jay Y. Lee Visits UAE to Expand Samsung's Middle East AI Data Center Push - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI Memory Boom Is Funding China's Chip Catch-Up
stories.Summary:
Chinese memory chipmakers are closing the gap with their Korean rivals, and industry watchers say the AI memory boom is paying for it. According to a Seoul Economic Daily report published on October 23, 2026, ChangXin Memory Technologies, a Chinese DRAM maker, and Yangtze Memory Technologies, a NAND flash producer, are expanding capacity and moving into each other's main business lines. The report says CXMT is pursuing NAND research while YMTC has started work on DRAM, suggesting both want to become full-line suppliers. The article's author is Seo Jong-gap, and industry watchers quoted in the piece say competition could intensify sharply once China's new fabs reach full operation in 2027 and 2028.

The growth figures are steep. CXMT's preliminary nine-month guidance, released on October 16, implies third-quarter revenue of 114.7 billion to 119.7 billion yuan, roughly seven times the year-earlier figure. Counterpoint Research put CXMT's share of global DRAM revenue at 10 percent in the second quarter, up from 4 percent a year earlier. SemiAnalysis projects CXMT's monthly DRAM wafer capacity will rise from about 350,000 wafers at the end of this year to 500,000 by the end of 2028. YMTC has reached third place globally in NAND shipment share and is targeting a 20 percent share over the long term.

Analysts attribute the windfall to a DRAM supply shortage and price increases driven by AI server investment, and the companies are reinvesting it. YMTC reportedly has 4,796 R&D staff, has spent 14.2 billion yuan on R&D over three years, and holds 5,611 registered invention patents. It is using its Xtacking wafer bonding technology to work around U.S. export controls on advanced chipmaking equipment. The article notes that Samsung Electronics reportedly signed a related patent licensing agreement with YMTC last year. The report also says CXMT's July stock market listing raised a large sum that adds to its investment capacity.

The article cautions that a rising market share does not yet mean the technology gap is closing. CXMT's DDR5 products are reported to carry manufacturing costs per unit of data capacity more than 30 percent higher than those of Korean and U.S. producers. Analysts quoted in the report say the threat to Korean companies depends on when China's capacity additions take full effect, with some pointing to 2028 as the turning point. If large volumes of new Chinese output arrive as AI investment growth slows, the article says, commodity memory prices could come under downward pressure.

Articles.Title: AI Memory Boom Is Funding China's Chip Catch-Up - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: TSMC advances CoPoS packaging at Taoyuan Longtan site
stories.Summary:
TSMC's Longtan Science Park Phase 3 in Taoyuan is restarting after nearly three years of delays. Taiwan's National Development Council approved the development plan for the site on September 17, 2026. The report, published by Digitimes on October 23, 2026, ties this approval to the company's advancing CoPoS packaging work at the location. The article's visible text is limited, and much of it is navigation, subscription prompts and site boilerplate rather than reporting. Because the body of the story sits behind a paywall, the full details of the packaging plan are not available in the material provided.

The text available says only that the approval and restart mark a change after a long stretch of delay at the Phase 3 site. It does not state the size of the investment, the number of jobs, the production capacity, or the timeline for CoPoS output at Taoyuan. The article's summary gives no figures beyond the September 17 approval date and the three years of delay. Readers should not assume further specifics from the headline alone. Any changes to the site's scope or schedule that the full article may describe are not included in the excerpt provided.

The approval came from Taiwan's National Development Council, which the excerpt names as the body that cleared the development plan. The excerpt does not include any statement from TSMC or from government officials explaining the reasons for the delay or the restart. It also does not say who else, if anyone, has been named as responsible for the earlier setbacks. The site belongs to TSMC, and the report frames the company as the party advancing the packaging work.

Beyond that, the material does not attribute remarks to specific people. The surrounding page shows other recent coverage about TSMC, including reports on wafer price increases for 2027 and talks about possible involvement in Elon Musk's Terafab project, but the excerpt does not connect these stories to the Longtan approval. The available text does not say what comes next for the Phase 3 site or when construction or CoPoS production is expected to begin. More to follow.

Articles.Title: TSMC advances CoPoS packaging at Taoyuan Longtan site - digitimes

stories.Headline: Amkor triples Gwangju investment as AI packaging demand grows
stories.Summary:
Amkor Technology has announced that it is tripling its planned investment in Gwangju, South Korea, to expand its advanced packaging capacity for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing chips. The project is part of South Korea's southwestern development strategy, and the report was published on October 20, 2026. The article describes the move as a response to growing demand for advanced packaging tied to AI hardware. Beyond that, the details available in the reporting are limited, and the full text is restricted to paid subscribers.

The expansion brings a semiconductor project into the region's development plans and concentrates it on the packaging stage that links chips to the systems that use them. Advanced packaging has become a bottleneck in AI hardware production, so added capacity of this kind is aimed at meeting that demand. The reporting frames the investment as a tripling of what Amkor had previously planned for the site. The specific dollar figures, timelines, and job numbers are not visible in the portion of the article available here.

Amkor Technology is the company behind the investment, and its plans were reported by DIGITIMES. The article does not include direct statements from company executives or government officials in the visible text. The Gwangju project is linked to South Korea's effort to spread semiconductor activity beyond its established hubs. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Amkor triples Gwangju investment as AI packaging demand grows - digitimes

stories.Headline: Micron opens second Taiwan advanced packaging plant as HBM supply tightens
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology opened Micron Advanced Assembly and Test Taiwan 2 (AATT2) in Taichung on October 15, 2026. The facility is the company's second advanced assembly and test site in Taiwan. The opening was attended by Micron President and Chief Operating Officer Manish Bhatia, Donghui Lu, who heads Micron Taiwan, and Taiwan President Lai Ching-te. The article's text beyond the opening paragraph is not available in the copy provided.

The article gives no further figures on the plant's capacity, investment, or staffing in the material available. Its headline ties the opening to tightening supply of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is the reason the new packaging capacity matters. The surrounding page text describes unrelated industry stories and subscription features, so no additional details about the plant can be drawn from it. Because the substance of the article is cut off, the description of what the facility requires or changes cannot be expanded beyond what is stated.

Beyond the opening itself, the only responsibility the available material assigns is to the company, which opened the plant, and to the three officials pictured at the event. The material does not record any statements those officials made about the facility. Nothing further about the plant's operations, timing of production, or next steps is reported in the sources provided. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Micron opens second Taiwan advanced packaging plant as HBM supply tightens - digitimes

stories.Headline: Nvidia lines up six suppliers to expand substrate, packaging, and testing capacity
stories.Summary:
Nvidia said on October 21, 2026, that it is working with six supply chain partners to expand manufacturing capacity in several parts of its production chain. The company named four areas where capacity is being added: substrates, advanced packaging, testing, and optical engines. The expansion is meant to meet growing demand for its accelerated computing and AI factory platforms. The report was published by DIGITIMES on October 22, 2026, and the announcement itself came the day before.

The articles provide no further figures, dates, or names for the six suppliers, and they do not specify how much capacity will be added or over what timeframe. What they do establish is the direction of the move, which is that Nvidia is bringing more outside manufacturers into the process of building the hardware behind its AI systems. The four areas named cover the steps that sit between chip design and finished products. Because the report is brief, it offers little detail on how the new arrangements will be structured.

The articles attribute the announcement to Nvidia itself, which described the partnerships as a way to support its accelerated computing and AI factory offerings. Beyond that statement, the report does not include comments from the suppliers or from any independent analysts. The text on the page is largely navigation and subscription material, so no additional remarks from the company are available in the source material. The article therefore rests on Nvidia's own description of its plans.

The surrounding coverage on the same site points to a broader industry context of tight packaging and foundry capacity. Other stories listed alongside this one discuss advanced packaging expansion and chipmaker pricing for 2027, though the articles do not connect those developments directly to Nvidia's announcement. The source material does not say what the next steps will be or when more details on the six suppliers will be released. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nvidia lines up six suppliers to expand substrate, packaging, and testing capacity - digitimes

stories.Headline: AI in Higher Education Internal Audit: 2026 Survey Results
stories.Summary:
A 2026 survey of higher education internal audit leaders, run by EisnerAmper with the Association of College and University Auditors (ACUA), found that AI use in these offices is moving faster than the governance around it. The survey was facilitated for participating ACUA institutions through a 34-question instrument, and the results were published on October 23, 2026. Of the institutions that responded, 34 were counted in the findings. Respondents pointed to data quality and staff AI literacy as the main barriers to broader adoption, while only 3% named leadership buy-in as their primary obstacle.

Internal audit teams are using AI mainly for writing and planning work. Seventy-one percent use it to write and edit audit reports, 68% use it for risk assessments and audit planning, and 68% use it for regulatory and policy research. Far fewer use it for analytical work, with 35% applying it to data analysis and continuous monitoring and fewer than 9% using it to review contracts and vendor agreements. The authors suggest teams worry about accuracy and security because contracts hold sensitive information, and they recommend starting any such work in a secure, institution-approved environment with human verification of the results.

Governance is lagging behind use. Only 12 of the 34 responding institutions have a formal AI policy or guidelines, and half are still developing one. Technology leaders own AI governance at 44% of institutions, while 24% report no single owner or structure. None of the responding internal audit leaders lead or co-lead governance, and 62% are only informed of it or not involved. The authors also note that 41% of institutions have a policy on students' use of generative AI, even though 65% of respondents cite academic integrity as a significant concern.

Respondents rated nine AI risk categories on a one-to-five scale. The highest concerns were cybersecurity risks from AI and over-reliance on unvetted AI output, each rated four or five by 76% of respondents. Data privacy and FERPA compliance came next at 74%, with 56% giving it the top rating of five. Building team AI literacy and skills is the top priority for the next 12 to 18 months, and four respondents, or 12%, said AI is not a current priority. The article recommends three starting steps: building an AI inventory with IT and procurement, placing AI auditing in both the skills plan and the audit plan, and documenting how AI-assisted work is verified before it reaches a report.

Articles.Title: AI in Higher Education Internal Audit: 2026 Survey Results

stories.Headline: Kansas State hosting Heartland AI Symposium
stories.Summary:
The Heartland AI Symposium, titled "Our Society in the Age of AI," is set to take place November 10 to 12 at Kansas State University, according to a report published by WIBW on October 23, 2026. The event is described as a wide-ranging discussion that has grown over four years from an initial exploration of what artificial intelligence is to a broader look at what it can do. A free townhall discussion will open the event from 6:30 to 8 p.m. on November 10 at the Manhattan Public Library. The main symposium sessions are held at the K-State Student Union.

Attendance costs $150 in person and $125 online, with discounts available for students, educators and K-State staff. The agenda covers topics including education, language, security and ethics. Full agenda and registration details are posted at k-state.edu/ai-symposium. Those interested are directed to that site for the complete schedule and sign-up information. Raelynne Hale, a professor of modern languages at K-State, serves as the symposium director.

She described the scope of the agenda in an interview on Eye on NE Kansas, the WIBW program that previewed the event. The article reports her remarks as an overview of the topics planned for the three days. It does not give further detail on specific speakers or sessions. The article does not describe any changes or new requirements tied to the event beyond the registration and attendance details already noted. It also does not state any outcomes or follow-up plans for the symposium.

Articles.Title: Kansas State hosting Heartland AI Symposium

stories.Headline: Redmond-based startup develops new robot weeder using AI technology
stories.Summary:
A Redmond-based startup called Aigen has developed a solar-powered robot weeder that uses AI to tell weeds apart from crops, according to a report published by KUOW on October 23, 2026. The machine, known as the Element Gen 2, looks like a drafting table on wheels and has a solar panel on its top surface that powers it. Four metal arms underneath pluck weeds and fling them behind the machine as it rolls through a farm plot. The company's cofounder, Richard Wurden, said the aim was to control weeds without diesel or chemical sprays.

Conventional weeding of low-cost crops often relies on herbicides, the article explains, and that approach has drawbacks. Rui Liu, an assistant professor of weed science at Washington State University, is quoted saying that repeated herbicide use can produce resistant weed strains, which makes the chemicals less effective over time. Liu added that growers need diverse management strategies to keep weeds under control in the long term. The Aigen founders said their interest in non-toxic weed control was personal, since Wurden has Type 1 diabetes and cofounder Kenny Lee has non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and both conditions have been linked to pesticide use.

Wurden said the company chose solar power so the machine would not need refueling, which he described as making it truly autonomous, in contrast to equipment that has to be trucked out and filled. The article notes that rising fuel prices have brought the company more than 30 orders for its solar-powered models. Aigen is not the only startup working on farm technology, as the report points out that Seattle-based Carbon Robotics uses AI detection and laser weeding. The article also observes that many companies still depend on diesel to run their equipment.

Articles.Title: Redmond-based startup develops new robot weeder using AI technology

stories.Headline: AI devours a fifth of companies’ IT budgets
stories.Summary:
According to a new study by the research firm Forrester, AI will account for 20% of corporate technology spending in 2027. At the same time, more than half of IT executives are expected to miss their return-on-investment targets. The findings were reported by The Register and originally appeared in Computer Sweden. The study points to a gap between the money companies are putting into AI and the results they are getting back from it.

In the survey, 45% of AI decision-makers said investments must produce a positive return within one year to be considered successful. Only 22% reported a positive effect on their company's operating profit over the past year. Forrester attributes part of the problem to companies buying AI technology without also changing their organizations and work processes. As a result, financial gains tend to show up only within individual use cases rather than across the business.

Forrester expects companies to increasingly turn to open AI models in the future, since they are cheaper to run. More expensive and advanced models are expected to be kept for more critical tasks. Together, these shifts are presented as ways to keep AI costs under control. The articles provide no further figures on how quickly this change is expected to happen.

Articles.Title: AI devours a fifth of companies’ IT budgets

stories.Headline: Turmoil hits AI build-out as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO
stories.Summary:
Investor concern about the artificial intelligence build-out pushed markets lower this week, with neocloud providers taking some of the steepest losses. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN each fell sharply and were down well over 30% for October, while CoreWeave's credit default swap spreads widened past 11%, a level generally seen as distress. Yields on CoreWeave's 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes topped 15%. Elsewhere, Elice Group in South Korea fell 30% in its market debut on Tuesday, and Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after cutting its annual earnings forecast.

On Thursday, SK Hynix said it was withdrawing its planned initial public offering for Solidigm, its U.S.-based unit that makes NAND and SSD storage for data centers. The company cited market volatility and recent share price trends in its release, and said the IPO had been expected to ease investment burdens and expand capacity for shareholder returns. Meta's stock fell 7% on Thursday after it reported negative free cash flow of over $2 billion in the third quarter and raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditure to $135 billion from $130 billion. Meta also said it plans to spend about $825 billion over the coming years on leases and contracts, with more than $450 billion of that in non-cancellable take-or-pay agreements.

Credit markets reflected the strain. Meta's five-year credit default swap spreads reached all-time highs above 124 basis points, while spreads on Nvidia and Oracle also hit records at 126 and 343 basis points this week. Oracle's stock has lost more than a third of its value this year, and the company faces the risk of a credit rating downgrade. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, speaking at a conference in Berlin, said demand for neoclouds is "off the charts" and that the demand for capital exceeds its availability, a shortage he expects will be resolved. Analysts at Gartner, meanwhile, predict that 80% of neocloud companies will either cease operations or be absorbed by 2030.

Market participants are watching how the trade plays out, and investors are increasingly looking for ways to hedge their exposure. John Williams of law firm Milbank LLP said the scale of spending makes risk management tools appropriate regardless of whether an investor is bullish or bearish. Portfolio manager Brian Stutland of Equity Armor Investments said the pressures are interconnected and voiced concern that the strain could spread to the broader Nasdaq. Alphabet, which reports third-quarter earnings next week along with Microsoft and Amazon, had been the worst performer among the hyperscalers, with its shares falling 6% ahead of that report.

Articles.Title: Turmoil hits AI build-out as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO

stories.Headline: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend
stories.Summary:
Block, the payments company led by Jack Dorsey, has announced an AI model called Dessa that it says was trained "from scratch on nothing but human conversation." To show what it can do, the company shared chat exchanges with people that are sometimes natural and sometimes a little awkward or uncanny. In one example shared by Dessa lead Ragavan Thurairatnam, the model briefly mistakes the speaker for someone named "Ronaldo" before the conversation settles into a mostly natural back and forth. The article was published on October 23, 2026.

The Dessa website describes the model as a true speech-to-speech system whose knowledge came entirely from human speech, and it says the model can run locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max or better. Other examples on the site include a discussion of Christopher Nolan's films that drifts into an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer's Superman films, and a conversation in which the model responds to news of a surprise trip to Paris with what the site describes as teary gratitude. A clip also pits Dessa against OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 voice model, and the article says Dessa comes across as more natural in that exchange. The article notes that the clips can be heard in an accompanying video.

The Dessa team gives three reasons for building the model: curiosity, better understanding between humans and AI, and safety. On safety, the team argues that current voice AI flattens speech into text and cannot respond to emotion in people's voices, which it describes as a problem as AI gains power and independence. The team says it will give "a small group of AI safety researchers" early access to the model. The articles do not say when broader access will be available or whether Block plans a public release.

Articles.Title: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend

stories.Headline: AI alerts help win over skeptical drivers, fleet execs say
stories.Summary:
At the American Trucking Associations' Management Conference & Exhibition in Charlotte, N.C., on Oct. 19, a panel discussed how artificial intelligence and connected vehicle data can support safety, driver coaching, fueling and back-office work. Austin Henderson, vice president of innovation and engineering at Werner Enterprises and FirstFleet, joined Gary Johnson of Motive and Jared Whitson of Bennett Family of Cos. in a session titled "The Rise of Physical AI in Trucking." Henderson recalled a skeptical driver who admitted that an AI-enabled distracted-driving alert had saved his life. The system detected the distraction, alerted the back office, and staff spoke with the driver, who later watched the video and recognized the danger.

Bennett uses forward-facing cameras on about 2,500 trucks, mainly to detect and review events. Whitson also described location-based alerts that notify staff when a truck with a critical fault code enters a shop's geofence. He said the system could eventually go further and generate a repair work order automatically. Henderson described a prescriptive fueling tool that uses fuel prices, fuel levels and truck location to recommend stops in real time, and it suggests an alternative when a driver skips a planned stop. Whitson said AI can gather the relevant information for an event review, turning a process that once took four or five minutes of research into a check of about 30 seconds.

The panelists stressed that adoption is as much cultural as technical. Henderson said organizations need to explain what they are doing and why, or employees may assume the technology is meant to replace them. He recalled a veteran driver who opposed the technology until video showed he was not at fault in a highway incident. Henderson also said about 97% of the videos in the company's coaching process are viewed the same day the event occurs, and the company uses digital avatars of regional safety managers to deliver coaching.

The panel urged fleets to invest in reliable systems, communicate clearly and ensure data connects across platforms. Johnson summed up the panel's message by saying that AI does not replace judgment but protects the time needed for it. Werner Enterprises ranks No. 19 on the Transport Topics Top 100 list of the largest for-hire carriers in North America. The article itself reports no further developments beyond the conference discussion.

Articles.Title: AI alerts help win over skeptical drivers, fleet execs say

stories.Headline: AI-Native: Redesigning Automotive's Next Era
stories.Summary:
Two pieces of industry commentary, both dated October 2026, argue that automotive companies need to change how they adopt artificial intelligence. One, published by NTT DATA on October 23, says most organizations are still layering AI onto existing processes and functional structures, which produces pockets of efficiency without improving end-to-end results. The other, published by Cox Automotive on October 22 after a panel at the Automotive News Congress, focuses on how to scale AI across the enterprise in ways that create measurable business value. Neither piece describes a single event or a new regulation, so the story is one of industry direction rather than a dated incident.

NTT DATA's central recommendation is to redesign work around outcomes rather than tasks, processes or traditional functional boundaries. It says becoming AI-native means organizing people, software and AI agents into connected, end-to-end workflows that span multiple functions. The article lists four things readers will learn, including why applying AI to existing processes often yields only incremental gains and where automotive leaders should focus to move from isolated use cases to enterprise performance. The article does not provide figures, timelines or specific case results.

Cox Automotive's piece reports on a panel moderated by its President Steve Rowley, with Marianne Johnson, its Chief Product Officer, Oliver Parker of Google Cloud's Generative AI go-to-market team, and Jeff Rachor, CEO of Berkshire Hathaway Automotive. Johnson argued that connected data matters most, because AI needs context and disconnected data simply automates wrong answers faster. Parker described agentic AI as systems that link reasoning, memory and action across multiple systems, and said this can free employees for higher-value work while cutting costs. Rachor stressed that deployments must be tied to business outcomes, that scaling requires governance, trusted partners, interoperability and a clear return on investment, and that the aim is to augment employees rather than eliminate them.

Both sources frame the current moment as a shift from early experimentation toward enterprise-wide scale. Cox Automotive describes the first phase as understanding what the technology could do and the next as connecting AI to trusted data, embedding it in business processes and extending its reach across the organization. The panel's speakers note that the pace of change is fast and that organizations are no longer asking whether AI belongs in their business. Neither article gives specific forecasts or next steps beyond these recommendations, and the NTT DATA piece is primarily a gated resource offering a download. Cox Automotive describes itself as the world's largest automotive services and technology provider, with more than 29,000 employees.

Articles.Title: AI-Native: Redesigning Automotive's Next Era

stories.Headline: KOP Mall worker accused of taking upskirt photos and creating AI child porn
stories.Summary:
Robert Mayberry, a 41-year-old man from Prospect Park, Pennsylvania, who worked at the Therabody store in the King of Prussia Mall, was arrested on October 21, 2026, and charged with several counts tied to AI-generated child sexual abuse material, upskirt photography, and invasion of privacy. The investigation began on June 18, 2026, when a woman contacted West Goshen Police after seeing AI-generated child pornography videos and upskirt photos on Mayberry's cellphone. Police obtained a search warrant that day, stopped Mayberry on Paoli Pike near the Route 202 ramps in West Goshen Township, and seized his MacBook, iPhone, flash drive, and SD cards. Between June 26 and August 14, investigators reportedly found hundreds of AI-generated child sexual abuse videos and photos, additional non-AI child pornography, and more than 150 upskirt videos of women and teen girls.

According to the criminal complaint, the images were taken at the King of Prussia Mall, parks, a zoo, convenience stores, and an aquarium. West Goshen Police Detective Kyle Maye said Mayberry was targeting girls and females on escalators and walking around the mall. In one case, police say Mayberry photographed a teen girl at West Goshen Community Park and used the AI app Grok to create child pornography. Mayberry was charged with multiple counts of photographing or depicting a computer sex act involving a child, child sexual abuse material, invasion of privacy, and criminal use of a communication facility. He posted bail after his arrest, and his next preliminary hearing is scheduled for October 30, 2026.

Therabody, the store's employer, said it takes the allegations extremely seriously, that customer and staff safety is its top priority, and that the employee has been placed on leave effective immediately. Sources told NBC10 that Mayberry has been banned from the King of Prussia Mall. NBC10 said it had contacted Mayberry's attorney for comment and would add a response if one was provided. Anyone with additional information is asked to contact West Goshen Township Police.

Articles.Title: KOP Mall worker accused of taking upskirt photos and creating AI child porn

stories.Headline: Moonshot AI launches new flagship Kim K3.1 Pro model with 3T parameters
stories.Summary:
Moonshot AI, a Chinese artificial intelligence company, introduced Kim K3.1 Pro on October 23, 2026, as a new flagship large language model. The model is a post-trained, or upgraded, version of Kimi K3, which the company released in July. Kimi K3 contains 896 neural networks with 3 trillion parameters but activates only 16 of them at a time to reduce inference costs. The company says it ran the new model's post-training on an upgraded stack with automated quality checks and greater infrastructure efficiency. Moonshot AI reported that this post-training workflow consumed significantly more processing power than its earlier projects.

The model is available through Moonshot AI's paid cloud services from launch, and the company plans to release its weights as open source by November 4. Kimi K3.1 Pro scored 92.7 percent on the BenchCAD 3D model coding benchmark, within four percentage points of GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. It can also animate 3D models, and the company used it to produce a simulation of human motion and several 3D video games. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it reached 65.7 percent, more than 7 percent ahead of Astra but slightly behind Opus 5.5. It also outperformed both rivals on OfficeQA Pro v2, a test of complex financial analysis.

The model's results on popular cybersecurity benchmarks trail Astra and Opus 5.5 by a wide margin. Moonshot AI said it deliberately removed cybersecurity-related information from the post-training dataset to address safety risks. The company said it plans to give future models more advanced vulnerability analysis features. The articles credit Moonshot AI with these statements and do not describe any outside review of them. The article is a product announcement based on the company's own claims and internal evaluations.

Articles.Title: Moonshot AI launches new flagship Kim K3.1 Pro model with 3T parameters

stories.Headline: AI Tool of the Week: this ChatGPT feature turns audio into useful work notes
stories.Summary:
ChatGPT now accepts audio recordings and can turn them into transcripts, summaries or working drafts, according to a Mint column by Jaspreet Bindra and Anuj Magazine published on October 24, 2026. The feature, called ChatGPT Audio Uploads, is presented as a way for professionals to avoid replaying long conversations to find a price, deadline or commitment. The authors note that many useful workplace discussions happen without notes, such as over lunch, on a site visit or during a call taken while walking. A recording made with permission can be attached to a chat and questioned directly. The column describes this as a way to capture conversations that would otherwise be reconstructed from memory, sometimes inaccurately.

The column says the tool accepts a range of audio formats, including WAV, MP3, M4A, FLAC and AAC, so many phone recordings can be uploaded without conversion. Users attach a file and state what they need, such as a transcript listing every price and delivery commitment or a recap with decisions, open questions and next steps. The article gives an example of a procurement head who finishes a 40-minute supplier negotiation and has a leadership review at 4 pm, then asks for commitments in a table with item, owner and date. The same chat can then produce a follow-up email to the supplier or a three-line summary for a director. The authors also say the transcript becomes a conversation, so follow-up questions can replace manual searching of the audio.

The article attributes the feature to OpenAI and says it is included in Enterprise workspaces, where OpenAI states that customer content is not used to improve its models. The authors state that the tools and analysis in their weekly section reflect their own internal testing and that their recommendations are independent and not influenced by the tool creators. Bindra is identified as co-founder and CEO of AI&Beyond, and Magazine as its co-founder. The piece is excerpted from Leslie D'Monte's weekly TechTalk newsletter, according to the article. The column does not describe any expansion plans, pricing changes or further product updates beyond the features it lists.

Articles.Title: AI Tool of the Week: this ChatGPT feature turns audio into useful work notes

stories.Headline: Decade-old PHP bug puts websites at risk: How AI uncovered it, who is vulnerable and how to stay safe | Explained
stories.Summary:
Two critical flaws in PHP, the programming language behind around 70% of websites worldwide, were disclosed on 21 October 2026 by Wiz Research, alongside PHP security updates. Dubbed PHP2Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the bugs sit in PHP's core engine and could let attackers run code remotely and steal data without logging in. Google, OpenAI, Amazon Web Services and other tech firms worked with the researchers on analysis and safeguards. Amazon's MadPot threat intelligence system said it caught attack attempts before the flaws were made public.

Both flaws are memory-safety bugs that can lead to sensitive data leaks or remote code execution. Researchers demonstrated successful attacks against WordPress, Drupal and Joomla, though the weaknesses lie in PHP itself, so any site running an affected version may be exposed. An attacker could reach passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and other data held in server memory. Affected versions go back to PHP 5.4, so software more than 10 years old may be vulnerable. The companies involved built detection tools and offered temporary protections for systems that could not be patched quickly.

Wiz Research said frontier AI models helped its investigators find the vulnerabilities and turn complex memory errors into working exploits, using Wiz Atlas, Google's Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. According to the report, the AI was also used to study failures, refine exploitation techniques and test security patches, work that would otherwise have required extensive manual testing and expert effort. The findings suggest that the same tools that help defenders find weaknesses can also lower the skill attackers need. Amazon said it does not know how the attackers learned of the flaws before they were widely known.

Articles.Title: Decade-old PHP bug puts websites at risk: How AI uncovered it, who is vulnerable and how to stay safe | Explained

stories.Headline: Harmful Partial Interventions and Benign Leakage in Concept-based Models
stories.Summary:
This arXiv preprint, posted on October 24, 2026, by Gregory Verghese, Christopher J. Soelistyo, Mateo Espinosa Zarlenga, Alessandro Barp and Christopher R.S. Banerji, examines concept-based models, a type of artificial intelligence system built to let people inspect and correct human-understandable intermediate concepts. The authors describe a failure they call intervention harm, in which a human correction to those concepts makes downstream predictions worse. They separate harm that appears once every concept has been corrected from harm that appears when only some concepts are corrected, which they regard as the more likely real-world situation. The paper argues that models often reach high accuracy by carrying extra task-relevant information inside their concept representations, a practice known as leakage.

The authors state that earlier work held such leakage to be benign when concept representations meet two conditions, sufficiency and localisation, but they prove those conditions do not guarantee that corrections help. In their experiments, across controlled and real-world settings, incomplete concept supervision went together with more intervention harm. They report that a previously proposed objective, which optimises the model when all concepts are corrected, lowers harm at the endpoint but does not reliably stop harmful partial corrections. To address this, they introduce a monotonic intervention objective that penalises any rise in task loss along partial correction paths. According to the abstract, combining the two training objectives substantially reduces how often and how severely partial interventions cause harm, while keeping concept and task prediction performance intact.

The work is attributed to the five named authors, who present it as a contribution to making AI systems deployed in high-risk settings more amenable to meaningful human oversight. The articles provide no further detail on institutional affiliations, funding, or any response from others in the field. The paper is a preprint and has not been described in the source as peer reviewed or published in a journal. The source does not say what follow-up work or adoption is planned.

Articles.Title: Harmful Partial Interventions and Benign Leakage in Concept-based Models

stories.Headline: OpenAI shifts value to US$1.25 trillion as funding talks finalise
stories.Summary:
OpenAI is finalising a fresh funding round of around US$30 billion, and according to sources familiar with the matter it is now targeting a valuation of US$1.25 trillion as negotiations enter their final stages. The figure has come down by US$150 billion from the US$1.4 trillion discussed earlier in the talks. Sources who asked for anonymity said the fund-raising discussions are still ongoing and the details could change. The ChatGPT maker last raised US$122 billion in March at an US$852 billion valuation, including that money.

Coatue Management is in talks to co-lead the round, according to the sources, and OpenAI has also been speaking with several investment funds from the United Arab Emirates. Bloomberg previously reported that other firms, including BlackRock, are part of those discussions. Coatue did not immediately respond to a request for comment. One person said the company expects investor commitments to be finalised by the end of next week. CNBC had earlier reported the US$1.25 trillion valuation.

The timing comes as technology stocks have fallen this week after mixed quarterly results from companies including Meta Platforms and Tesla raised investor concerns that heavy spending on artificial intelligence has gone too far. Many investors are closely watching how the initial public offering of OpenAI rival Anthropic, which is expected in November, will be received. OpenAI has pushed back its own plans for an IPO until 2027, citing its focus on AI safety efforts. The articles do not say whether the new round will change that timeline.

Articles.Title: OpenAI shifts value to US$1.25 trillion as funding talks finalise

stories.Headline: Hong Kong badly lags peers in Greater Bay Area AI supply chains
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong ranks near the bottom of the Greater Bay Area's 11 cities in meeting growing demand for artificial intelligence supply chains, according to a major index released on Thursday. The finding comes from the Greater Bay Area Industry Development Index 2026, jointly published by think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation and Dah Sing Bank. The index assessed each city across key sectors including trade and logistics, construction, real estate, innovation, technology and financial services. Hong Kong still posted the strongest overall growth of the 11 cities, with expansion of 5.1 per cent across six key industries this year.

The index ranks Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Dongguan as the top three cities for benefits from surging AI supply chain demand and advanced, high-technology manufacturing. Its results suggest that Hong Kong's position in this area lags well behind its neighbours even as its wider economy grows. The article reports the sectoral findings but gives no further breakdown of where Hong Kong falls short. It also does not say what measures, targets or timelines follow from the index.

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of Our Hong Kong Foundation, spoke about the results and identified the three mainland cities at the top of the AI supply chain category. The article attributes the index's conclusions to the foundation and Dah Sing Bank as joint publishers. Shui's comments focus on the rankings themselves, and the report does not provide any further remarks from the bank or other officials. The piece was written by Vivian Au and published by the South China Morning Post on October 22, 2026.

Articles.Title: Hong Kong badly lags peers in Greater Bay Area AI supply chains

stories.Headline: U.K. politicians are testing their messages on AI-generated focus groups
stories.Summary:
British politicians are now testing their policy messages on AI-generated focus groups, according to a Japan Times report published on October 22, 2026. Startups Electric Twin and Artificial Societies, along with more established research firms GWI and Toluna, use data from real focus groups and surveys to build AI personas that can react to political messages within minutes. London-based Synthetic Respondents also offers the service, charging $16 (£12) per project. The company says this is a thousandth of the cost of a traditional focus group study.

The arrangement changes how politicians can gauge public reaction, since the tools make it quicker and cheaper to predict how real voters might respond to a policy. The article notes that this also gives backbench lawmakers access to analysis that might otherwise have been beyond their budgets. Critics, however, warn that depending on these synthetic panels could pull politicians away from the views of actual people. The report does not give further figures on how widely the tools are being used across Parliament.

The article names Kanishka Narayan as one early adopter, a politician elected to Parliament in 2024 who is now Britain's AI minister. It does not provide direct statements from Narayan or from the firms about how the tools have been applied in practice. The report instead frames the question as one of balance between speed and affordability on one side and the risk of detachment from voters on the other. It does not say whether any regulation or guidance is planned for such use.

Articles.Title: U.K. politicians are testing their messages on AI-generated focus groups

stories.Headline: Rubric Judgments Lack Uncertainty: Conformal Weighting for LLM Evaluation
stories.Summary:
Researchers Licheng Pan, Haocheng Yang, Haoxuan Li, and seven others posted a paper on October 24, 2026, describing a new method for scoring large language model outputs. The work addresses rubric-based evaluation, in which an output is broken into several criteria and an LLM verifier gives each one a binary judgment. The authors observed that the certainty of these judgments differs widely from one criterion to another, yet existing methods combine them into a single score as if every judgment were equally reliable. The proposed approach, called Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW), is a training-free framework that measures how uncertain each criterion-level judgment is.

It draws a soft uncertainty signal from a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates and turns that signal into a weight for each criterion using split-conformal p-values, which the authors say come with provable coverage guarantees. The weights let uncertain judgments count for less instead of feeding into reward estimation undifferentiated. The authors argue that this matters because such judgments could otherwise produce misleading training signals for downstream reinforcement learning. According to the abstract, the authors ran extensive experiments showing that URW consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy.

They also report stronger downstream reinforcement learning alignment when the method is used. The paper's full text is available as a PDF and in HTML form on arXiv, and the authors frame the work as a fix for a limitation in current aggregation practices rather than as a new evaluation benchmark. The article gives no further details on the specific datasets, models, or effect sizes used in the experiments, and it does not say whether the work has been peer reviewed or adopted elsewhere. Readers wanting those specifics would need to consult the full paper, which the abstract indicates contains the complete experimental results.

Articles.Title: Rubric Judgments Lack Uncertainty: Conformal Weighting for LLM Evaluation

stories.Headline: Japan weighs rebranding energy, AI as defense spending under Trump pressure
stories.Summary:
Japan is considering counting a wider range of expenditures as defense spending beginning next fiscal year, including energy and some development assistance, according to Nikkei. The move comes as the United States presses Tokyo for larger defense budgets. The proposals would bring Japan closer to the goal of spending 3.5% of its gross domestic product on defense. The reported changes would reclassify spending that is not traditionally military, so that it counts toward the defense total. Energy and some development aid are the categories named in the report.

Nikkei's reporting describes these as proposals under consideration rather than settled policy. The article does not give specific yen amounts or the exact categories beyond those named. The article does not identify a specific official who made these proposals, and it does not provide direct statements from Japanese officials. Its central claim is that the U.S. has demanded bigger budgets, which is the stated reason behind the reclassification effort.

Nikkei's reporting presents the rebranding as a way to meet that demand while the government decides what to include. The article is framed within broader pressure from Washington on allies to raise defense outlays, and it notes that Japan has been working on a stronger security posture. It does not say when a final decision will be made or what the budget process will look like. The source offers no further details on how the proposals would be implemented or whether they will be approved.

Articles.Title: Japan weighs rebranding energy, AI as defense spending under Trump pressure

stories.Headline: GS Caltex showcases AI-driven workplace innovations
stories.Summary:
GS Caltex held its fourth annual Deep Transformation Day on Thursday at GS Tower in southern Seoul, showcasing artificial intelligence-driven workplace projects. The event was attended by Vice Chairman and CEO Hur Sae-hong and other executives and employees. It featured 15 exhibition booths built by staff to raise productivity and change how the business operates. Outside experts also spoke on industrial AI, humanoid robots and shifts in the global business environment.

The exhibits covered AI-powered training tutors that use the Socratic method of questioning, physical AI applications such as drones, robots and smart helmets, and a multi-agent AI system meant to automate research report writing. Other projects included energy-saving work at the Yeosu refinery, data-driven catalyst procurement, a planned overhaul of the enterprise resource planning system and a co-processing system for biofuel production. One highlight grew from digital and AI concepts Hur had shared internally, which employees turned into tools such as AiQ+, a program that combines 12 job training courses in the Mobility & Marketing division. Staff also built a Socratic AI tutor for junior production engineers and a finance training assistant. The event was organized around the theme "We," stressing employee-led innovation and continuous improvement.

Hur said that individual challenges and initiatives together shape the company's future, and that when those changes spread across the organization they can drive growth. GS Group Chairman Huh Tae-soo, who also attended, argued that business processes should be redesigned around digital technology from the outset rather than adding digital tools to existing work. He urged employees to use digital tools to improve collaboration, respond to change and deliver stronger business results. The articles frame the event as part of the company's continuing push to build innovation from within. They do not say what further steps are planned beyond the projects displayed.

Articles.Title: GS Caltex showcases AI-driven workplace innovations

stories.Headline: Lee showed how he uses AI. Trump isn't telling
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea drew criticism after publicly sharing how he used Google's Gemini chatbot to back his position in a political dispute. The dispute concerned whether the heads of investigative agencies should attend Cabinet meetings. Around the same time, U.S. President Donald Trump acknowledged using artificial intelligence but declined to explain how. When reporters asked him about his personal use of AI aboard Air Force One last month, he replied that he did not want to say.

Lee's disclosure prompted opposition politicians to question his reliance on a chatbot for legal and constitutional matters. The presidential office responded that Lee had used Gemini to verify legal facts and not to make government decisions. The article notes that Trump's public use of AI-generated imagery, including fabricated images and videos posted on his social media accounts, is well documented, but his remarks did not show whether he consults chatbots on policy or legal questions. Other American lawmakers have been more open about their own use of the technology.

Among the examples cited, Senator Tommy Tuberville, a Republican from Alabama, told The Washington Post in August that he consults ChatGPT during long drives to learn about issues such as Medicare and Medicaid. Representative Anna Paulina Luna, a Florida Republican, defended her staff's use of AI after a summary accompanying a defense bill amendment included text generated by Anthropic's Claude. Researchers Danaé Metaxa and Alex Engler, writing in an August analysis for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, described chatbots' influence on political discourse as a critical new frontier of modern politics. They also noted that chatbots can give different answers to identical questions.

That variation surfaced in the Korean dispute as well. Representative Na Kyung-won of the main opposition People Power Party said she had also asked Gemini about the issue and received a response warning that justifying the attendance of investigative agency chiefs through presidential supervisory authority could threaten their political neutrality. Na accused Lee of framing his question to obtain a favorable answer. The article describes the growing use of AI in politics as raising questions about accuracy, transparency and accountability, particularly when officials rely on chatbot output in their work.

Articles.Title: Lee showed how he uses AI. Trump isn't telling

stories.Headline: Not X, but When: Diagnosing a Mandarin LLM Writing Tic through Contextual Appropriateness
stories.Summary:
Researchers Yihang Peng, Yi Jing, Dewen Liu, Weihan Meng and Ying Liu posted a paper on October 24, 2026, examining a recurring phrase in text written by large language models. The phrase is a Mandarin corrective construction, bushi X, ershi Y, which translates roughly as "not X, but Y." The authors argue that such expressions are often treated as signs of machine authorship even though most of them serve legitimate purposes. The question they pursue is whether a model knows when the construction is called for. The paper was published on arXiv and carries the identifier 2610.22249.

To test this, the authors built a decision tree that sorts each use of the construction into one of three groups: substantive, optional, or defective. The sorting depends on whether the context makes X a live alternative and whether rejecting X gives the reader any information. Five commercial models used the construction between 2.5 and 9.2 times as densely as a human reference. Of 307 annotated uses, 1.30 percent were defective, while 52.8 percent were optional, meaning correct but unneeded. The authors conclude that the models fall short on appropriateness far more often than on correctness.

The paper also reports that several reward models favor the construction even over variants of matching quality, and that an LLM judge favors it even where the context does not support it. According to the authors, both supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization tended to raise how often open-weight models used the construction. The authors say they hope the work encourages the development of models that pay closer attention to whether their expressions suit the context. The article does not name any of the five commercial models tested.

Articles.Title: Not X, but When: Diagnosing a Mandarin LLM Writing Tic through Contextual Appropriateness

stories.Headline: Microsoft Teams to get AI-powered, context-aware phishing detection
stories.Summary:
Microsoft says Teams will begin using AI-powered phishing detection in early November 2026 to spot malicious behavior in messages. The rollout is a targeted release phase expected to end by mid-November, with the feature likely reaching general availability worldwide between early and mid-December. Microsoft first disclosed the capability in a Microsoft 365 Roadmap entry the previous week. The feature analyzes conversation context to catch phishing and suspicious activity in higher-risk scenarios, such as chats from external users contacting someone for the first time.

The detection targets phishing, social engineering, impersonation attempts, and deceptive intent, including threats that carry no malicious links or files. Microsoft says IT administrators do not need to take any action to turn it on, and it will focus mainly on external first-contact chats for most users. The company also says the system will not retain customer message content for model training or other secondary uses. According to Microsoft, the analysis is used only for security protection and not for productivity, summarization, advertising, or user monitoring.

The announcement came in a Microsoft 365 Message Center update that Microsoft published on Wednesday. Microsoft presents the feature as part of a broader set of Teams security changes. Earlier, the company said administrators could lock out external users through the Defender portal starting in January, a step meant to stop cybercrime groups, including ransomware gangs, from abusing Teams in social engineering attacks against employees. Microsoft also began rolling out a meeting protection policy in August that lets admins automatically block identified external bots from joining meetings.

The wider series of changes also includes blurring QR codes sent by external senders, which Microsoft said it would introduce last month, and a way for users to report suspicious guest invitations directly within Teams. In early October, the company announced plans to add support for third-party deepfake detection tools and impersonation protection in Teams meetings. Together these measures address attacks that begin with outside contact and then exploit trust inside the platform. The articles do not say what results the new phishing detection will produce once it is widely available.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Teams to get AI-powered, context-aware phishing detection

stories.Headline: Designing Human-AI Collaborative Science: The 9A Framework
stories.Summary:
A preprint posted on arXiv and listed through doi.org on October 24, 2026 by Zihan Zheng, Linyue Pan and Xin Lan proposes a new way to think about artificial intelligence in science. The authors argue that AI for Science is usually described as a path from tools that assist humans toward AI systems that work more and more autonomously, but they point to a further mode in which human and AI contributions both shape scientific reasoning and the direction of inquiry. The paper says existing research covers work division, coordination between humans and AI, and system evaluation, yet it has not clearly explained how these pieces interact. To address that gap, the authors present what they call the 9A Framework for Human-AI Collaborative Science, abbreviated HACS. The article does not report any experiment that tests the framework in practice.

The framework is organized into three layers, each made up of three elements that begin with the letter A. The organization layer covers Activity, which asks what scientific work is required, Actor, which asks who performs it, and Authority, which asks who holds power over consequential decisions. The coordination layer covers Awareness, meaning how participants reach relevant research information, Accountability, meaning how work moves through repeated cycles of proposal, execution, examination, revision and resolution, and Adaptability, meaning when collaborative arrangements should change. The evaluation layer covers Achievement, which defines effective performance, Attribution, which concerns how comparisons can isolate the effects of organizational and coordination choices, and Assurance, which concerns the evidence behind the conclusions drawn. The authors say these layers together treat HACS as a system-design problem. They describe the framework as a basis for designing collaborative scientific workflows and for comparing their effectiveness empirically.

The authors are Zihan Zheng, Linyue Pan and Xin Lan, and the article presents their framework as their own proposal rather than a finding backed by outside parties. The abstract describes the work as an effort to connect considerations that have so far been treated separately. The article does not name any institution, funder or reaction from other researchers. It also does not say whether the authors plan follow-up studies, released tools, or revisions. What the material establishes is a conceptual framework posted publicly on October 24, 2026, that invites others to design and test collaborative scientific systems against its criteria.

Articles.Title: Designing Human-AI Collaborative Science: The 9A Framework

stories.Headline: Meta AI ad edits put liability on brands
stories.Summary:
The articles are a full report with enough detail for a standard story, so I'm writing it as requested, not as a breaking brief. Meta advertisers are discovering unexpected AI changes to their live ad creative, and some have pulled campaigns to fix them. Adweek reported on October 22 that online bookseller Bookshop.org and digital agency Exverus both found ad changes they had not intended to publish. Bookshop.org said an automated account update enrolled it in a generative AI ad feature that inserted an AI-generated illustration into an ad originally made by people. Exverus saw a wider set of alterations, including extra sitelinks, translated copy, generated pictures and carousel variations, some of which buyers said they had never selected.

Meta's revised Commercial Terms take effect on October 30, 2026, and their section on AI features says automated outputs can be inaccurate or unsuitable and that businesses assume responsibility for assessing and using the resulting content. Advertisers already had obligations under Meta's generative AI ad terms, but the key question raised by Adweek's reporting is whether those obligations cover changes applied without a buyer's deliberate choice. Ryan Adams, a paid search and social specialist at Exverus, said Meta auto-applies the enhancements and that the options can be hard to find inside collapsed menus. That leaves a gap between the creative a brand approves and the version users actually see.

Meta told Adweek that the update consolidates its existing advertising AI terms and that individual creative options can be disabled. In its own description of the change, the company is allocating risk by contract, which does not settle how any particular dispute would be decided under applicable law. Meta's October 6 advertising announcement also described expanded Ads Creative Studio access and tests of a business assistant that generates imagery and text and recommends campaign adjustments, with some of those tests including previews and approvals. The reported cases suggest that an account's existing enhancement settings may not reliably match what an advertiser believes it has approved.

Advertisers are being advised to treat AI-enhanced creative as a live output that needs its own checks. The steps include reviewing enhancement options across active campaigns, confirming whether account or campaign updates have changed their configuration, and previewing variations against approved claims and visuals. Agencies running several advertisers need a clear owner for these inspections and a fast escalation process when an unintended version is already live. Legal and brand teams are advised to review the updated terms before October 30, especially for regulated products, licensed creative and sensitive claims.

Articles.Title: Meta AI ad edits put liability on brands

stories.Headline: Meta delays its AI terms to November 20. The trust problem does not move
stories.Summary:
Meta has delayed the start date of its revised Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms from October 30 to November 20, 2026. A Meta spokesperson confirmed the change to Reuters by email on Friday, October 23, saying the extra three weeks would give the company time to explain what is changing and what is not. The move follows complaints from publishers and advertisers to antitrust authorities in the EU and the UK, who argued that the contract gives Meta an unlimited right to use their content for its AI services. Meta has not amended the text itself, and regulators have not said they have suspended or closed anything.

The clauses still in the document are the ones critics find most troubling. The crawling clause still covers websites tied to a business's products or services, still allows test credentials to reach those sites, and still makes no commitment to honour robots.txt files. The AI training sentence has been removed, and the clause now names a purpose of "advertising and business products" instead. Businesses must still indemnify Meta against claims of any kind, Meta may change or discontinue its products without notice, and continued use counts as acceptance, with no way to accept only part of the terms. US businesses keep a 30-day window to opt out of arbitration, which would close around December 20 if acceptance falls on November 20.

The European Commission welcomed the delay, while the European Publishers Council wants the terms suspended during an investigation. Its executive director, Angela Mills Wade, argued that a business page or advertising subscription should not grant general rights over a publisher's website. In the UK, Theo Bamber of the News Media Association called the postponement a pause rather than a solution and asked the Competition and Markets Authority to secure public commitments from Meta. The News/Media Alliance, led by Danielle Coffey, has separately asked Meta to withdraw the terms and set conditions for talks, with a reply requested by October 26. Meta's own UK preview page reportedly still showed October 30 at one point, and Bamber said the CMA had confirmed the pause, so it is not yet clear which document governs.

The episode sits alongside a broader debate over whether robots.txt can control AI use of content. Google has said the protocol governs access rather than what a system does with data after crawling, and Google's own tools split search, AI features and training into separate controls. Regulators are also moving: the EDPB has issued draft guidance on web scraping for generative AI, with comments due October 30, and the CMA's publisher conduct requirements take legal force in the UK on December 3, 2026. Advertisers have also raised complaints that Meta's AI tools altered their ads without consent, which led some to pull campaigns, and Meta's terms place the responsibility for those changes on the advertiser. Whether the revised terms restore trust will depend on what Meta publishes before November 20.

Articles.Title: Meta delays its AI terms to November 20. The trust problem does not move

stories.Headline: Learning the self-energy through equivariant neural networks
stories.Summary:
A research team has published a paper on arXiv, dated October 24, 2026, describing a machine-learning method for predicting the electronic self-energy of molecules. The authors are Wudong Shen, Yang Zhong, Min-Ye Zhang, Xinyang Dong, Hongjun Xiang and Xinguo Ren, and their work centers on the self-energy matrix from a G_0W_0 calculation. The paper explains that this quantity sets the single-particle Green's function and, through it, quasiparticle energies and spectral functions. Computing it from first principles is costly, which is why the authors treat it as a machine-learning target. They report that the target is complex-valued, matrix-valued in a local-orbital basis, and dependent on a continuous frequency.

The model they describe is an E(3)-equivariant message-passing network that takes atomic species and coordinates as input and predicts the dynamical correlation part of the imaginary-frequency self-energy matrix. The architecture itself enforces rotational covariance of the orbital-space matrix, and the static exchange part is taken from the density-functional reference. Frequency is supplied either as an explicit input or through frequency-specific output heads. The predicted matrices are then continued to the real axis in a representation where causality and a non-negative spectral density hold by construction. The authors state that the frequency-conditioned model reproduces matrix elements to below 1 meV on the imaginary axis for the systems studied.

According to the paper, that accuracy carries over after continuation to the real axis. For water clusters, including a tetramer absent from the training set, and for chemically diverse molecules from the QM9 dataset, the reconstructed spectral functions follow the G_0W_0 reference peak by peak. The frontier quasiparticle levels are recovered to within a few tens of meV. The authors conclude that, once trained and given the density-functional reference the model is built on, a new geometry requires no explicit G_0W_0 calculation. The article itself does not describe any broader consequences, planned follow-up work or responses from other researchers.

Articles.Title: Learning the self-energy through equivariant neural networks

stories.Headline: Will the A.I. Assistant Wars Produce a SuperApp?
stories.Summary:
Meta, OpenAI and a growing group of startups are racing to move artificial intelligence beyond chatbots and into everyday tasks delivered through text messages. Products such as Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots, Wajo's Fo, Town, Hark and Instinct are built to handle email, purchases, travel and other chores through familiar messaging interfaces. Their backers hope to create a new category of "SMS-based A.I. assistants" that people rely on for nearly everything on their to-do lists. The market has grown from nothing to millions of users in a matter of weeks. Meta's Muse, launched in September, reached 10.9 million downloads in its first 40 days and roughly 2.5 million daily active users.

The author argues that this is not the moment when a single A.I. super app takes over, and expects the market to fragment into specialized categories. Consumers have long preferred separate tools for messaging, money, travel and work, even when one platform can handle several jobs. The author also points to Adam Smith's argument in The Wealth of Nations that dividing labor into specialized tasks raises productivity. As underlying models become more interchangeable, advantage is expected to come from specialized workflows, integrations, user experience and proprietary data. Within each category, the author expects a few leaders to emerge, while a coordinating layer may eventually link different agents together.

The author identifies three areas where text-based assistants stand out. The first is handling tasks on the go, such as planning a party and ordering supplies with user approval before purchase. The second is coordinating multistep plans for travel and dining, which involve comparing options, checking schedules and making reservations. The third is ordering services that would otherwise require a phone call, such as canceling a flight and requesting a refund with United Airlines or booking a nail salon appointment. The author notes that Assistant Benchmark currently ranks Meta's Muse first, followed by Hark and Instinct, though the rankings are described as a snapshot rather than a forecast.

The article names several bottlenecks that could limit the category, including access to user accounts, permissions, secure payments and handling exceptions when websites or businesses behave unexpectedly. The author suggests that startups solving this "messy last mile" could become essential infrastructure for the broader ecosystem. The author, who identifies as an investor, says the category is still early enough that leading business models and interfaces are unsettled. Over the next year, the author says, observers will learn which assistants can turn curiosity into habitual use and which categories can support durable businesses.

Articles.Title: Will the A.I. Assistant Wars Produce a SuperApp?

stories.Headline: The Wrap: Anthropic Gets Heavyweight Backup; AI Defense Gets Bipartisan Backing; AI Graduates From Pilot Mode
stories.Summary:
Seventeen former national security officials, including former Director of National Intelligence Avril Haines and former national security advisers Jake Sullivan and Susan Rice, have urged a federal appeals court to reconsider its decision upholding the supply chain risk designation placed on Anthropic. The dispute started when Anthropic objected to the Pentagon using its Claude model for mass surveillance and fully autonomous weapons. After negotiations collapsed, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth moved to designate the company a supply chain risk. The former officials argue that AI safeguards should not become grounds for punishment and say the Pentagon put its decision ahead of its justification.

They warn the precedent could drive away advanced AI capabilities as the United States competes with China for technological leadership. On October 22, Reps. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., and George Whitesides, D-Calif., introduced the AI Cyber Defense Act. The bill proposes a two-pronged cyber strategy that protects American AI models from foreign exploitation and helps critical infrastructure operators use AI to strengthen their defenses.
